meta.title: The Complete Writer's Compendium — Master JSON
meta.subtitle: Das Vollständige Schreibhandbuch
meta.description: All compendium content in a single machine-readable structure: chapters, craft examples, editor notes, attributions, web sources, SVG asset manifest, and multilingual language notes.

sections.title: Why Rules Exist — And When to Break Them
sections.summary: Fiction writing has no absolute laws — only craft principles distilled from thousands of works. The goal is to understand WHY a principle exists before deciding to break it.
key_points: Master the rules first, then transcend them (Picasso principle)
Reader expectations are built from genre conventions — defy them intentionally or invisibly
Every rule has a reason; every exception needs justification

sections.title: The Reading Imperative
sections.summary: Every master writer is first a voracious reader. Reading in your genre teaches pacing, convention, and expectations. Reading outside imports unexpected techniques.
key_points: Read 50–100 books in your genre before writing your first novel
Read recent bestsellers to understand current market expectations
Read literary fiction to study prose style and interiority
Read nonfiction in your theme area for authentic detail

sections.title: Consistency & The Writing Habit
sections.summary: Great writing is built in small daily increments. A first draft does not need to be perfect — it needs to exist.
key_points: Write 500 words every morning before checking email — 120 days = a novel draft
Waiting for inspiration produces 3 pages a year
Discipline, persistence, and willingness to revise separate published authors from perpetual first-drafters
10% talent, 90% craft — James N. Frey

sections.title: Setting the Frame — Defining Your Story's Terms
sections.summary: The one who defines the terms of conflict, responsibility, and meaning controls the story. Framing isn't about legal blame — it's about narrative clarity: deciding what your characters control, what the world imposes, and what readers should hold them accountable for.
key_points: Stop automatic blame: separate what a character is truly responsible for from what circumstance, upbringing, or society forced on them. This creates nuanced protagonists.
Signal self-respect through action: let characters set boundaries without over-explaining. A character who calmly defines their limits becomes active rather than reactive.
Force precision in conflict: vague accusations fuel melodrama. Make characters demand specificity — 'What exactly did I do?' — to raise stakes and deepen tension.
Keep it fair, not manipulative: when characters set the frame honestly — neither defensive nor aggressive — their choices feel earned.
Define systemic responsibility in the world: who is accountable — the ruler, the system, the gods? Clarify where blame and credit lie so readers understand the rules.
Precision in stakes: a bounded, specific crisis is more compelling than a vague world-ending threat. Frame exactly what is at risk, for whom, and why.
sections.key_insight: Not the loudest wins — the one who sets the frame. Frame clearly, and your characters and world will follow.

sections.title: Uncommon Story Ideas
sections.summary: A prompt bank of premises that subvert reader expectation.
key_points: A series told from the villain's point of view — but at first you don't realise they are the villain. The reveal lands as a twist near the end, and the reader discovers they've been rooting for the wrong side all along.

sections.title: The Three Dimensions of Character
sections.summary: Every memorable character operates on three levels: External Want (goal), Internal Need (emotional), and Fatal Flaw/Wound (obstacle). Missing any dimension produces flatness.

dimensions.name: External Want
dimensions.strong_example: Katniss wants to keep her sister alive

dimensions.name: Internal Need
dimensions.definition: Emotional truth the character must learn
dimensions.strong_example: Katniss needs to trust others and allow herself to be loved
dimensions.weak_example: No inner conflict; character is already complete at page 1

dimensions.name: Fatal Flaw / Wound
dimensions.definition: The broken thing that creates internal obstacle
dimensions.strong_example: Katniss's distrust of vulnerability born from her father's death
dimensions.weak_example: Clumsy, shy, awkward (surface traits with no emotional root)

sections.title: Character Voice — Making Everyone Sound Different
sections.summary: Voice is the single most powerful differentiator. Build it from: vocabulary level, sentence rhythm, what the character notices, what they care about, and what they are blind to.
key_points: Give each major character 5 FORBIDDEN WORDS — things they would never say
Two characters should never sound interchangeable even in unmarked dialogue
Voice is tied to milieu, class, education, trauma history

sections.title: Character Arc — Transformation or Revelation
sections.summary: A character arc is the internal journey from Point A to Point B. Not all arcs mean growth — tragedy arcs have characters refuse change and fall.

arc_types.description: Character overcomes their flaw and moves toward their need
arc_types.example: Ebenezer Scrooge — miser → generous

arc_types.description: Character doubles down on their flaw and loses everything
arc_types.example: Walter White — chemistry teacher → drug lord

arc_types.description: Character is already complete; the world around them changes instead
arc_types.example: Atticus Finch

arc_types.description: Character begins noble and is twisted by events or choices
arc_types.example: Anakin Skywalker

sections.title: Avoiding Common Character Mistakes
sections.summary: The Mary Sue, the villain without motivation, and the exposition sidekick are the three most commonly cited character failures in editorial feedback.

common_mistakes.name: Mary Sue / Gary Stu
common_mistakes.description: A character with no real flaws who excels at everything and is universally loved
common_mistakes.fix: Give them a flaw that costs them something real, and make it thematically linked to their strength

common_mistakes.name: Evil-for-evil's-sake Villain
common_mistakes.description: Antagonist with no coherent worldview or motivation
common_mistakes.fix: Give the villain a wound and a logic that makes sense from inside their perspective

common_mistakes.name: As-You-Know-Bob Sidekick
common_mistakes.description: Character who exists only to prompt exposition the protagonist already knows
common_mistakes.fix: Deliver exposition through action, environment, and conflict — not explained dialogue

sections.title: Hero Archetypes — Types of Protagonists
sections.summary: Protagonists are not interchangeable. The type of hero you choose determines the story's emotional register, the nature of the conflict, and what the reader is rooting for. Understanding archetypes helps you write a hero with a clear function — not just a character who does things.

arc_types.description: Ordinary person thrust into extraordinary circumstances. Readers identify because the hero is recognisably themselves. Works by proximity: we ask 'what would I do?' The everyman's weakness is ordinariness — they must compensate with extraordinary resourcefulness, loyalty, or moral clarity.
arc_types.example: Bilbo Baggins (The Hobbit), Katniss Everdeen (The Hunger Games)

arc_types.description: Destined for greatness by prophecy, birth, or cosmic selection. Creates high stakes from page one. Risk: passive protagonists who are dragged through plot. The best Chosen Ones resist, doubt, or reinterpret their destiny — they choose to fulfil it.
arc_types.example: Harry Potter, Frodo Baggins, Paul Atreides (Dune)

arc_types.description: Morally compromised, selfish, or outright criminal protagonist who nonetheless commands our sympathy. Works through honesty: we recognise their faults because we share them. The arc often moves toward redemption — or deliberately away from it (tragedy).
arc_types.example: Walter White (Breaking Bad), Raskolnikov (Crime and Punishment), Jay Gatsby

arc_types.description: Defined by extraordinary skill rather than virtue. Reader pleasure is watching mastery in action. Needs human vulnerability to avoid coldness — the best competence heroes are undone by their blind spots, not their incompetence.
arc_types.example: James Bond, Sherlock Holmes, Lisbeth Salander (The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo)

arc_types.description: A fundamentally great person destroyed by a fatal flaw (hamartia). The reader knows from early on that disaster is coming — the tragic pleasure is watching the flaw operate despite good intentions. Requires the flaw to feel both inevitable and avoidable.
arc_types.example: Macbeth, Jay Gatsby, Michael Corleone (The Godfather)

arc_types.description: Does not want the role. Must be pushed, dragged, or cornered into action. The reluctance is the characterisation — it reveals what they value more than heroism. The moment of decision (when they finally choose to act) is the emotional core of the story.
arc_types.example: Rick Blaine (Casablanca), Atticus Finch, Samwise Gamgee

key_points: Mix archetypes — most compelling protagonists blend two or more (the Everyman who is also Reluctant; the Anti-Hero who is also Competent).
The archetype should match the genre: thrillers favour the Competence Hero; literary fiction favours the Tragic or Anti-Hero; YA often uses the Chosen One or Everyman.
A hero's archetype implies their internal arc. The Reluctant Hero must choose. The Tragic Hero must fall. The Anti-Hero must decide whether to change.
Avoid the 'Mary Sue' trap in any archetype: the hero must have a cost, a limit, or a genuine flaw that the story takes seriously.

sections.title: Villain Archetypes — Designing Antagonists
sections.summary: A story is only as strong as its villain. The antagonist defines the protagonist — they are the force that tests whether the hero's values are real. Great villains are not evil for evil's sake: they have coherent worldviews, genuine grievances, or compelling motivations. The reader should be able to articulate why the villain believes they are right.
key_points: The villain should be the hero of their own story. Give them a motivation you can argue for even if you disagree with it.
Menace requires competence: a villain who keeps failing stops being threatening. Let them win — at least for a while.
Mirror the protagonist: the best villains share the hero's desires but pursue them through opposite means, or share the hero's flaws taken to an extreme.
Avoid 'evil because evil' — even pure-evil figures (Hannibal Lecter, the Joker) work because they embody something real: meaninglessness, chaos, the thrill of transgression.
The villain's defeat should feel earned. If the hero wins through luck, the thematic promise of the conflict is broken.

arc_types.description: The dark reflection of the hero — same desires, same gifts, different choices. Forces the protagonist to confront what they could have become. Creates thematic resonance because the conflict is really about the hero's values.
arc_types.example: Magneto vs. Professor X, Javert vs. Valjean (Les Misérables), Commodus vs. Maximus (Gladiator)

arc_types.description: A villain driven by ideology — often convinced they are saving the world. Dangerous because their logic is internally consistent. Most challenging to write: the author must understand the ideology well enough to make it genuinely persuasive before dismantling it.
arc_types.example: Thanos (Avengers), Dolores Umbridge (Harry Potter), Judge Holden (Blood Meridian)

arc_types.description: Created by damage — trauma, betrayal, or injustice turned outward. Sympathy is possible; the reader understands how they got here. The risk: sympathy becomes excuse. The wound explains without justifying.
arc_types.example: Jaime Lannister (Game of Thrones), Gollum (The Lord of the Rings), Heathcliff (Wuthering Heights)

arc_types.description: Not a person but an institution, ideology, or social structure. No single villain to defeat — the conflict is with something larger than any individual. Requires the protagonist to change the system or be changed by it.
arc_types.example: The Capitol (The Hunger Games), the Party (Nineteen Eighty-Four), society itself (Crime and Punishment)

arc_types.description: Disarming, likeable, socially adept — the danger is hidden under warmth or charisma. Works through dramatic irony: the reader sees what other characters do not. Forces the protagonist (and reader) to question their own judgment.
arc_types.example: Amy Dunne (Gone Girl), Patrick Bateman (American Psycho), Iago (Othello)

common_mistakes.name: The Incompetent Villain
common_mistakes.description: The antagonist keeps failing, losing henchmen, monologuing — they pose no real threat. The hero's victory feels unearned.
common_mistakes.fix: Let the villain succeed at something important before the climax. Give them at least one moment where they are genuinely more capable than the hero.

common_mistakes.name: The Moustache-Twirler
common_mistakes.description: Evil for no reason, no coherent worldview, no human dimension. A placeholder, not a character.
common_mistakes.fix: Write a one-page internal monologue in the villain's voice justifying everything they do. If you can't make the argument convincingly, the character isn't ready.

common_mistakes.name: The Villain as Plot Device
common_mistakes.description: The antagonist only appears when the plot needs them, with no consistent presence or goal of their own.
common_mistakes.fix: Give the villain a separate story running in parallel. What are they doing when they're not bothering the protagonist?

sections.title: Supporting Characters — The Ensemble
sections.summary: Supporting characters are not furniture. They exist to reflect, challenge, and complicate the protagonist — and to carry their own weight as human beings. A cast of flat supporting characters makes even a strong protagonist feel isolated and unconvincing. The goal is a world that feels inhabited, not staged.

arc_types.description: Provides wisdom, tools, or moral clarity to the protagonist. Must be limited — either in knowledge, power, or lifespan — or the hero has no reason to grow. The mentor's limitation creates the protagonist's necessity.
arc_types.example: Gandalf, Dumbledore, Yoda, Atticus Finch (as mentor to Scout)

arc_types.description: Committed to the hero's cause, often before the hero is. Tests the protagonist's capacity to receive love and trust. The best allies have independent motivation — they're not just helping the hero; they have their own stakes.
arc_types.example: Samwise Gamgee, Horatio (Hamlet), Dr Watson

arc_types.description: Contrasts with the protagonist to highlight specific qualities. Not an antagonist — may be friendly. The contrast should illuminate both characters, not just one.
arc_types.example: Laertes and Fortinbras (vs. Hamlet), Ron and Hermione (vs. Harry), Jane Bennet (vs. Elizabeth Bennet)

arc_types.description: Chaos agent — may help or hinder the protagonist unpredictably. Introduces irony, humour, and unexpected solutions. Serves the story by refusing to let it take itself too seriously.
arc_types.example: Puck (A Midsummer Night's Dream), Loki, the Cheshire Cat

arc_types.description: Not a prize or a reward — a person with independent goals that complicate and enrich the protagonist's world. The best love interests challenge the hero's assumptions and are changed by the relationship as much as the hero is.
arc_types.example: Elizabeth Bennet (from Darcy's perspective), Ilsa Lund (Casablanca)

arc_types.description: Tests the hero before they can advance — gatekeepers, bureaucrats, sceptics, rivals. Temporarily an obstacle, often later an ally or a neutral force. Represents the social cost of change.
arc_types.example: The doorman, the rival, the examiner, the unbelieving parent

key_points: Every named character needs a want that exists independently of the protagonist. Ask: what does this character do when the hero isn't around?
Supporting characters should disagree with the protagonist occasionally — a cast that always agrees is just the hero talking to themselves.
Give minor characters one vivid, specific detail — a habit, a contradiction, a specific way of speaking — that makes them feel real rather than functional.
Avoid the 'Smurfette principle': token diversity of any kind (one woman, one person of colour, one comic relief) flattens your world. Build an ensemble with genuine variety of perspective.
The rule of 'every character is the hero of their own story' applies especially to supporting roles. If you can't summarise their internal life in two sentences, they need more development.

common_mistakes.name: The Exposition Bot
common_mistakes.description: A character who exists only to deliver information to the protagonist (and the reader). No personality, no want, appears and disappears as needed.
common_mistakes.fix: Give every exposition-delivering character a conflicting motivation. What do they want from the protagonist in return for this information?

common_mistakes.name: The Disposable Friend
common_mistakes.description: A character introduced so they can die and make the protagonist sad. The reader sees the function before the funeral.
common_mistakes.fix: Make the character so vivid and interesting that their death is a genuine loss, not a narrative beat. If readers don't grieve, the sacrifice means nothing.

sections.title: Anti-Hero Archetypes
sections.summary: The anti-hero lacks conventional heroism yet carries the story. Each type pressures the reader's sympathies in a different way.

arc_types.description: Lacks the conventional qualities of heroism — cowardly, selfish, or reluctant. Readers relate to their familiar fears and failings.
Arrogant and self-destructive, haunted by guilt or a secret past. Magnetic darkness: readers know not to trust them yet cannot look away.
Knows what's right but approaches everything through a thick coating of cynicism. They'll do the right thing — and complain the entire way.
Operates by a different moral code, doing whatever needs to be done. Every choice pressures the reader's own ethics.
The villain given the protagonist's seat, forcing readers to empathise with terrible acts. Perspective becomes a weapon for rationalisation.
Has rejected the world's values entirely — no causes, no people, no systems. Every circumstance tests whether the cynicism is as total as they claim.

sections.title: Morally-Gray Archetypes
sections.summary: Characters who resist the hero/villain binary. Their moral ambiguity is the engine of tension.

arc_types.description: Genuinely wants to save the world — and has decided the cost is acceptable, even when it isn't. Their logic is airtight, which is exactly what makes them terrifying.
Once believed completely; the world broke that belief. Now operates by colder, harder rules built from the wreckage of who they used to be.
Every terrible thing was done for someone they love. The line between devotion and destruction blurred so gradually they never noticed crossing it.
Fights for survival and advantage, not good or evil. Loyalty lasts exactly as long as it's useful, keeping every alliance dangerously uncertain.
The system failed, so they replaced it with themselves. Hero or villain depends entirely on which side of their justice you stand.
Trying to become better while responsible for things that cannot be undone. Every step toward redemption is shadowed by what it can never erase.
Follows orders without question — not from cruelty but devotion to something larger. The story asks whether blind loyalty is a virtue or the most dangerous flaw of all.

sections.title: Villain Motivation
sections.summary: A villain's motive should be simple and universal, grounding an epic conflict in human psychology. Simple motivation, complex execution.

arc_types.description: Useful once, then forgotten. Now mercy feels insulting — they remember what kindness costs.
Flaws offend them; chaos feels unbearable, so they reshape life itself. People become the price.
Once powerless, and that memory never left. Now control feels holy and cruelty feels safe.
They miss a world that died. Instead of grieving it, they punish the future. Nostalgia becomes violence.

sections.title: Redeeming a Villain — Five Methods
sections.summary: Redemption that costs nothing is performance. These five moves make a turn feel earned rather than handed over.

arc_types.type: Let Them Save the Wrong Person
arc_types.description: Not the hero, not the kingdom — someone small, someone nobody else would have bothered with. Redemption that costs them their reputation is real.

arc_types.type: Show the Child They Used to Be
arc_types.description: A toy never thrown away, a song hummed without realising, the promises made at seven. They're redeemed not by backstory but by the moment the reader sees who that kid wanted to be.

arc_types.type: Let Them Fail at Being Good
arc_types.description: A smooth redemption arc is a costume change. Let them try, get it wrong, be cruel out of habit and hate themselves after. Readers trust villains who become trying, not saints.

arc_types.type: Make Them Refuse Their Own Redemption
arc_types.description: The hero forgives them; the reader forgives them; they refuse to forgive themselves and walk away from the arc the author handed them. That refusal is the most redeeming thing they'll ever do.
They turn at the last second, save the day, and don't get to live in the world they helped fix. The reader closes the book furious — and remembers them longer than the hero.

sections.title: The Iceberg Principle
sections.summary: For every detail on the page, ten must exist in the author's mind. The reader senses depth even when they don't see it.

pillars.name: Settings / Geography
pillars.questions: Where do characters live, travel, and fight? What does the landscape demand physically and psychologically?
pillars.common_mistake: Map that exists but never affects plot or characters' bodies.

pillars.name: History & Lore
pillars.questions: What happened before the story? Who won the last war?
pillars.common_mistake: History invented on the fly, contradicting itself across chapters.

pillars.name: Factions & Power
pillars.questions: Who holds power? Who wants it? What do groups compete over?
pillars.common_mistake: Everyone agrees on everything — no conflict.

pillars.name: Rules (Magic / Tech)
pillars.questions: What can the system do AND what can't it do?
pillars.common_mistake: Magic that fixes every problem — deus ex machina.

pillars.name: Culture & Society
pillars.questions: What do people eat, celebrate, fear? What's taboo?
pillars.common_mistake: Medieval world where everyone thinks like modern Westerners.

pillars.name: Language & Communication
pillars.questions: Are there dialects, class registers, sacred languages?
pillars.common_mistake: Every character speaks identical anachronism-free modern English.

sections.title: Writing Lore Without Info-Dumping
sections.summary: Lore is always a story a character would tell — not a Wikipedia article the author is inserting.

sections.title: Setting as Character
sections.summary: The best settings actively shape mood, mirror character psychology, and create or solve plot problems.
key_points: Weather should reflect or contrast emotional tone
A character's home reveals their psychology
Settings that change across a story mirror character change
Every sensory detail should earn its place by doing double duty

sections.title: World-Building Question Sets
sections.summary: Prompt banks for interrogating a world at three scales — world, country, city — plus the obscure details that make a place feel lived-in. Answer only what serves the story; the rest is iceberg.

questions.question: One country or an entire world? If a whole world, ask these questions for each country you create.
Do you need a map? Name every country and location — it builds ideas and aids visualization.
Who populates your world? How do the species differ, and do they have different climate needs?
What are the major climates and landscapes? Research how mountains affect climate and how rivers run — take liberties, but keep it sensible.
What kinds of governments exist across the world and its countries? This drives international politics later.
What kind of economy? This ties into government and politics; consider imports and exports.
What religions do people follow? Does it differ by culture, country, species? It feeds politics, holidays, customs.
What is the military structure, and how does it shape domestic and international politics?
Does your world have magic? Who has it, where does it come from, what is the system?
How technologically advanced is it, and how do magic and technology interact?
Topography — major landforms and their lore, bodies of water, where are the major cities?
What is the capital, and why was it chosen — religion, military strategy, history?
What are the other major cities, and why?
What type of government — democracy, monarchy, oligarchy, dictatorship?
Who rules, and how do they come to power? Do they rule alone or with a court/cabinet?
What is the economy — command, traditional, market, mixed? What does it import and export?
Socioeconomic makeup — even across classes or sharp disparity, and why?
Religious makeup — one god or a pantheon, and how does it shape politics and daily life?
What customs and traditions is the country known for?
What are the major holidays?
Does magic exist, what type, and is it feared or revered?
How technologically advanced, and what are the views on science?
What else is it known for — landmarks, delicacies, a signature plant?
What does daily life look like — common jobs, ordinary routines? A world feels real when life exists beyond the protagonist.
Who are its allies internationally, and why?
Who are its historical enemies, and why?
What animals are found here?
What plants are found here?
What are the positives of living here?
What are the negatives? These can seed conflict in your plot.
Topography — major landforms and their lore, water, and why was this location chosen?
What is the weather like?
Who runs the city?
Where does the ruler live, and what are the political buildings?
When was the city founded?
Who founded it?
What is the population?
Who inhabits it?
What is the main street, why is it the main street, and what's on it?
What is the socioeconomic makeup?
What is the religious makeup, and where are the religious buildings?
What is the culture — customs and traditions?
What is the city known for?
What are the districts and what is each known for (merchant, university, industrial…)?
What is this city's role in your story, and why do these details matter?
Is there indoor plumbing and a sewer system? If not, what do they do with excrement?
How do they dispose of trash?
What does your country/city sound like?
What does it smell like?
Are there healers or doctors, and what is the level of medical advancement?
What language(s) do people speak? Is there a common tongue?
Where do the dead go — buried, cremated, a pyre? What are the death rites?
Where does food come from?
How do they clean water — do they?
What are the popular books in your world?

sections.title: Tiny Details That Sell a World
sections.summary: The fastest way to get a reader emotionally invested in a fictional place is rarely the grand map — it's the small, specific texture that implies a world older than page one.

arc_types.description: An innkeeper who turns every coin face-up before bed; a road no one will take; a fisherman who won't sail on the seventh of the month. Tiny, specific, and they make a world feel ancient.
Language carries culture and history. The second people swear differently, the reader is more invested than any info-dump could manage.

arc_types.type: Multiple versions of the same historical event
arc_types.description: History is propaganda, always told by people desperate to keep control. Conflicting accounts make readers reflect on their own perception of truth.

arc_types.type: Smells, fauna, or visuals that mark a region
arc_types.description: A scent or animal that becomes associated with a place; its absence or abundance as characters travel builds a world of distinct cultures.
A common truth no one questions — until new information flips it, sending you back to the beginning to re-read the clues. (Not the same as a hidden identity or a faked event.)

sections.title: Empire, Government & Power
sections.summary: Who holds power, how they got it, and how they keep it — the machinery a world runs on. Pick a form of government, then pressure-test it with the questions that make it feel real rather than a label on a map.

pillars.name: Forms of Government
pillars.questions: Monarchy (hereditary rule), theocracy (rule by religious authority), oligarchy (rule by a few — nobles, merchants, elders), democracy/republic (rule by citizens or their representatives), dictatorship/autocracy (rule by one, often by force), feudalism (layered oaths of loyalty and land), tribal/clan confederation (kinship-based), technocracy (rule by experts), and corporatocracy (rule by corporations). Most real polities are hybrids.
pillars.common_mistake: Naming the system ('a kingdom') without showing how it actually decides anything.

pillars.name: Legitimacy — Why People Obey
pillars.questions: What gives the rulers the right to rule in the eyes of the ruled — divine mandate, bloodline, conquest, election, wealth, competence, fear? When legitimacy cracks, you have the seed of rebellion or civil war.
pillars.common_mistake: Rulers whose authority is never questioned by anyone, anywhere.

pillars.name: Succession & Transfer of Power
pillars.questions: How does power pass on — primogeniture, election, appointment, coup, trial by combat, a council's vote? Contested succession is one of the most reliable engines of political plot.
pillars.common_mistake: A stable throne with no rivals, heirs, or ambitious second sons.

pillars.name: Enforcement & the Monopoly on Violence
pillars.questions: Who enforces the ruler's will — a standing army, a city watch, secret police, mercenaries, feudal levies, a religious order? Who do they answer to, and what happens when they stop obeying?
pillars.common_mistake: Laws with no visible means of enforcement.

pillars.name: Money & Administration
pillars.questions: How is the state funded — taxes, tribute, tariffs, plunder, state monopolies? Who collects it, and who skims it? Bureaucracy, corruption, and record-keeping are where power meets daily life.
pillars.common_mistake: An empire with armies and palaces but no visible economy paying for them.

pillars.name: Factions & Counter-Power
pillars.questions: Who checks the ruler — nobles, guilds, temples, the mob, a rival court, neighbouring states? Every stable power has rivals it must manage; map them and you map your intrigue.
pillars.common_mistake: A monolithic government with no internal disagreement.

pillars.name: Empire — Ruling the Conquered
pillars.questions: How does a power administer peoples it absorbed — direct rule, client kings, colonies, forced assimilation, tolerated autonomy? How does it move goods, troops, and messages across distance? Empires are held together by roads, coin, and fear as much as by armies — and they fall when any of the three fails.
pillars.common_mistake: A vast empire that behaves like a single small kingdom.

critical_notes: You don't need every answer on the page — but you should know them. Government is iceberg like everything else: readers feel the nine-tenths you never show.

sections.title: Story Structure — The Foundation
sections.summary: Structure is the skeleton your story stands on. Defying conventions requires extraordinary craft or intentional artistic choice.

sections.title: Pacing — The Speed of Story
sections.summary: Pacing is the rate at which information and events are delivered. Vary it: sprint through action, walk through quiet moments.

sections.title: The Flashback Problem
sections.summary: Flashbacks must move the story forward — revealing information that changes how we understand the present. A flashback that only explains backstory is an info-dump in costume.
key_points: Earn the flashback: create mystery/urgency in present, then let flashback resolve it
The present scene must earn reader's permission to time-travel
Never open a story with a flashback — earn it first

sections.title: Plot, Story & Premise — Telling Them Apart
sections.summary: Three words writers use interchangeably, to their cost. Premise is the concept; plot is the sequence of events; story is what those events mean.
key_points: Premise — the central 'what if', usually one sentence. The Hunger Games: 'A teenage girl must compete in a televised fight to the death to save her sister and survive an oppressive government.'
Plot — the sequence of events. The Hunger Games: 'After volunteering, Katniss travels to the Capitol, trains, and fights to survive the games before becoming a symbol of rebellion.'

Story — what the events mean, the emotional and thematic journey. The Hunger Games: 'A young woman learns that protecting the people she loves is worth risking everything, and that small acts of defiance can change the world.'
sections.key_insight: Most stuck manuscripts have plot without story, or premise without plot.

sections.title: Diagnosing a Scene That Feels 'Off'
sections.summary: When a scene isn't landing, run it through five questions. The fault is usually one of them.

questions.question: What changes? If the character, relationship, situation, or information is identical at the end, the scene may not be pulling its weight.
What does the character want right now? A character who wants something creates movement; one who wants nothing creates drift.
What's creating resistance? Something should push back and make the goal harder to reach.
What is the scene really about? A scene about dinner might be about forgiveness; a job interview might be about self-worth.
What emotion should the reader be left with? Besides information, what emotional residue does the scene leave?

critical_notes: If it feels off, the answer is usually: no change, no goal, no resistance, no deeper meaning, or no emotional residue.

sections.title: Seven Ways to Open a Chapter
sections.summary: Openings that aren't waking up or looking in a mirror. Each creates a different pull.

arc_types.description: Drop readers into something already happening — a chase, an argument, a scramble to fix a mistake. Action creates immediate momentum.
Start with a conversation already underway. Readers have to catch up, which pulls them in.
'The smell of burnt coffee made her stomach twist.' Reveals setting and emotional state at once.
Open on internal conflict — a character wanting two opposing things. Internal tension becomes narrative tension.

arc_types.type: A time or place shift in one clean line
arc_types.description: 'Three days later, the city was burning.' Readers wonder what happened in the gap.

arc_types.type: The aftermath of an off-page event
arc_types.description: Show the shattered room, the broken friendship, the fresh scar — not the event. Readers become curious about the cause.
A character decides to leave, confess, lie, or fight. Decisions force the story in a new direction.

sections.title: Overused Action Scenes (and What to Use Instead)
sections.summary: Five action beats readers have seen a thousand times — and fresher alternatives that keep the tension.

arc_types.description: The antagonist sprints across rooftops and only the hero can keep up. Instead: set the chase somewhere unexpected — a workplace or a museum.
A single fight resolves the entire conflict. Instead: have the protagonist attempt a desperate rescue while the villain fights to stop them, so the fight isn't the point.
Both armies throw everything they have. Instead: give the heroes a crisis to solve, such as repairing a bridge before refugees fleeing an army arrive.
Effective but overused, especially to open a story with a setback. Instead: use a public confrontation (a debate, a wedding) where violence isn't an option, no matter how much everyone wants it.
Tense but very familiar. Instead: use a slow-changing environment — crossing a frozen lake as the ice cracks, or a desert as heat rises. Spread the tension over time.

sections.title: Raising Lethal Stakes
sections.summary: Shattering narrative safety creates visceral engagement — but apply it deliberately, not chaotically. Six principles for making mortal danger land.

arc_types.description: Establish early that even beloved central characters can die unexpectedly. Remove plot armour for everyone; let consequences be final and unpredictable.
Ambition and influence carry brutal trade-offs. Balance any gain in status, strength, or control with proportional loss or sacrifice. No victory is clean.
Life is chaotic and unfair. Allow random, senseless, anti-climactic events — not every death serves the arc; sometimes fate is simply cruel.
Build strong attachment before introducing danger. Invest in relationships and vulnerability; the deeper the connection, the more devastating the threat.
Treat every choice as having weight. Show ripple effects — intended and unintended — across characters, factions, and time.

arc_types.type: The Long Memory of the World
arc_types.description: The past is never past. Weave old grudges, prophecies, and unresolved trauma into current events; let history constrain the present.

critical_notes: Caveat: full brutal unpredictability during a first draft can cause paralysis and break coherence. These principles are for shaping a story you understand — use them with intent, not as chaos.

sections.title: Plotting Hints for Long-Form & Series
sections.summary: Structural habits that keep a multi-book saga coherent and propulsive.

arc_types.description: Structure each installment around three main mysteries or conflicts to keep pacing tight and discovery constant.
A protagonist's greatest strength should also be their greatest flaw, so mistakes flow from character and the plot feels organic.
Plant seeds in early installments that don't pay off until much later. Rewards re-reading and signals meticulous planning.
The setting is a character and a device: use the rules of the world to create and resolve conflicts, not just as backdrop.
A secondary thread — a friendship or romance — provides emotional grounding, relief, and often the solution to the main conflict.
The whole saga should orbit one powerful central theme; every major beat and arc reinforces it.
Draft the first book with momentum while leaving threads open to expand. Over-planning a saga before writing book one is the fastest route to writer's block.

chapters.title: Prose Style — Dos, Don'ts & Editor's Notes

sections.title: Cutting Description — The Vivid Line Rule
sections.summary: Description drags when we try to show everything, so the reader remembers nothing. Cut roughly 30% by choosing the one image that carries weight.

arc_types.description: Readers need the single detail that matters, not the whole room. ✗ 'The kitchen was small, cramped, cluttered with mismatched dishes, overflowing trash, and yesterday's coffee.' → ✓ 'Yesterday's coffee sat cold in the pot.'
Delete 'saw', 'noticed', 'there was', 'it felt like'. ✗ 'She noticed the clouds gathering.' → ✓ 'The clouds gathered.'
Descriptions are strongest when they pull emotional weight. ✗ 'The hallway was quiet and dim.' → ✓ 'The empty hallway swallowed all sound.'

arc_types.type: Remove anything that could apply anywhere
arc_types.description: If the line could fit another story, sharpen it. ✗ 'The sun was bright.' → ✓ 'The sun glinted against the cracked tile.'

arc_types.type: Make every line earn its place
arc_types.description: Ask: does this image reveal tone, emotion, or character? If not, revisit or delete it.

sections.key_insight: Better description isn't about writing less — it's about writing what matters.

sections.title: Dialogue That Does Double (or Triple) Duty
Dialogue Tags — Said Is Not Dead
Subtext in Depth — Displacement & Deflection
sections.summary: Subtext is the gap between what a character feels and what they say — the truth hiding beneath the surface. Humans are terrified of emotional nakedness, so they displace a massive emotion (fear of abandonment) into a tiny, safe container (a seasoning problem).
key_points: Let dialogue be polite, not honest. 'Of course I'm fine. Why wouldn't I be?' is flat alone — but said while cutting chicken a little too aggressively, the contradiction does the work.
Make the body contradict the words. Subtext lives in what the body leaks: shaky hands, gritted teeth, a character controlling the scene while their body betrays them.

Use objects and actions as emotional proxies. A character aligning every object on the table before speaking isn't 'tidy' — they're trying not to explode. Objects let emotion become physical without being explained.
critical_notes: Worked example — Sarah cooked for three hours; Mark arrived forty minutes late, no apology. On-the-nose: 'I'm pretty sure you're sleeping with your assistant.' Subtext: she grits her teeth — 'It needs salt.' He lifts his gaze — 'I like it this way.' The text is about dinner; the subtext is a relationship crumbling.
When you hide the truth, the reader becomes a detective and connects the dots themselves — and an emotional conversation is never just in the conversation. It always needs salt.

editing_levels.name: Story Level
editing_levels.focus: Structure, plot logic, character arc, theme
questions: Does every scene move the story forward?

editing_levels.name: Scene Level
editing_levels.focus: Scene goals, POV consistency, pacing, dialogue
questions: Does every scene have a goal that changes by the end?
Is the dialogue doing double duty?

editing_levels.name: Line Level
editing_levels.focus: Sentence craft, word choice, passive voice, adverbs, clichés
questions: Is every word earning its place?

sections.title: The Editor's Most Common Manuscript Notes
Working With Editors — The Two Rules
rules: Take the edit seriously — the editor is almost certainly responding to a real problem
You don't have to take the editor's specific solution — find your own. It's your book.

sections.title: The Four Drafts Most Authors Actually Write
sections.summary: Revision isn't one pass — most finished books move through four distinct drafts, each with a single job.

arc_types.description: Figure out what the book actually is. Plot holes, inconsistent characters, and messy scenes are all normal. Goal: not perfection — discover your story.
Rebuild the bones. Scenes get added, deleted, combined, or moved. Goal: pacing, plot progression, stakes — make the whole thing work.
Focus on the people. Does every character sound distinct? Are motivations consistent and reactions believable? Goal: strengthen arcs and make each voice unique.
Sentence-level work — tighten prose, sharpen dialogue, cut repetition, fix grammar. Goal: the story already works; now make it shine.

sections.title: Writer Warning Labels — Your Bad Habits Are Strengths
sections.summary: Every 'bad habit' is a strength expressed too loud. Diagnose yours, then learn to adjust the volume.

arc_types.description: Symptom: your first chapter is 40% world-building, 60% story. Strength: the freshest takes on complicated worlds — readers will obsess once you cut the fluff.
Symptom: you use em dashes — constantly — for everything. Strength: naturally dynamic pacing and rhythm; learn when a dash adds something vs. punctuation anxiety.
Symptom: 847 uses of 'had' in 80k words. Strength: solid grasp of timeline and backstory — express it without leaning on past perfect.
Symptom: five sentences to describe one room. Strength: real voice and lyricism — learn when to pull back and let readers breathe.
Symptom: every line has a tag ('said angrily', 'whispered softly'). Strength: distinct character voices — you're just over-explaining what readers already get.
Symptom: 'she saw', 'he felt', 'I realized' everywhere. Strength: naturally introspective — show interiority directly instead of narrating the noticing.
Symptom: scenes begin three pages before anything happens. Strength: you build atmosphere and stakes — cut to the moment that matters.
Symptom: 'She did X. He said Y. They felt Z.' Strength: clear, easy-to-follow pacing — vary length and structure for dynamism.
Symptom: the character's whole childhood by page 50. Strength: deep grasp of motivation — layer that information instead of front-loading it.
Symptom: the second act sags; nothing escalates. Strength: solid character work and emotional beats — keep adding complications so stakes rise.

sections.key_insight: The goal isn't to stop being yourself — it's to be yourself more effectively. Your flaws are your strengths turned up too loud; learn to adjust the volume.

sections.title: Instagram & Social Media Accounts for Writers

accounts.description: Literary Hub — literary journalism, criticism, essays, and author interviews. The single best feed for serious literary culture.
The Paris Review — home of the Art of Fiction interview series since 1953. Essential craft conversations with major living writers.
Penguin Classics — the canonical library in daily posts. Classical context, quotes, and cover art from world literature.
The Tolkien Society — official account. Events, scholarship, and discussion of Tolkien's work and legacy. See also tolkiensociety.org.
NYRB Classics — New York Review Books imprint for overlooked masterworks from world literature. Excellent editorial curation.
Writer's Digest — craft tips, market news, and community. The oldest continuously running writing resource in the US (est. 1920).
Reedsy — professional editing resources, craft articles, and a vetted community of editors and published authors.
K.M. Weiland's craft site — deep dives into structure, character arc, and story theory. One of the most thorough free resources online.

classical_resources.title: On Fairy-Stories
classical_resources.author: J.R.R. Tolkien
classical_resources.description: Tolkien's foundational essay on the nature of fantasy, the 'secondary world,' eucatastrophe, and the mythopoeic function of story. Essential for any writer of speculative fiction — and for anyone thinking seriously about why story matters at all.
classical_resources.available_in: Tree and Leaf (1964); The Monsters and the Critics and Other Essays (1983, HarperCollins)
classical_resources.note: PDF widely shared online; for the authoritative text use the HarperCollins collected edition.

classical_resources.title: Le Roman experimental / The Experimental Novel
classical_resources.author: Emile Zola
classical_resources.description: Zola's theoretical manifesto for literary naturalism: fiction should apply the scientific method to human behaviour and society. His 20-novel Rougon-Macquart cycle is the result. Even sceptics of naturalism gain from Zola's insistence on rigorous observation as the writer's first discipline.
classical_resources.note: Public domain. French original and English translations available on Project Gutenberg.

classical_resources.title: Poetics
classical_resources.author: Aristotle
classical_resources.description: The oldest surviving work of dramatic theory. Aristotle introduced mythos (plot), ethos (character), anagnorisis (recognition), and peripeteia (reversal) — vocabulary still used in writers' rooms today. Every modern beat structure traces its lineage here.
classical_resources.note: Public domain. The Bywater (Oxford) or Halliwell translations are recommended.

classical_resources.title: The Art of Fiction
classical_resources.author: Henry James
classical_resources.description: James's manifesto for the novel as a serious art form: 'A novel is in its broadest definition a personal, a direct impression of life.' Argues for consciousness, selectivity, and the author's angle of vision as the fundamental tools of fiction.
classical_resources.note: Public domain. Full text freely available.

classical_resources.title: Aspects of the Novel
classical_resources.author: E.M. Forster
classical_resources.description: Source of the flat/round character distinction and the test: 'Can a character surprise us convincingly?' Forster's Clark Lectures remain one of the most readable introductions to how fiction actually functions — and what distinguishes it from history.
classical_resources.note: Public domain. Available on Internet Archive.

classical_resources.title: The Craft of Fiction
classical_resources.author: Percy Lubbock
classical_resources.description: The first systematic study of point of view in the novel. Lubbock's analysis of Tolstoy, Flaubert, and Henry James established the critical vocabulary — 'showing vs. telling,' 'pictorial vs. dramatic' — that every subsequent craft book has inherited.
classical_resources.note: Public domain. Available on Internet Archive.

chapters.title: Draft Planning & Beat Structures
chapters.subtitle: From Blank Page to Structured Blueprint
chapters.summary: Beat structures are not cages — they are maps. They encode what thousands of successful stories have in common, making that wisdom available before you write the first word. This chapter covers the six most widely used plotting frameworks, explains what each does well and poorly, and shows how to choose or combine them for your project.
chapters.key_insight: All beat structures describe the same underlying shape: a character begins in one state, is forced through escalating pressure to change, and arrives somewhere different at the end. The frameworks differ in granularity, origin, and emphasis — not in fundamental purpose.
chapters.planner_vs_pantser_note: Beat structures work for both planners (outline before draft) and pantsers (discover while drafting). Planners use them as blueprints; pantsers use them as diagnostic tools during revision. Neither approach is superior — the question is which produces your best work.

sections.title: The Three-Act Structure
sections.origin: Aristotle, Poetics (c. 335 BCE); codified for modern screenwriting by Syd Field (Screenplay, 1979)
best_for: Identifying macro-level structural problems in existing drafts
weaknesses: Too broad for detailed planning — doesn't specify what happens inside each act
Easy to produce a sagging middle without more specific waypoints
sections.description: The oldest and most universal framework. Divides a story into three movements of roughly equal weight. Does not tell you what happens — only that something must happen at each transition point.

beats.name: Act I — Setup
beats.function: Establish protagonist, world, and status quo. End with the protagonist committing to the story's central journey.
key_events: End: protagonist crosses the threshold — no going back
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss wakes in District 12, hunts with Gale, attends the Reaping — Prim is chosen — Katniss volunteers. She is on the train.

beats.name: Act II — Confrontation
beats.function: Protagonist pursues the goal across escalating obstacles. Midpoint shifts the story's direction. Ends at the lowest point (All Is Lost).
key_events: Protagonist tests their skills and flaws
Dark Night of the Soul — all seems lost
beats.example_hunger_games: Training, the chariot parade, interviews. Alliance with Peeta. Arena entry. Rue's death. Tracker jacker attack. Rule change announced — two tributes from the same district can win.

beats.name: Act III — Resolution
beats.function: Protagonist uses what they have learned to confront the central conflict. Climax. New equilibrium.
key_events: Optional: brief denouement showing the changed world
beats.example_hunger_games: Mutts chase, Cato battle at Cornucopia. Gamemakers announce rule reversal. Katniss and Peeta threaten mutual suicide with nightlock. Both survive. Return home.

critical_notes: The 25/50/25 split is a guideline, not a rule. Literary fiction often has longer first acts; thrillers often have shorter ones.
The most common failure mode: a weak Act II with no midpoint shift. Without a true Midpoint, the middle sags.
Act II should be two distinct halves: II-A (protagonist adapts, reactive) and II-B (protagonist in crisis, flaw fully exposed).

sections.title: Save the Cat! — The 15-Beat Sheet
sections.origin: Blake Snyder (Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need, 2005); adapted for novels by Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel, 2018)
best_for: Writers who need detailed structural scaffolding
weaknesses: Can feel formulaic if followed too rigidly — produces 'paint-by-numbers' plots
Percentage targets can paralyse writers who fixate on hitting exact word counts
Less suitable for experimental, literary, or non-conflict-driven narratives (see Kishōtenketsu for those)
Originally designed for 110-page screenplays; novel adaptation requires flexibility
sections.description: The most prescriptive widely-used framework. Provides 15 named plot points with percentage targets across a story's total length. Originally a screenwriting tool but now the dominant planning method in commercial fiction.
sections.name_origin: The title comes from an early scene type in Hollywood films where the hero does something immediately likeable — 'saves a cat' — to make the audience root for them before the plot begins.

beats.name: Opening Image
beats.function: A single scene that captures the protagonist's current state — the 'before' photograph. Sets tone, genre, and the problem.
beats.question: What single image or moment shows the reader what 'normal' looks like — and what feels missing?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss wakes in her grey, cold house in District 12 next to her sleeping sister.
beats.craft_note: Should mirror or contrast the Final Image at the end. The two images together show how far the character has travelled.

beats.name: Theme Stated
beats.function: A character (often not the protagonist) states the story's core truth — but the protagonist doesn't understand it yet. This is the lesson they will learn by the end.
beats.question: What is the one thing your protagonist needs to learn? Who plants that seed early?
beats.example_hunger_games: Peeta tells Katniss he doesn't want the Games to change who he is. She doesn't understand this yet.
beats.craft_note: Don't make this a lecture or a thesis statement. It should feel like casual dialogue — a seed, not a lesson.

beats.name: Set-Up
beats.function: Establish the protagonist's world, supporting characters, and — crucially — the flaws and problems that need to be fixed by the story's end.
beats.question: What is broken in your protagonist's world that the story will repair or destroy?
beats.example_hunger_games: The Reaping, Katniss's hunting, her relationship with Gale, her mother's distance, Prim's vulnerability.
beats.craft_note: Plant everything here that will be paid off later. The Set-Up is the promise; the rest of the story is the delivery.

beats.name: Catalyst
beats.function: The inciting incident. The single event that disrupts the protagonist's world and kicks the story into motion. Should be unmistakable — if a reader can't point to your Catalyst, it is not strong enough.
beats.question: What one event forces your protagonist's world to change in a way they cannot ignore?
beats.example_hunger_games: Prim's name is called at the Reaping.
beats.craft_note: The Catalyst happens TO the protagonist. They do not choose it. Their first choice is the next beat: the Debate.

beats.name: Debate
beats.function: The protagonist reacts to the Catalyst with hesitation, doubt, or resistance. The 'should I go?' phase. Shows the cost of committing to the journey.
beats.question: Why would your protagonist NOT want to take this journey? What does refusing feel like?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss volunteers but must say goodbye to Gale and Prim, board the train, begin to grasp what the Games demand.
beats.craft_note: Skipping the Debate makes the protagonist seem naive or reckless. The hesitation earns their eventual commitment.

beats.name: Break into Two
beats.function: The protagonist makes a definitive choice to enter Act II — the 'new world.' This is the threshold crossing. The old rules no longer apply.
beats.question: What irreversible decision does your protagonist make that closes the door to the old world?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss arrives in the Capitol. The Games are real. She is no longer in District 12.
beats.craft_note: Must be a CHOICE, not an accident. If the protagonist is pushed into Act II rather than stepping in, the story loses agency.

beats.name: B Story
beats.function: A secondary relationship or storyline that carries the story's emotional and thematic weight. Often the love interest — but can be mentor, rival, or ally. The B Story is where the theme actually lives.
beats.question: Who or what helps your protagonist learn what they need to learn? How does this relationship carry your theme?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss's relationship with Peeta deepens. He is kind; she is strategic. Together they represent the tension between humanity and survival.
beats.craft_note: The B Story must intersect with the A Story. Subplots that run parallel without influencing the main plot are dead weight.

beats.name: Fun and Games
beats.function: The 'promise of the premise' — the section readers picked up the book for. The hero explores the new world, tests themselves, and pursues the goal. Stakes are building but not yet critical.
beats.question: What did your readers expect when they picked up this book? Are you delivering that here?
beats.example_hunger_games: Training sessions, chariot parade, TV interviews, strategy with Haymitch. The spectacle of the Capitol. Alliance with Rue.
beats.craft_note: This is where most genre expectations are paid off (the detective solving clues, the romance's will-they-won't-they tension, the wizard learning magic). Do NOT skip to danger too fast.

beats.name: Midpoint
beats.function: The exact middle of the story. Either a 'false victory' (protagonist seems to have won — but a bigger problem is coming) or a 'false defeat' (protagonist seems to have lost — but it galvanises them). Stakes rise permanently.
beats.question: At the exact middle, what flips? What does your protagonist think they know that is about to be proven wrong?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss and Peeta form their alliance. The Gamemakers announce that two tributes from the same district can win — the first apparent hope.
beats.craft_note: This is NOT just a big event. A strong Midpoint gives the second half of the story a new charge. Ask: does everything after the midpoint feel different from before it?

beats.name: Bad Guys Close In
beats.function: The pressure tightens on every front. External antagonists advance; internal flaws compound the problem. Every choice costs more. Every mistake leaves a mark.
beats.question: How does the protagonist's own flaw make the external problem worse during this section?
beats.example_hunger_games: Tracker jacker attack, Rue's death, Peeta fighting with Cato's group. Katniss's self-sufficiency prevents her from trusting allies.
beats.craft_note: The 'bad guys' don't have to be villains. They can be circumstance, internal doubt, allies proving unreliable, or time running out.

beats.name: All Is Lost
beats.function: The lowest point. Something or someone is lost — possibly permanently. The protagonist's old approach has completely failed. Often involves a symbolic (or literal) death.
beats.question: What is the worst thing that could happen at this point that is directly caused by your protagonist's flaw?
beats.example_hunger_games: Rue is killed. Katniss's alliance is gone. She is alone, injured, and the Gamemakers cancel the rule change.
beats.craft_note: The 'whiff of death' is Blake Snyder's term — this beat often involves a literal death, but it can be the death of a belief, relationship, or plan. Something must be lost, not just threatened.

beats.name: Dark Night of the Soul
beats.function: The protagonist sits with the loss. This is the emotional trough — deeper than the All Is Lost moment. They must confront their flaw, grief, or failure before finding the will to continue.
beats.question: What does your protagonist realise about themselves when everything has failed?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss grieves Rue. Sings to her. Covers her body with flowers — a human act in an inhuman game. This is her internal turning point.
beats.craft_note: Do not rush through this beat. The Dark Night of the Soul is the emotional permission slip for the finale. Readers need to feel the depth of the pit before the climb out means anything.

beats.name: Break into Three
beats.function: The protagonist finds the answer — usually through the B Story's theme. They choose to change. This is the internal shift that enables the external climax.
beats.question: What does your protagonist decide to do — and why is this decision only possible because of what they have learned?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss decides that survival at the cost of her humanity isn't survival worth having. She will fight on her own terms.
beats.craft_note: The solution to the Act III problem must come from the protagonist's internal change — not from external rescue, coincidence, or a new tool arriving conveniently.

beats.name: Finale
beats.function: The protagonist executes the new plan using what they have learned. Synthesises A Story and B Story. The antagonist is defeated — or the protagonist fails trying. The world is permanently changed.
beats.question: How does your protagonist use their internal change to resolve the external conflict?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss and Peeta threaten mutual suicide with nightlock berries. The Gamemakers yield. Both survive as co-victors.
beats.craft_note: The finale should feel both surprising and inevitable. Readers should not see exactly what is coming, but in retrospect it should seem like the only possible outcome.

beats.name: Final Image
beats.function: The closing snapshot. The 'after' photograph. Shows — does not tell — how the protagonist's world and inner state have changed from the Opening Image.
beats.question: What single image shows the reader who your protagonist has become?
beats.example_hunger_games: Katniss and Peeta return to District 12. Peeta holds her hand. She is no longer alone — but she knows the Capitol is not finished with them.
beats.craft_note: The Final Image should echo the Opening Image. Same location or object, different emotional meaning. The contrast is the story.

practical_usage.for_planners: Fill in each beat before you write. For each beat, write: (1) the external event, (2) the internal pivot, and (3) the consequence. If you cannot name the consequence, the beat is a topic, not a beat.
practical_usage.for_pantsers: Use after your first draft as a diagnostic tool. Map your draft onto the 15 beats. Missing beats indicate structural gaps; beats in the wrong position indicate pacing problems.
practical_usage.for_revision: The most common problems: missing or weak Midpoint; no true All Is Lost; protagonist does not make the Break into Three choice — they are carried into Act III rather than choosing it.

sections.title: The Hero's Journey (Monomyth)
sections.origin: Joseph Campbell (The Hero with a Thousand Faces, 1949, 17 stages); distilled to 12 stages for writers by Christopher Vogler (The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers, 1992)
best_for: Stories with a clear mentor figure and threshold-crossing
Writers interested in the psychological / archetypal dimension of story
weaknesses: Less suited to intimate, domestic, or conflict-free narratives
Literal application can make stories feel mythic when they are actually contemporary or realistic
The 'Return with the Elixir' stage often does not map cleanly to modern commercial fiction
Campbell's original 17 stages are studied by mythologists; Vogler's 12 are the writer's working tool
sections.description: Campbell identified a pattern across myths from unconnected cultures: a hero leaves a familiar world, survives trials in a special world, transforms, and returns with a gift for their community. Vogler trimmed this to 12 stages specifically for storytellers. The Hero's Journey differs from STC in emphasis: where STC focuses on plot mechanics, the Hero's Journey maps the psychological transformation of the protagonist against archetypal character types (Mentor, Threshold Guardian, Shadow, Trickster, Herald, Shapeshifter).

three_movements.name: Departure
three_movements.description: The hero leaves the ordinary world. Corresponds roughly to Act I.

three_movements.name: Initiation
three_movements.description: The hero is tested, transformed, and receives their reward. Corresponds to Act II.

three_movements.name: Return
three_movements.description: The hero brings the gift back. Corresponds to Act III.

beats.name: Ordinary World
beats.function: Establish the hero in their familiar environment before the adventure begins. This is the baseline against which all change will be measured.
beats.example: Harry Potter lives in the cupboard under the stairs at Number 4 Privet Drive. The ordinary world must be shown — not just named.
beats.craft_note: The richer and more specific the Ordinary World, the more meaningful every departure from it will feel.

beats.name: Call to Adventure
beats.function: Something disrupts the Ordinary World and presents the hero with a challenge they cannot ignore. The stakes and goal of the adventure become clear.
beats.example: Harry receives a letter from Hogwarts. Luke Skywalker receives Princess Leia's message via R2-D2.
beats.craft_note: The Call can come from many sources: an external event, an encounter, even an internal restlessness. What matters is that it makes the old life no longer possible.

beats.name: Refusal of the Call
beats.function: The hero hesitates, doubts, or actively refuses. This is not weakness — it shows what is being risked and makes the eventual commitment meaningful.
beats.example: Harry is told he cannot go to Hogwarts by the Dursleys. Luke initially refuses to join Obi-Wan, wanting to stay with his family.
beats.craft_note: Without refusal, the hero seems foolhardy. With it, the eventual crossing is earned.

beats.name: Meeting the Mentor
beats.function: The hero encounters a guide who provides knowledge, tools, or confidence for the journey ahead. The mentor does not solve problems — they prepare the hero to face them.
beats.example: Obi-Wan Kenobi, Gandalf, Haymitch Abernathy, Dumbledore.
beats.craft_note: The mentor cannot accompany the hero all the way — they must eventually step back, die, or become unavailable. This is what forces the hero to discover their own strength.

beats.name: Crossing the First Threshold
beats.function: The hero commits to the adventure and enters the Special World. An irreversible decision. This is the Break into Two.
beats.example: Harry boards the Hogwarts Express at Platform 9¾. Luke leaves Tatooine after his family is killed.
beats.craft_note: Threshold Guardians — characters or forces that block the entry — test whether the hero is ready. They should not be easily defeated.

beats.name: Tests, Allies, and Enemies
beats.function: The hero navigates the Special World. They meet potential allies, face enemies, and learn the new world's rules. Equivalent to Fun and Games.
beats.example: Harry meets Ron and Hermione, encounters Draco, learns magic at Hogwarts.
beats.craft_note: This is often the longest section. Do not rush. The audience picked up the book to spend time in this world — earn the adventure before the crisis.

beats.name: Approach to the Inmost Cave
beats.function: The hero moves toward the central ordeal. Preparation, gathering allies, addressing doubts. The last moment before the point of no return.
beats.example: Harry, Ron, and Hermione plan to retrieve the Sorcerer's Stone before Snape (as they believe) can steal it.
beats.craft_note: The Inmost Cave is not just a place — it is the location of the hero's greatest fear. Identify what that fear is and build toward it.

beats.name: The Ordeal
beats.function: The hero faces their greatest crisis. A 'death-and-rebirth' moment. They must confront their deepest fear or flaw. The protagonist should break down and come out the other side stronger — or not come out at all (tragedy).
beats.example: Harry faces Quirrell/Voldemort at the Mirror of Erised. Katniss watches Rue die.
beats.craft_note: This is not necessarily the climax. It is the point of maximum danger in Act II — the moment that reshapes everything. Campbell called it 'the belly of the whale.'

beats.name: Reward (Seizing the Sword)
beats.function: Having survived the Ordeal, the hero receives a reward: an object, knowledge, reconciliation, or a new understanding. The trophy of having survived.
beats.example: Harry retrieves the Sorcerer's Stone. Katniss's act of defiance earns her — and Peeta — survival.
beats.craft_note: The Reward is often only the beginning. Now it must be brought back safely — and the road back is rarely easy.

beats.name: The Road Back
beats.function: The hero must return to the Ordinary World — but the antagonist often pursues, or returning home proves more complicated than leaving did.
beats.example: Harry escapes the trap. Frodo and Sam's long march back from Mordor. Katniss boards the train as a victor.
beats.craft_note: In many modern stories this stage collapses into the Resurrection. For shorter works, do not linger.

beats.name: Resurrection
beats.function: The climax. The hero is tested one final time — often in a way that echoes the Ordeal but requires their new self. A final 'death' and 'rebirth' before full integration.
beats.example: Harry wakes in Dumbledore's office, saved by his mother's love. The Gamemakers yield to Katniss and Peeta's nightlock threat.
beats.craft_note: The hero who faces the Resurrection should be different from the hero who entered the Ordinary Cave. If they are the same person, the story has failed to produce transformation.

beats.name: Return with the Elixir
beats.function: The hero returns to the Ordinary World transformed, bringing something that benefits their community. The 'elixir' can be a literal object, knowledge, hope, freedom, or a changed self.
beats.example: Harry returns to Privet Drive knowing he has people who love him. Frodo returns to the Shire — but cannot stay unchanged.
beats.craft_note: The elixir the hero initially sought often becomes secondary. What they bring back is always, at root, a new version of themselves.

archetypal_characters.name: Mentor
archetypal_characters.function: Guide who prepares but cannot complete the journey for the hero

archetypal_characters.name: Threshold Guardian
archetypal_characters.function: Tests the hero before they can enter or advance — not always a villain

archetypal_characters.name: Herald
archetypal_characters.function: Delivers the Call to Adventure; signals that change is coming

archetypal_characters.name: Shapeshifter
archetypal_characters.function: Character whose loyalty is unclear; creates doubt and complexity

archetypal_characters.name: Shadow
archetypal_characters.function: The antagonist; often represents the hero's own dark potential

archetypal_characters.name: Trickster
archetypal_characters.function: Provides comic relief, disruption, and unexpected insight; questions the status quo

archetypal_characters.name: Ally
archetypal_characters.function: Supports the hero; can include the love interest, sidekick, or found family

practical_usage.for_planners: Map your characters to archetypes first. Then sequence the 12 stages. A character who fulfils multiple archetypes (e.g., a mentor who becomes a threshold guardian) creates richer complexity.
practical_usage.for_pantsers: Use after draft to check whether your protagonist is reactive (hero's journey not working) or proactive. The journey breaks when the hero is carried by events instead of choosing to meet them.
practical_usage.for_revision: Check the Mentor stage: do they leave or become unavailable before the climax? Check the Resurrection: is your hero genuinely different, or merely victorious?

sections.title: Dan Wells' Seven-Point Story Structure
sections.origin: Dan Wells, presented at a writing conference and documented on the Writing Excuses podcast (Season 7, Ep. 41); structure adapted from a role-playing game sourcebook
best_for: Character-driven stories where the arc is paramount
Writers who want symmetry between character start and end states
Subplots (the 7 points can be applied to each subplot independently)
weaknesses: Too skeletal for detailed planning without supplementary scene-level work
The two Pinch Points can feel mechanical if not properly motivated
Does not specify the structure inside 'Fun and Games' equivalent
sections.description: A lean, symmetrical seven-beat framework that begins at the ending and works backward. Its core insight: the Hook (opening state) should be the mirror opposite of the Resolution (ending state). The story is the distance between those two poles. Unlike STC, Wells does not specify what happens — only what function each point must serve.
sections.key_insight: Start with your Resolution. Then write your Hook as its opposite. The story is the journey between them. Every other point exists to make that journey believable.
sections.design_order: Wells recommends designing in this order: Resolution → Hook → Midpoint → Plot Turn 2 → Plot Turn 1 → Pinch 2 → Pinch 1. Write in reverse so every element serves the ending.

beats.name: Hook
beats.function: Introduce the protagonist in their starting state. Crucially, this state should be the OPPOSITE of where they end up at the Resolution. The contrast between Hook and Resolution IS the character arc.
beats.question: If your protagonist ends brave and open-hearted, where must they start? Fearful and closed. Design the Hook last — after you know your Resolution.
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry is powerless, unloved, ignorant of his identity, living in a cupboard.
beats.example_design_note: If your Resolution is 'Marta has learned to trust people,' your Hook must show Marta unable to trust anyone.

beats.name: Plot Turn 1
beats.function: The inciting incident. The event that kicks the story into motion and commits the protagonist to the main path. Introduces the central conflict.
beats.question: What one event disrupts the protagonist's starting state and commits them to the story's journey?
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry receives his Hogwarts letter — discovers he is a wizard.

beats.name: Pinch Point 1
beats.function: A moment of pressure. Often the first direct encounter with the antagonist or the true scale of the conflict. Raises stakes and forces the protagonist into action.
beats.question: What demonstrates the power of the forces working against your protagonist? The antagonist shows their hand.
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry learns Voldemort is in the school. The threat is real, immediate, and personal.
beats.craft_note: The Pinch Points are not about action — they are about demonstrating what the protagonist is up against. Make the stakes visceral.

beats.name: Midpoint
beats.function: The exact centre of the story. The protagonist shifts from REACTIVE (responding to events) to PROACTIVE (driving events). Everything changes direction here.
beats.question: At exactly the halfway point, what decision or realisation turns your protagonist from someone things happen to into someone who makes things happen?
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry decides he must go after the Stone himself — he cannot wait for adults to act.
beats.craft_note: The Midpoint in a detective story can come very early (when the detective takes the case, they move from reactive to proactive). Adjust for genre. The function, not the timing, is fixed.

beats.name: Pinch Point 2
beats.function: A second, harder squeeze. More serious than Pinch 1. The 'jaws of defeat' — everything seems lost. Mentors vanish, plans fail, allies prove unreliable.
beats.question: What is the worst possible thing that happens to your protagonist right before they find the solution?
beats.example_harry_potter: Ron and Hermione are stopped by the traps; Harry must face Quirrell alone.
beats.craft_note: This beat corresponds to All Is Lost in STC. It should feel like the floor has fallen out. If it doesn't, your Pinch 2 is not hard enough.

beats.name: Plot Turn 2
beats.function: The protagonist receives or discovers the last piece needed to resolve the conflict. Often an internal realisation — 'the power was in them all along.' The bridge from darkest moment to Resolution.
beats.question: What does your protagonist realise or receive that makes the Resolution possible?
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry understands that his motives are pure — and this protects him from Quirrell's touch (Lily's sacrificial love).
beats.craft_note: Wells calls this 'The power is in you!' — the hero's last insight before the climax. It must be earned by everything that came before.

beats.name: Resolution
beats.function: The climax and its aftermath. The protagonist resolves the central conflict — or fails. Note the change from the Hook state. This beat was designed first; everything in the story was built to earn it.
beats.question: Who is your protagonist now, compared to who they were at the Hook? Show the distance.
beats.example_harry_potter: Harry defeats Quirrell/Voldemort. Returns to Privet Drive knowing he has friends, belonging, and identity.

sections.subplot_usage: The 7 points can be applied independently to each subplot. Line up subplots' Pinch Points and Resolutions with the main arc's equivalents to create powerful moments where multiple threads converge.
sections.tragedy_variant: For tragedy, reverse the arc: the Hook begins at a high state, and the Resolution ends at the lowest. Plot Turns move the character toward destruction rather than growth.

sections.title: Nigel Watts' Eight-Point Story Arc
sections.origin: Nigel Watts (Write a Novel — And Get It Published, Teach Yourself Books, 1996)
best_for: Writers who want a gentle framework without prescriptive percentages
weaknesses: More descriptive than prescriptive — does not specify what should happen at each point
The 'Quest' stage is deliberately vague, which helps literary fiction but frustrates genre writers
Less widely known than STC or Hero's Journey; fewer learning resources available
sections.description: A gentle eight-stage arc derived from Watts's analysis of successful novels. Unlike STC, it does not provide percentage targets. Unlike the Hero's Journey, it does not require a mythic framework. It emphasises the evolution of the protagonist's internal QUEST — which should change shape over the course of the story as the character learns what they actually need.
sections.key_insight: The protagonist's quest should not remain the same throughout the story. What begins as a quest for money might evolve into a quest for love, then a quest for survival. The arc is not just the journey — it is the evolution of the hero's understanding of what they are actually seeking.

beats.name: Stasis
beats.function: The protagonist's ordinary life — business as usual. Shows what the character has to gain or lose. Must be established before it can be disrupted.
