beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: The Bennet family in their Hertfordshire home. The social world, the mother's anxiety about marriage, the five daughters.
beats.craft_note: Stasis is not static — it should already contain the seeds of the coming disruption. The best stasis shows a character already at the edge of change.

beats.name: Trigger
beats.function: An event beyond the protagonist's control that disturbs the stasis and starts the chain of events that makes up the story. Can be dramatic or quiet.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Bingley and his party arrive at Netherfield. The social dynamic — and Elizabeth's world — shifts.
beats.craft_note: Unlike STC's Catalyst, the Trigger does not have to be a dramatic inciting incident. A subtle change that builds over time qualifies.

beats.name: Quest
beats.function: Because of the Trigger, the protagonist begins pursuing a goal. The Quest is the main bulk of the story. Crucially, it should evolve — the protagonist's understanding of what they actually need should deepen.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Elizabeth pursues truth and connection; the quest evolves from social observation to genuine love to reconciling her judgment errors.
beats.craft_note: Watts' most original contribution: the Quest is not fixed. A character who starts seeking money and ends seeking money has not grown. The Quest must evolve with the character.

beats.name: Surprise
beats.function: An unexpected event that complicates the Quest. Can be positive or negative, but must not be easily predictable. Forces the protagonist to adapt. Usually solidifies the conflict.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Elizabeth learns of Wickham's true character. Darcy's first proposal — completely unexpected. Each surprise forces her to re-examine her judgment.
beats.craft_note: Surprises must arise naturally from what has already happened — not feel random. A surprise that seems to come from nowhere breaks the story's internal logic.

beats.name: Critical Choice
beats.function: The protagonist must make a decision under maximum pressure. This choice reveals character and determines the course of the story. It should be genuinely difficult — no easy option available.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Elizabeth chooses to refuse Darcy's first proposal despite the social cost. Later: the choice to accept his second.
beats.craft_note: If the choice is obvious, it isn't a Critical Choice. The protagonist should have compelling reasons on both sides. What they choose tells us — and them — who they really are.

beats.name: Climax
beats.function: The point of maximum tension. The result of all previous Surprises and Critical Choices. The protagonist faces the consequence of their choices head-on.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Darcy's letter. Lydia's elopement. Elizabeth confronts her own misjudgement at precisely the moment her family's reputation is destroyed.
beats.craft_note: The Climax is not just the biggest action scene. In literary fiction it is often an internal confrontation — a moment of radical self-knowledge.

beats.name: Reversal
beats.function: The situation changes fundamentally as a result of the Climax. The protagonist's world — internal and external — is permanently altered. The reversal is the direct consequence of the Critical Choice.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Darcy helps resolve the Lydia crisis. Elizabeth's pride and prejudice are reversed. Her understanding of herself and Darcy is transformed.
beats.craft_note: The Reversal must flow causally from the Critical Choice and Climax. If it could have happened regardless of the protagonist's choices, it is not a Reversal — it is an accident.

beats.name: Resolution
beats.function: The new stasis. The protagonist's world settles into a new equilibrium. Should mirror — and contrast with — the opening Stasis.
beats.example_pride_and_prejudice: Elizabeth and Darcy are engaged. The family is transformed. The opening social anxiety is resolved — but the resolution has been earned, not merely delivered.
beats.craft_note: The Resolution does not have to be happy. It must be truthful — the natural consequence of everything that has come before.

sections.title: The Snowflake Method
sections.origin: Randy Ingermanson (advancedfictionwriting.com, 2003; developed over subsequent years into a 10-step process)
best_for: Fantasy, science fiction, thriller with intricate world-building or plotting
Writers with ambitious first projects who need help managing scope
weaknesses: Very time-intensive — the full 10-step process can take weeks before a word of prose is written
Can create an illusion of progress without actual story discovery
The fractal expansion process can produce over-detailed outlines that feel more like summaries than blueprints
Less useful for character-discovery writers who find their story by writing it
sections.description: Unlike beat frameworks, the Snowflake Method is a planning process rather than a story structure. It begins with a single sentence and expands outward in ten steps, each one adding detail to the previous. The process is named after the mathematical fractal: each iteration reveals more complexity while maintaining the same fundamental shape.
sections.key_insight: The method forces writers to test their story at every level of abstraction — from single sentence to scene-by-scene outline — before committing prose. Each step reveals weaknesses in the previous one.

steps.name: One-Sentence Summary
steps.description: Write a single sentence summarising your novel. Aim for about 15 words. No character names — use descriptors. This is your 'elevator pitch.'
steps.example: 'A teenage girl in a dystopian future must fight to the death to save her family and expose the cruelty of her government.' (The Hunger Games)
steps.craft_note: If you cannot summarise your novel in one sentence, you do not yet know what it is about. The sentence reveals the central character, their goal, and the conflict.

steps.name: One-Paragraph Summary
steps.description: Expand the sentence into a paragraph of five sentences: setup, Act I disaster, Act II disaster (first half), Act II disaster (second half), and Act III ending.
steps.example: One sentence each for: protagonist's starting situation → first major turning point → midpoint reversal → all-is-lost moment → resolution.
steps.craft_note: This is a rough version of the Three-Act Structure in miniature. It forces you to have something at each major structural juncture before you begin.

steps.name: Character Summaries
steps.description: For each major character, write a one-page summary covering: name, arc, motivation (surface goal), ambition (deeper need), conflict (internal obstacle), and epiphany (what they learn).
steps.craft_note: This step often reveals that your antagonist is more interesting than your protagonist — or that a secondary character is actually carrying your theme.

steps.name: Expanded Story Summary
steps.description: Expand the one-paragraph summary to a full page. Resolve any contradictions revealed in step 3. Each of the five sentences becomes a paragraph.
steps.craft_note: The expansion often breaks things that seemed fine in summary. A character motivation that worked in one sentence may collapse when examined across a paragraph.

steps.name: Character Charts
steps.description: For each major character, write a detailed profile: birthdate, physical description, history, personality, motivation, goal, conflict, and their story arc in one paragraph.
steps.craft_note: Include each character's version of the story's events. Every character believes they are the protagonist of their own story.

steps.name: Four-Page Synopsis
steps.description: Expand the one-page story summary to four pages. Go through the story beat by beat at a chapter-level view.
steps.craft_note: This is where most structural problems become visible. A four-page synopsis forces you to commit to what happens in every part of the book.

steps.name: Full Character Narratives
steps.description: Write the story from the perspective of each major character, in their own voice, covering all the events of the novel from their point of view.
steps.craft_note: Optional but valuable for multi-POV novels or any story where the antagonist's perspective matters.

steps.name: Scene List
steps.description: List every scene in the novel in a spreadsheet. For each scene: POV character, scene summary (2-3 sentences), what changes by the end.
steps.craft_note: If a scene does not change something — if the protagonist exits in the same state they entered — that scene should be cut or combined.

steps.name: Scene Expansions
steps.description: Expand each scene into a multi-paragraph description of what happens, including dialogue beats, emotional beats, and sensory detail.
steps.craft_note: This step is optional. Some writers find it so detailed that they lose energy for the actual prose. Stop here if writing the expansions feels like writing the book.

steps.name: First Draft
steps.description: Write the novel. The outline is a guide, not a cage. If the story demands a scene you did not outline, write it. The outline exists to serve the story — not the other way around.
steps.craft_note: Ingermanson emphasises that the outline should evolve as you write. Rigidly following a finished outline is as bad as having no outline at all.

sections.title: Freytag's Pyramid
sections.origin: Gustav Freytag (Die Technik des Dramas, 1863), German playwright and novelist
best_for: Understanding classical structure in existing works
weaknesses: Designed for classical tragedy — the falling action is long and extended denouement rarely suits modern commercial fiction
The symmetrical pyramid shape implies equal weight for rising and falling action, which most modern stories do not follow
Does not address character arc in useful planning terms
sections.description: The oldest formal European story framework, derived from Freytag's analysis of Greek and Shakespearean tragedy. Visualised as a pyramid: the story rises through conflict to a climax, then descends through consequences to resolution. Standard in literary education; less used as a planning tool but widely relevant as analytical vocabulary.

beats.name: Exposition (Einleitung)
beats.function: Introduction of characters, setting, and background. The world before the story begins.
beats.example: Macbeth establishes the Scottish court, Macbeth's reputation, and the king's trust in him.

beats.name: Rising Action (Steigende Handlung)
beats.function: A series of events and complications that build tension toward the climax. The protagonist encounters obstacles.
beats.example: The witches' prophecy; Macbeth's ambition kindled; the murder of Duncan; increasing paranoia.

beats.name: Climax (Höhepunkt / Umkehr)
beats.function: The turning point. The moment of maximum tension. In classical tragedy, the point at which the protagonist's fate is sealed.
beats.example: Macbeth's murder of Duncan. After this, there is no return.

beats.name: Falling Action (Fallende Handlung)
beats.function: The consequences of the climax unfold. The protagonist's situation deteriorates. Forces of antagonism advance toward the tragic conclusion.
beats.example: Macbeth's increasing tyranny, Banquo's murder, Lady Macbeth's breakdown, the march of Malcolm's forces.

beats.name: Denouement / Resolution (Katastrophe)
beats.function: The final outcome. In tragedy: destruction or death. In other genres: resolution of the central conflict and establishment of a new order.
beats.example: Macbeth's death; Malcolm restored to the throne. Order reimposed on a shattered world.

sections.modern_adaptation: Modern fiction rarely uses the symmetrical pyramid. Act III (resolution) is typically much shorter than Act II (rising action). Freytag's Pyramid is most useful for understanding classical dramatic structure and analysing existing works, not as a primary planning tool.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Framework
sections.description: No framework is universally superior. The question is which tool fits your story, your genre, and your working style.

comparison_table.key_strength: Universal foundation; works with all other frameworks
comparison_table.key_weakness: Too broad for detailed planning alone

comparison_table.key_strength: Highly prescriptive; excellent for debut commercial fiction
comparison_table.key_weakness: Can feel formulaic; poor fit for literary/experimental work
Return stage often doesn't fit modern commercial fiction

comparison_table.key_strength: Symmetry; works beautifully on subplots; backward-design insight
comparison_table.key_weakness: Too skeletal without supplementary scene planning

comparison_table.key_strength: Quest evolution concept; gentle; works for non-genre fiction
comparison_table.key_weakness: Less prescriptive than genre writers often need

comparison_table.key_strength: Manages complexity; forces scope testing early
comparison_table.key_weakness: Time-intensive; can produce inert, over-outlined drafts
Poor fit for modern commercial pacing expectations

combination_strategies.name: STC + 7-Point
combination_strategies.description: Use the 7-Point Structure on each major subplot independently, then align subplot pinch points with STC's main-story bad-guys-close-in sequence. Powerful moments emerge where arcs collide.

combination_strategies.name: Hero's Journey + Snowflake
combination_strategies.description: Use the Hero's Journey to define the protagonist's arc and archetypal character roles, then use the Snowflake Method to expand from sentence to scene list.

combination_strategies.name: Watts + Three-Act
combination_strategies.description: Use the Three-Act Structure as your macro framework, then use the 8-Point Arc inside each act to track the evolution of your protagonist's quest.
combination_strategies.best_for: Literary fiction; character-driven domestic or psychological fiction

combination_strategies.name: STC as Revision Diagnostic
combination_strategies.description: Write freely (pantsing), then map your draft onto the 15 STC beats. Missing or weak beats reveal structural problems. Use STC as a revision framework rather than a planning one.
combination_strategies.best_for: Discovery writers working in commercial genres

common_planning_mistakes.mistake: Confusing framework compliance with good storytelling
common_planning_mistakes.fix: Frameworks describe what successful stories have in common — they do not cause success. Character, voice, and theme are not in any beat sheet. They live in the prose.
common_planning_mistakes.attributed_to: Kindlepreneur.com: 'The beat sheet is most useful when it helps you see the shape of your novel, not when it starts bossing you around like a tiny clipboard-holding tyrant.'

common_planning_mistakes.mistake: Hitting beat percentages before writing a compelling scene
common_planning_mistakes.fix: The Midpoint should be placed where it makes narrative sense, not at word 40,000 of an 80,000-word novel. Percentages are guidelines that point to common reader expectation — not laws.
common_planning_mistakes.attributed_to: penwise.ai: 'The fix is usually missing thresholds, unclear stakes — not wrong page numbers.'

common_planning_mistakes.mistake: Using an outline as a cage after story discovers a better path
common_planning_mistakes.fix: The outline exists to serve the story. If the story demands a scene you didn't outline, write it. The best outlines are revised continuously during drafting.
common_planning_mistakes.attributed_to: Reedsy / Jennifer C. (editor): 'Once you begin drafting, the story should be primary. If the story demands a scene you didn't outline, that's what you need to do.'

common_planning_mistakes.mistake: Forcing mythic structure onto intimate, domestic, or conflict-free stories
common_planning_mistakes.fix: Not all stories are hero stories. Kishōtenketsu (Japanese/Chinese 4-part structure) and similar non-conflict-based frameworks exist for stories that progress through revelation and juxtaposition rather than antagonism.
common_planning_mistakes.attributed_to: authorflows.com: 'If your story lives in fragments, nonlinearity, or mood over plot, STC may fight your intent.'

common_planning_mistakes.mistake: Planning all subplots with the same framework as the main arc
common_planning_mistakes.fix: Subplots often function better at a different granularity than the main arc. Use the 7-Point Structure on subplots; use STC or Hero's Journey on the main arc.
common_planning_mistakes.attributed_to: Dan Wells / Writing Excuses: 'Plots, subplots and character arcs can each be mapped out with the Seven-Point System.'

chapters.title: Genre & Subgenre Wiki
chapters.subtitle: A field guide to the major fiction genres, their subgenres, and the worlds they build — a toolkit, not a set of cages.

sections.title: How to Use Genres
sections.summary: Genres are labels for a cluster of features — useful for readers, marketing, and shelving, but their borders are porous and shift over time and place. The most memorable works blend, subvert, and transcend them. Treat this wiki as a toolkit, not a set of cages.
key_points: Six very broad families of fiction are commonly named: literary, action/adventure, speculative (SF/fantasy/horror), crime, romance, and historical — with thousands of subgenres nested inside.
Most books are hybrids. 'Historical romantic suspense' or 'cosy paranormal mystery' are normal; a book usually lands in several categories at once.
Subgenre is a promise to the reader about the experience — cosy vs. hardboiled, epic vs. sword-and-sorcery — so choosing one sets expectations you must then honour or deliberately subvert.
critical_notes: Speculative Fiction — the umbrella for all fiction that departs from realism: SF, fantasy, horror, magical realism, superhero, alternate history, utopia/dystopia, fairy tale, and the various '-punks'.

Fantastique (French tradition) — stories where characters, like the reader, cannot accept the supernatural as real, producing doubt and fear; distinct from fantasy, where the supernatural is accepted as normal within the world.

sections.title: Fantasy
sections.summary: Fiction set in worlds where magic or the supernatural is real. It ranges from fully invented secondary worlds to magic hidden in our own, and spans the mythic grandeur of epic fantasy to the personal grit of sword-and-sorcery.

subgenres.name: High / Epic Fantasy
subgenres.description: Grand-scale, world-ending stakes in a fully secondary world with its own physical and magical laws; a hero or band of heroes; often spans many volumes.
subgenres.examples: The Lord of the Rings, A Song of Ice and Fire, The Wheel of Time, Malazan Book of the Fallen

subgenres.name: Low Fantasy
subgenres.description: Set in the real world, but intruded on by magical elements that shock the characters — the magic is not considered normal.
subgenres.examples: Harry Potter (hidden from Muggles), Buffy the Vampire Slayer

subgenres.name: Sword & Sorcery
subgenres.description: Personal, fast-paced conflict over world-ending stakes; violent action, often a romantic thread; a reluctant protagonist of humble origin.
subgenres.examples: Conan the Barbarian, Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd & the Gray Mouser

subgenres.name: Dark Fantasy
subgenres.description: Fantasy fused with horror — a gloomy atmosphere, dread, and supernatural villains.
subgenres.examples: Stephen King's Dark Tower, Anne Bishop's Black Jewels, Clive Barker

subgenres.name: Grimdark
subgenres.description: Bleak, morally pessimistic worlds where political scheming and bloody violence take precedence over enchantment.
subgenres.examples: George R.R. Martin, Joe Abercrombie, Mark Lawrence, Glen Cook's Black Company

subgenres.name: Urban Fantasy
subgenres.description: Magic and magical creatures woven into the interstices of a (usually contemporary) city.
subgenres.examples: Charles de Lint's Newford, Patricia Briggs' Mercy Thompson, The Dresden Files

subgenres.name: Historical Fantasy
subgenres.description: A real historical period seeded with magic, the supernatural, or anachronistic technology.
subgenres.examples: Guy Gavriel Kay, Naomi Novik's Temeraire, Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell

subgenres.name: Fairy Tale / Folkloric
subgenres.description: Traditional tales — trolls, dragons, witches — retold, often for adults, drawing on world folklore.
subgenres.examples: Neil Gaiman, Mercedes Lackey, Naomi Novik's Uprooted

subgenres.name: Magical Realism
subgenres.description: Magical events treated as an ordinary, unremarked part of the real world; the author never explains them.
subgenres.examples: Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, Isabel Allende

subgenres.name: Contemporary / Modern Fantasy
subgenres.description: Present-day consensus reality where magic exists in the cracks or leaks from other worlds.
subgenres.examples: Philip Pullman, Charles de Lint, J.K. Rowling

subgenres.name: Comic / Light Fantasy
subgenres.description: A light, humorous tone that parodies or gently mocks fantasy convention.
subgenres.examples: Terry Pratchett's Discworld, Terry Pratchett & Neil Gaiman's Good Omens

subgenres.name: Hard Fantasy
subgenres.description: Magic built on logical, rational, consistent internal rules — a 'magic system' you could diagram.
subgenres.examples: Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere, Mistborn

subgenres.name: Portal / Isekai / LitRPG
subgenres.description: A protagonist crosses into a secondary world, often one resembling a game with in-universe levels or ranks; isekai adds reincarnation with real-world knowledge.
subgenres.examples: The Chronicles of Narnia, Sword Art Online, Ready Player One

subgenres.name: Superhero Fantasy
subgenres.description: Heroes with powers of supernatural (rather than scientific) origin; frequently blends SF and fantasy.
subgenres.examples: DC & Marvel Universes, My Hero Academia

subgenres.name: Paranormal Romance
subgenres.description: Fantasy fused with the romance genre — a central love story with supernatural or magical elements and a guaranteed emotional payoff.
subgenres.examples: Twilight, Patricia Briggs' Mercy Thompson

subgenres.name: Bangsian Fantasy
subgenres.description: Famous historical or literary figures interacting in the afterlife; named for John Kendrick Bangs.
subgenres.examples: Riverworld (Philip José Farmer)

subgenres.name: Fables & Legends
subgenres.description: Fables teach a moral truth (often via talking animals); legends embroider a national hero or folk figure with a kernel of history.
subgenres.examples: Aesop's Fables, Arthurian legend, Robin Hood

subgenres.name: Romantasy
subgenres.description: High-fantasy world-building carrying equal weight to a central romance with a happily-ever-after; an explosively popular crossover.
subgenres.examples: Sarah J. Maas (A Court of Thorns and Roses), Rebecca Yarros (Fourth Wing)

world_profiles.name: High Fantasy (Tolkienesque)
world_profiles.core_themes: Good vs. evil, destiny, the hero's journey, ancient prophecy, fall and redemption.
world_profiles.world: A vast, detailed secondary world at pre-industrial (medieval or earlier) technology, with distinct kingdoms, forests, mountains, and ancient ruins. Magic is woven into the fabric of the world.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Humans plus elves, dwarves, orcs, goblins, dragons and other mythic races — distinct cultures with long histories, languages, and grudges.
world_profiles.society: Feudal monarchies and rigid class structures; honour, lineage, and oaths are paramount; guilds and ancient orders hold power.
world_profiles.technology: Pre-gunpowder — swords, bows, plate armour, siege engines. Magic rivals or replaces technology; knowledge lives in ancient texts.
world_profiles.mood: Grand, mythic, sweeping — wonder and dread at forces beyond mortal understanding.
world_profiles.examples: The Lord of the Rings, The Wheel of Time

world_profiles.name: Fairy Tale / Folkloric
world_profiles.core_themes: Morality, transformation, cunning over strength, bargains with dangerous powers, the wild vs. the civilised.
world_profiles.world: Rooted in our world but adjacent to a hidden realm — the woods, the Otherworld. Dreamlike and symbolic: forests that move, cottages that come and go.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Humans alongside fairies, witches, talking animals, tricksters, and changelings; characters are often archetypal rather than psychologically complex.
world_profiles.society: Small villages, isolated cottages, fragile royal courts. Outcasts, youngest children, and the clever poor are the usual protagonists.
world_profiles.technology: Pre-industrial — hearths, spinning wheels. The magic is old, natural, and always comes with a price.
world_profiles.mood: Whimsical yet dark; beauty over lurking danger; morally ambiguous, with consequences for every action.

world_profiles.name: Science Fantasy
world_profiles.core_themes: The blurred line between magic and science, the nature of reality, the power of belief, the fall of empires.
world_profiles.world: A universe where 'magic' is a codified science and starships may run on psychic energy; ancient ruins hold power beyond understanding.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Psychic knights, technomancers, mutant creatures, and 'gods' who are really aliens.
world_profiles.society: Often a mix of feudal orders and high-tech guilds atop a fallen empire in a technological dark age; power comes from knowledge and will.
world_profiles.technology: Enchanted blasters, spirit-AIs, runic cyborgs — it works because the story's internal logic says so.
world_profiles.mood: Psychedelic, mind-bending, philosophically provocative; the boundaries of reality are flexible.
world_profiles.examples: Star Wars, Dune, Gideon the Ninth

sections.title: Science Fiction
sections.summary: Fiction extrapolated from science and technology — from the rigorously plausible (hard SF) to the frankly mythic (space opera). It asks 'what if?' about the future, the cosmos, and what technology does to us.

subgenres.name: Hard Science Fiction
subgenres.description: Rigorously plausible science and technology; the speculation obeys known physics as far as possible.
subgenres.examples: Andy Weir's The Martian, Kim Stanley Robinson's Mars trilogy, Greg Egan

subgenres.name: Soft Science Fiction
subgenres.description: Foregrounds the social sciences — psychology, sociology, politics — over hard technical accuracy.
subgenres.examples: Ursula K. Le Guin's The Left Hand of Darkness, Octavia Butler

subgenres.name: Space Opera
subgenres.description: Grand adventure across a galaxy — empires, aliens, FTL travel, interstellar war; scale and romance over rigor.
subgenres.examples: Star Wars, Dune, The Expanse

subgenres.name: Cyberpunk
subgenres.description: 'High tech, low life': near-future dystopias of cybernetics, AI, and corporate control, in noir-soaked neon cities.
subgenres.examples: Neuromancer, Blade Runner, Cyberpunk 2077

subgenres.name: Steampunk
subgenres.description: 19th-century steam technology and Victorian aesthetics in an alternate history of airships and clockwork.
subgenres.examples: The Difference Engine, Gail Carriger's Parasol Protectorate

subgenres.name: Dieselpunk
subgenres.description: Interwar / WW2-era Art Deco meets heavy industry — zeppelins, armoured machines, noir cities on the brink of war.
subgenres.examples: Iron Sky, The Rocketeer

subgenres.name: Solarpunk
subgenres.description: The optimistic counter to cyberpunk: sustainable, community-first futures in harmony with nature.
subgenres.examples: Becky Chambers, A Psalm for the Wild-Built

subgenres.name: Biopunk
subgenres.description: Speculation centred on biotechnology, genetic engineering, and biotech corporations.
subgenres.examples: Paolo Bacigalupi's The Windup Girl, Margaret Atwood's Oryx and Crake

subgenres.name: Military Science Fiction
subgenres.description: War fought with future technology, told from a soldier's or command perspective; tactics and duty at the fore.
subgenres.examples: Starship Troopers, The Forever War, Old Man's War

subgenres.name: Time Travel
subgenres.description: Movement through time as the central device, exploring paradox, causality, and consequence.
subgenres.examples: The Time Machine, 11/22/63, This Is How You Lose the Time War

subgenres.name: Alternate History
subgenres.description: A past that diverged from ours, following the implications into a changed present.
subgenres.examples: The Man in the High Castle, Fatherland

subgenres.name: Apocalyptic / Post-Apocalyptic
subgenres.description: The catastrophe itself, or the struggle of survivors in its aftermath — plague, war, collapse.
subgenres.examples: The Stand, The Road, Station Eleven, Mad Max

subgenres.name: Dystopian / Utopian
subgenres.description: An oppressive (or ideal) society used to critique the present.
subgenres.examples: 1984, The Handmaid's Tale, Brave New World, The Dispossessed

subgenres.name: Climate Fiction (Cli-Fi)
subgenres.description: Stories grappling with climate change and its human consequences, often near-future.
subgenres.examples: The Ministry for the Future, Flight Behavior

subgenres.name: First Contact / Alien Invasion
subgenres.description: Humanity's encounter with extraterrestrial intelligence — as wonder, threat, or both.
subgenres.examples: Arrival / Story of Your Life, The War of the Worlds, Project Hail Mary

subgenres.name: Mundane SF
subgenres.description: Deliberately plausible near-future stories that avoid FTL and other 'impossible' technologies.
subgenres.examples: Gattaca, much of Black Mirror

subgenres.name: Weird / New Weird
subgenres.description: Uncanny, boundary-dissolving fiction blending SF, fantasy, and horror.
subgenres.examples: China Miéville's Perdido Street Station, Jeff VanderMeer's Annihilation

world_profiles.name: Cyberpunk
world_profiles.core_themes: Corporate control, alienation, transhumanism, identity in a digital age, the gap between rich and poor.
world_profiles.world: A near-future dystopia of dark, neon-lit, rain-slicked mega-cities; a decaying physical world beside a sprawling, lawless cyberspace, under corporate arcologies.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Hackers, mercenaries, cybernetically enhanced outcasts, corporate drones, and AI — the line between human and machine blurred.
world_profiles.society: Hyper-capitalist and corrupt; nations are weak and corporations are the real governments; information is currency.
world_profiles.technology: Cybernetics, neural interfaces, AI, VR, genetic engineering — cheap and pervasive, but controlled by the powerful.
world_profiles.mood: Gritty, paranoid, fast — rebellion against an uncaring system, and the question of what it means to be human.

world_profiles.name: Steampunk
world_profiles.core_themes: Science vs. nature, obsession, empire and colonialism, the romance of discovery and invention.
world_profiles.world: An alternate Victorian/Edwardian era of advanced steam technology — smog, brass, gears, and airships filling the sky.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Eccentric inventors, explorers, rogue airship captains, aristocrats, and clockwork automatons.
world_profiles.society: A sharp Victorian class system in tension between tradition and progress; secret societies and criminal underbellies thrive.
world_profiles.technology: Steam-powered everything — difference engines, clockwork prosthetics, airships, diving suits — in brass, copper, and leather.
world_profiles.mood: Gritty but optimistic; adventure and boundless possibility — the future is a machine waiting to be built.

world_profiles.name: Solarpunk
world_profiles.core_themes: Community, sustainability, environmentalism, collective action, harmony with nature, hope amid crisis.
world_profiles.world: A near or far future that has solved (or is solving) climate change: green cities of vertical gardens, solar arrays, and art-nouveau-meets-high-tech architecture.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Organisers, scientists, artisans, and activists — diverse, collaborative, and community-focused.
world_profiles.society: Egalitarian and decentralised; collective decision-making, open knowledge, global solidarity.
world_profiles.technology: Clean renewables, bioluminescence, vertical farming, elegant efficient machines designed to enhance life without harming the environment.
world_profiles.mood: Bright and hopeful — a celebration of colour, nature, and human ingenuity.
world_profiles.examples: A Psalm for the Wild-Built, Becky Chambers

world_profiles.name: Space Opera
world_profiles.core_themes: Good vs. evil, destiny, rebellion, grand romance, the vastness of space, contact with alien species.
world_profiles.world: A galaxy-spanning civilisation of single-biome worlds, empires and federations, ancient conflicts, and FTL travel.
world_profiles.inhabitants: Humans, humanoid aliens, ancient powers, AI and droids — often archetypes: the farm boy, the smuggler, the princess, the dark lord.
world_profiles.society: Grand imperial or republican structures, or feudal systems at galactic scale; rivalries between species and noble houses.
world_profiles.technology: Starships, blasters, energy shields, FTL drives, advanced robotics — often near-magical in effect and aesthetic.
world_profiles.mood: Grand, mythic, thrilling — wonder and scale, adventure across the stars.

sections.title: Horror
sections.summary: Fiction designed to evoke fear, dread, and unease. Subgenres differ mainly in the source of the fear — the supernatural, the mind, the body, the cosmos, or the community.

subgenres.name: Gothic Horror
subgenres.description: Brooding, atmospheric dread built on decay, old houses, family curses, and a romanticised past.
subgenres.examples: Frankenstein, Dracula, Mexican Gothic

subgenres.name: Supernatural / Paranormal Horror
subgenres.description: Ghosts, demons, hauntings, and forces beyond the natural order.
subgenres.examples: The Haunting of Hill House, The Exorcist

subgenres.name: Psychological Horror
subgenres.description: Fear from the mind — paranoia, unreliable perception, guilt, and dread rather than gore.
subgenres.examples: We Need to Talk About Kevin, The Turn of the Screw

subgenres.name: Cosmic Horror
subgenres.description: Existential terror before vast, indifferent, incomprehensible forces that reduce humanity to insignificance.
subgenres.examples: H.P. Lovecraft's The Call of Cthulhu, Annihilation

subgenres.name: Body Horror
subgenres.description: Fear rooted in the violation, mutation, or degeneration of the body.
subgenres.examples: The works of Clive Barker, films of David Cronenberg

subgenres.name: Slasher
subgenres.description: A stalking killer picks off a group one by one; suspense and set-piece kills.
subgenres.examples: Halloween, Scream (as fiction/film tradition)

subgenres.name: Folk Horror
subgenres.description: Dread drawn from isolated communities, old rituals, pagan belief, and the land itself.
subgenres.examples: The Wicker Man, Starve Acre, Harvest Home

subgenres.name: Splatterpunk
subgenres.description: Extreme, graphic, transgressive gore; coined 1986 by David J. Schow.
subgenres.examples: Clive Barker's Books of Blood, Richard Laymon

subgenres.name: Quiet / Literary Horror
subgenres.description: Restrained, ambiguous, slow-building dread that lingers rather than shocks.
subgenres.examples: Shirley Jackson, The Fisherman by John Langan

subgenres.name: Occult / Demonic
subgenres.description: Rituals, possession, cults, and pacts with dark powers.
subgenres.examples: Rosemary's Baby, The Exorcist

subgenres.name: Monster Horror
subgenres.description: A central creature — vampire, werewolf, kaiju, or the wholly new — as the engine of fear.
subgenres.examples: Dracula, The Terror, classic creature features

subgenres.name: Comedy Horror
subgenres.description: Fear braided with laughter; parody, satire, or gleeful excess.
subgenres.examples: Good Omens (adjacent), Shaun of the Dead, John Dies at the End

sections.title: Mystery & Crime
sections.summary: Fiction built around a crime and its investigation. Mystery emphasises the puzzle and the reveal; crime fiction ranges from the cosy to the pitch-black, defined by tone, sleuth, and how much the darkness is allowed to show.

subgenres.name: Cosy Mystery
subgenres.description: Low on violence, high on puzzle; a small, charming community and an amateur sleuth, with a light tone.
subgenres.examples: Agatha Christie's Miss Marple, Richard Osman's Thursday Murder Club

subgenres.name: Whodunit / Traditional Mystery
subgenres.description: The classic fair-play puzzle: clues, suspects, and a reveal the reader could in principle have solved.
subgenres.examples: Agatha Christie's Poirot, Knives Out

subgenres.name: Detective / Private Eye
subgenres.description: A professional or amateur investigator works a case through deduction and legwork.
subgenres.examples: Sherlock Holmes, Cormoran Strike

subgenres.name: Hardboiled
subgenres.description: Gritty, realistic crime with a tough, cynical detective in a morally ambiguous urban world.
subgenres.examples: Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe, Dashiell Hammett

subgenres.name: Noir
subgenres.description: Hardboiled taken darker: a corrupt system and a doomed protagonist on the margins, clinging to a personal code.
subgenres.examples: James M. Cain, Jim Thompson

subgenres.name: Police Procedural
subgenres.description: The process is the point — evidence, chain of custody, and the slow, documented build of a case by law enforcement.
subgenres.examples: Ed McBain's 87th Precinct, The Wire

subgenres.name: Legal Mystery / Courtroom
subgenres.description: Lawyers prove their cases; the justice system itself is almost a character.
subgenres.examples: Scott Turow's Presumed Innocent, Erle Stanley Gardner's Perry Mason

subgenres.name: Domestic Suspense
subgenres.description: Menace inside the home and marriage; unreliable narrators and buried secrets.
subgenres.examples: Gone Girl, The Girl on the Train

subgenres.name: Caper / Heist
subgenres.description: A crime planned and pulled off from the criminals' side, often with wit and ensemble flair.
subgenres.examples: The Lies of Locke Lamora, Ocean's Eleven (tradition)

subgenres.name: Historical Mystery
subgenres.description: A crime investigated in a richly reconstructed past.
subgenres.examples: The Name of the Rose, C.J. Sansom's Shardlake

subgenres.name: Locked-Room / Impossible Crime
subgenres.description: A crime that seems physically impossible, solved by revealing the trick.
subgenres.examples: The Hollow Man (John Dickson Carr), The Decagon House Murders

sections.title: Thriller & Suspense
sections.summary: Fiction driven by danger and momentum. Where mystery asks 'who did it?', the thriller asks 'will they survive / stop it in time?' — the protagonist is usually trying to prevent a catastrophe or save their own life.

subgenres.name: Psychological Thriller
subgenres.description: Suspense from unstable minds, manipulation, and shifting perception.
subgenres.examples: The Silence of the Lambs, Before I Go to Sleep

subgenres.name: Spy / Espionage
subgenres.description: Intelligence work, betrayal, and geopolitics; from gritty tradecraft to glamorous action.
subgenres.examples: John le Carré's Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, the James Bond novels

subgenres.name: Political Thriller
subgenres.description: Power, conspiracy, and intrigue at the level of governments and institutions.
subgenres.examples: The Manchurian Candidate, House of Cards

subgenres.name: Techno-Thriller
subgenres.description: Detailed, plausible technology and hardware at the centre of a high-stakes plot.
subgenres.examples: Tom Clancy's The Hunt for Red October, Michael Crichton

subgenres.name: Legal Thriller
subgenres.description: Suspense inside the machinery of justice; lawyers racing an unravelling case.
subgenres.examples: John Grisham's The Firm, A Time to Kill

subgenres.name: Action / Adventure Thriller
subgenres.description: Relentless pace, physical peril, and a capable protagonist against overwhelming odds.
subgenres.examples: Lee Child's Jack Reacher, The Bourne Identity

subgenres.name: Medical Thriller
subgenres.description: Danger from disease, medicine, or the healthcare system.
subgenres.examples: Robin Cook's Coma, Michael Crichton's The Andromeda Strain

subgenres.name: Conspiracy Thriller
subgenres.description: A hidden network or cover-up the protagonist must expose before it silences them.
subgenres.examples: The Da Vinci Code, Three Days of the Condor

subgenres.name: Military Thriller
subgenres.description: Combat and command under modern or near-future conditions; strategy and sacrifice.
subgenres.examples: Tom Clancy, Mark Greaney's Gray Man

subgenres.name: Domestic Thriller
subgenres.description: High-stakes suspense inside family and relationships; overlaps domestic suspense.
subgenres.examples: The Woman in the Window, Behind Closed Doors

sections.title: Romance
sections.summary: Fiction with a central love story and an emotionally satisfying, optimistic ending (the genre's 'HEA' — happily-ever-after — or 'HFN', happy-for-now). The largest-selling fiction category, defined more by that emotional promise than by setting.

subgenres.name: Contemporary Romance
subgenres.description: The largest subgenre — love stories set in the present, reflecting current mores.
subgenres.examples: Emily Henry, Christina Lauren

subgenres.name: Historical Romance
subgenres.description: Romance set in the past (often pre-1945), grounded in period detail — Regency, Victorian, and beyond.
subgenres.examples: Georgette Heyer, Julia Quinn's Bridgerton

subgenres.name: Romantasy
subgenres.description: Fantasy world-building and romance carrying equal weight, with a guaranteed emotional payoff — a booming crossover.
subgenres.examples: Sarah J. Maas, Rebecca Yarros's Fourth Wing

subgenres.name: Romantic Suspense
subgenres.description: A central love story braided with mystery, danger, or a threat to be solved.
subgenres.examples: Nora Roberts, Sandra Brown

subgenres.name: Paranormal Romance
subgenres.description: Supernatural love interests — vampires, shifters, the fae — and magical stakes.
subgenres.examples: Twilight, J.R. Ward's Black Dagger Brotherhood

subgenres.name: Erotic Romance
subgenres.description: Explicit intimacy central to the emotional arc, not merely incidental.
subgenres.examples: Sylvia Day, much of the 'spicy' contemporary market

subgenres.name: Small-Town / Cosy Romance
subgenres.description: Low-heat, community-centred love stories in close-knit places.
subgenres.examples: Debbie Macomber, Virgin River

subgenres.name: Sports Romance
subgenres.description: Athlete protagonists and the competitive world of sport as the backdrop for love.
subgenres.examples: Elle Kennedy's Off-Campus, Ali Hazelwood (adjacent)

subgenres.name: LGBTQ+ / Queer Romance
subgenres.description: Love stories centring queer protagonists across every heat level and setting.
subgenres.examples: Red, White & Royal Blue, Alexis Hall

subgenres.name: Inspirational / Clean Romance
subgenres.description: Low- or no-heat romance, often with faith or wholesome values foregrounded.
subgenres.examples: Christian romance imprints, many 'sweet' lines

subgenres.name: Dark Romance
subgenres.description: Morally grey love interests and taboo, high-tension dynamics; comfort is not the point.
subgenres.examples: Much of the contemporary 'dark' market

sections.title: Historical Fiction
sections.summary: Fiction set in a real past, reconstructing its customs, speech, and events with enough fidelity that the period feels lived-in. It cross-pollinates freely with romance, mystery, and fantasy.

subgenres.name: Traditional Historical Fiction
subgenres.description: A fictional story faithfully set in a documented period, event, or milieu.
subgenres.examples: Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall, Ken Follett's The Pillars of the Earth

subgenres.name: Family Saga
subgenres.description: Multiple generations of a family across a sweep of historical time.
subgenres.examples: Roots, Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits

subgenres.name: Biographical Fiction
subgenres.description: A real historical figure's life dramatised as narrative.
subgenres.examples: The Paris Wife, Wolf Hall (Cromwell)

subgenres.name: Wartime Fiction
subgenres.description: Lives shaped by a specific conflict, at the front or the home front.
subgenres.examples: All Quiet on the Western Front, The Nightingale, All the Light We Cannot See

subgenres.name: Nautical / Historical Adventure
subgenres.description: Seafaring and exploration in a historical age of sail or discovery.
subgenres.examples: Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey–Maturin, Hornblower

subgenres.name: Historical Romance / Mystery
subgenres.description: Historical settings foregrounding a love story or a crime — see also those genres.
subgenres.examples: Bridgerton (romance), The Name of the Rose (mystery)

subgenres.name: Alternate History
subgenres.description: A documented past diverged; explores the consequences (overlaps SF).
subgenres.examples: The Man in the High Castle, Fatherland

sections.title: Literary, Upmarket & Realistic
sections.summary: Fiction prizing language, character interiority, theme, and artistic ambition, usually set in a recognisable real world. 'Upmarket' sits between literary and commercial — book-club fiction with strong prose and a propulsive story.

subgenres.name: Literary Fiction
subgenres.description: Character- and theme-driven work emphasising style, ambiguity, and artistic merit over plot mechanics.
subgenres.examples: Toni Morrison, Kazuo Ishiguro, Marilynne Robinson

subgenres.name: Upmarket / Book-Club Fiction
subgenres.description: Elevated prose and depth married to an accessible, discussable story.
subgenres.examples: Celeste Ng, Ann Patchett, Tayari Jones

subgenres.name: Bildungsroman
subgenres.description: A coming-of-age story tracing a protagonist's psychological and moral growth.
subgenres.examples: Great Expectations, The Catcher in the Rye, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

subgenres.name: Satire
subgenres.description: Uses irony, exaggeration, and ridicule to critique society, politics, or human folly.
subgenres.examples: Catch-22, Animal Farm, A Modest Proposal (tradition)

subgenres.name: Metafiction
subgenres.description: Fiction that foregrounds its own artifice and the act of storytelling.
subgenres.examples: If on a winter's night a traveler, Slaughterhouse-Five

subgenres.name: Autofiction
subgenres.description: Autobiography reshaped as novel, blurring author and narrator.
subgenres.examples: Karl Ove Knausgård's My Struggle, Rachel Cusk

subgenres.name: Domestic / Women's Fiction
subgenres.description: The inner and relational lives of (often women) protagonists; family, identity, and change.
subgenres.examples: Jodi Picoult, Liane Moriarty

subgenres.name: Contemporary Realism
subgenres.description: Present-day, plausible lives with no speculative element; the texture of ordinary experience.
subgenres.examples: Sally Rooney, Jonathan Franzen

subgenres.name: Absurdist / Existential
subgenres.description: Meaning, alienation, and the irrational at the centre.
subgenres.examples: The Stranger, Waiting for Godot (tradition)

sections.title: Western, Adventure & Action
sections.summary: Fiction of frontier, exploration, and physical peril. The Western is a genre of place and myth (the American frontier); adventure and action share its appetite for movement, danger, and capable protagonists tested against the world.

subgenres.name: Classic Western
subgenres.description: Frontier justice, cowboys, outlaws, and the myth of the American West.
subgenres.examples: Louis L'Amour, Lonesome Dove (adjacent), Zane Grey

subgenres.name: Revisionist Western
subgenres.description: Interrogates the myth — moral ambiguity, the cost of violence, the perspectives it erased.
subgenres.examples: Blood Meridian, Unforgiven (tradition), Deadwood

subgenres.name: Weird West
subgenres.description: The Western fused with horror, fantasy, or the supernatural.
subgenres.examples: The Six-Gun Tarot, Territory

subgenres.name: Space Western
subgenres.description: Frontier tropes transposed to space — see also science fiction.
subgenres.examples: Firefly, The Mandalorian, Cowboy Bebop

subgenres.name: Adventure
subgenres.description: A quest or journey through danger and the unknown, driven by momentum and discovery.
subgenres.examples: Treasure Island, King Solomon's Mines, Indiana Jones (tradition)

subgenres.name: Survival
subgenres.description: A protagonist against a hostile environment, fighting to stay alive.
subgenres.examples: Robinson Crusoe, Hatchet, The Revenant

subgenres.name: Swashbuckler
subgenres.description: Dashing heroism, sword-play, and derring-do, often historical.
subgenres.examples: The Three Musketeers, The Princess Bride

subgenres.name: Lost World / Pulp Adventure
subgenres.description: Expeditions into hidden lands, ruins, or prehistoric enclaves.
subgenres.examples: The Lost World, Journey to the Center of the Earth

sections.title: Comedy, Satire & Humor
sections.summary: Fiction whose primary aim is to amuse — through wit, absurdity, exaggeration, or the puncturing of pretension. Comedy is often a mode layered onto other genres (comic fantasy, romantic comedy) as much as a category of its own.

subgenres.name: Satire
subgenres.description: Ridicule aimed at society, politics, or institutions to expose folly or vice.
subgenres.examples: Catch-22, Dr. Strangelove (tradition), Thank You for Smoking

subgenres.name: Parody
subgenres.description: Comic imitation that exaggerates the conventions of a work or genre.
subgenres.examples: Bored of the Rings, Galaxy Quest (tradition)

subgenres.name: Comic Fantasy
subgenres.description: Fantasy played for laughs, gently mocking the genre's own tropes.
subgenres.examples: Terry Pratchett's Discworld, Good Omens

subgenres.name: Romantic Comedy
subgenres.description: A love story foregrounding humour, banter, and comic misadventure.
subgenres.examples: Bridget Jones's Diary, Beach Read

subgenres.name: Black Comedy
subgenres.description: Humour drawn from grim, taboo, or tragic subject matter.
subgenres.examples: Catch-22, A Confederacy of Dunces

subgenres.name: Farce
subgenres.description: Improbable situations, mistaken identities, and escalating chaos.
subgenres.examples: The plays of Feydeau, Fawlty Towers (tradition)

subgenres.name: Picaresque
subgenres.description: Episodic misadventures of a roguish, low-born hero navigating a corrupt world.
subgenres.examples: Don Quixote, The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

sections.title: Age Categories (Cross-Genre)
sections.summary: Not genres but audience categories that cut across every genre, defined by the protagonist's age, content, complexity, and reader expectation. A fantasy can be middle-grade or adult; the category shapes voice, length, and theme.

subgenres.name: Picture Books & Early Readers
subgenres.description: For the youngest readers; illustration-led, simple language, gentle stakes.
subgenres.examples: Where the Wild Things Are, Elephant & Piggie

subgenres.name: Middle Grade (MG)
subgenres.description: Roughly ages 8–12; protagonists around 10–13, adventurous and hopeful, minimal graphic content.
subgenres.examples: Percy Jackson, Harry Potter (early), Holes

subgenres.name: Young Adult (YA)
subgenres.description: Roughly ages 12–18; teen protagonists, first experiences, identity and agency at the core.
subgenres.examples: The Hunger Games, The Fault in Our Stars, Six of Crows

subgenres.name: New Adult (NA)
subgenres.description: Late teens to twenties; college, early independence, often higher heat than YA.
subgenres.examples: Much of the contemporary romance crossover market

subgenres.name: Adult
subgenres.description: No age ceiling on content or complexity; the default for most genres above.
subgenres.examples: The bulk of the fiction market

sections.title: Hybrid & Emerging Genres
sections.summary: The most memorable worlds blend and subvert categories. These crossbreeds and newer labels sit deliberately across borders.

subgenres.name: Science Fantasy
subgenres.description: Combines SF and fantasy tropes — mystical elements given a scientific gloss, or the reverse.
subgenres.examples: Star Wars, Dune, Gideon the Ninth

subgenres.name: Space Western
subgenres.description: Science fiction fused with the Western.
subgenres.examples: Firefly, The Mandalorian

subgenres.name: Gaslamp / Neo-Victorian Fantasy
subgenres.description: A magical, gaslit 19th century of vampires, fae, and Victorian intertextuality; cousin to steampunk.
subgenres.examples: Gail Carriger, Erin Morgenstern's The Night Circus

subgenres.name: Speculative Evolution
subgenres.description: Hypothetical future or alternative evolution of life.
subgenres.examples: After Man: A Zoology of the Future

subgenres.name: Supernatural Fiction
subgenres.description: Plot devices that contradict a materialist worldview; overlaps paranormal, contemporary fantasy, and occult detective.
subgenres.examples: Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Stranger Things, The Vampire Diaries

subgenres.name: Slipstream
subgenres.description: Fiction between the literary and the fantastic that produces cognitive dissonance and strangeness.
subgenres.examples: The work of Kelly Link, Haruki Murakami (adjacent)

editor_notes.meaning: Stated emotion instead of experienced emotion
editor_notes.fix: Replace with action, body language, sensory detail

editor_notes.meaning: Multiple characters' thoughts in one scene without structural break
editor_notes.fix: One POV per scene; use chapter/section breaks to switch
Map scene-by-scene; each needs a mini-arc of tension and release

editor_notes.meaning: First page doesn't hook reader into a character + problem
editor_notes.fix: Start in media res; establish stakes by page 3

editor_notes.meaning: Blocks of background/history interrupt story momentum
editor_notes.fix: Distribute via action, dialogue, and sensory detail

editor_notes.meaning: Sentences weak because actor is buried or absent
editor_notes.fix: Audit every 'was/were + verb' construction; make actor the subject

editor_notes.meaning: Description so ornate it becomes the focus rather than serving story
editor_notes.fix: Cut to the most specific, surprising single detail; remove the rest

editor_notes.meaning: Characters say what they mean; no subtext or conflict
editor_notes.fix: Find what each character is NOT saying; build the scene around that absence

editor_notes.meaning: Reader told to feel something before story has made them care
editor_notes.fix: Establish character attachment before the emotional climax

editor_notes.meaning: Villain exists only to be defeated; has no interiority
editor_notes.fix: Give antagonist a coherent worldview and motivation the reader can understand

editor_notes.meaning: Protagonist saved by luck or coincidence, not their own choice
editor_notes.fix: Ensure protagonist's decision, skill, or change causes the resolution
Write a character bible: vocabulary, speech patterns, 5 forbidden words

editor_notes.meaning: Action scenes so detailed they slow momentum
editor_notes.fix: Shorten sentences in action; cut to essential beats; trust the reader

editor_notes.meaning: Scenes end in same state they began; nothing changed
editor_notes.fix: Every scene should end with something won, lost, or revealed

editor_notes.meaning: Chapter begins with weather, alarm clocks, waking up, or backstory
editor_notes.fix: Open with a character in motion, in conflict, or at a decision point

show_dont_tell.description: Conveying emotion, character, and situation through action, sensory detail, and dialogue rather than direct statement.

entries.principle: Show anger through body and behaviour, not label
entries.bad: She was angry.
entries.good: She slammed the door so hard the frame shuddered. In the kitchen she stood over the sink, gripping the counter with both hands, breathing through her nose.
entries.note: The reader infers the emotion; the writer doesn't need to name it.

entries.principle: Show stinginess through action, not character summary
entries.bad: He was a stingy, anxious man who worried constantly about money.
entries.good: He counted his change three times, checked the price on the menu again, and left the smallest possible tip.
entries.note: Three specific observations tell us everything about the character without editorialising.

entries.principle: Show wrongness through absence of the expected
entries.bad: He knew something was wrong the moment he walked in.
entries.good: He knew something was wrong the moment he walked in. The TV was off. Elena always had the TV on.
entries.note: The 'wrong' detail is more powerful than any adjective.

entries.principle: Show nervousness through body language, not filter words
entries.bad: She felt nervous as she waited for the interview.
entries.good: She'd read the poster on the waiting room wall four times. The same poster. She straightened her skirt. Read the poster again.
entries.note: Compulsive, repetitive behaviour shows nervousness more vividly than any adverb.

entries.principle: Show grief through observed physical detail
entries.bad: Tom was devastated by the news.
entries.good: Tom sat down. Not on the chair — just on the floor, right there in the hallway, still in his coat.
entries.note: The involuntary, slightly absurd physicality of grief is more affecting than the label.

entries.principle: Montrer la colère par le comportement, pas par étiquette
entries.bad: Elle était en colère.
entries.good: Elle posa la tasse avec une violence calculée. Le café déborda sur la nappe blanche. Elle ne dit rien.
entries.gloss_en: She placed the cup with calculated violence. The coffee spilled onto the white tablecloth. She said nothing.
entries.note_fr: L'acte révèle la maîtrise de soi brisée et une colère froide — bien plus menaçant que le simple label.
entries.note_en: The act reveals barely controlled rage — far more threatening than naming the emotion.

entries.principle: Montrer l'anxiété sans filtre narratif
entries.bad: Elle se sentait anxieuse en attendant.
entries.good: Elle avait relu le même paragraphe six fois. Les mots glissaient. Le tic-tac de l'horloge envahissait tout.
entries.gloss_en: She had read the same paragraph six times. The words slipped away. The ticking of the clock took over everything.
entries.note_fr: Supprimer le verbe-filtre 'se sentir' et remplacer par des détails sensoriels spécifiques.

entries.principle: Mostrare la tristezza attraverso il dettaglio fisico
entries.bad: Era triste. Pensava spesso a lei.
entries.good: Trovò il suo maglione in fondo all'armadio. Lo tenne tra le mani per qualche minuto, poi lo rimise esattamente dov'era.
entries.gloss_en: He found her sweater at the back of the wardrobe. He held it in his hands for a few minutes, then put it back exactly where it was.
entries.note_it: L'azione concreta — trovare, tenere, rimettere com'era — mostra il lutto più di ogni aggettivo.
entries.note_en: The concrete action — finding, holding, putting back exactly as found — shows grief more powerfully than any adjective.

entries.principle: Descrizioni che passano dall'emotività del personaggio
entries.bad: Il luogo era inquietante e misterioso.
entries.good: Le scale scricchiolavano a ogni passo, ma solo lui sembrava sentirle. Gli altri continuavano a parlare.
entries.gloss_en: The stairs creaked with every step, but only he seemed to hear them. The others kept talking.
entries.note_it: La descrizione passa attraverso la percezione selettiva del personaggio, rivelando il suo stato interiore.
entries.source: Principle: 'Le descrizioni devono passare dall'emotività e dal punto di vista del narratore.' — scritturacreativa.org

entries.principle: Mostrar miedo a través del cuerpo, no de la etiqueta
entries.bad: Tenía miedo.
entries.good: No podía abrir la mano. Llevaba diez minutos intentándolo. Los dedos no obedecían.
entries.gloss_en: He couldn't open his hand. He'd been trying for ten minutes. His fingers wouldn't obey.
entries.note_es: La pérdida de control corporal muestra el miedo de forma visceral.
entries.note_en: Loss of bodily control shows fear viscerally without naming it.

entries.principle: Mostrar la tensión entre personajes sin decirla
entries.bad: Entre ellos había mucha tensión desde el incidente.
entries.good: Le pasó la sal sin mirarlo. Él la cogió sin darle las gracias. Ninguno de los dos habló durante el resto de la cena.
entries.gloss_en: She passed him the salt without looking at him. He took it without thanking her. Neither spoke for the rest of the dinner.
entries.note_es: Los pequeños gestos cotidianos cargados de omisión revelan la ruptura más que cualquier resumen.

entries.principle: Mostrar raiva através de ação, não de rótulo
entries.bad: Ela estava com raiva.
entries.good: Ela fechou o punho com força, os olhos duros mirando o chão.
entries.gloss_en: She clenched her fist, her eyes hard, fixed on the floor.
entries.note_pt: Exemplo canônico no ambiente brasileiro de escrita criativa para ilustrar 'mostrar, não contar.'
entries.source: Widely used example in Brazilian craft communities; cited at tomaaiumpoema.com.br

entries.principle: Mostrar vergonha através de comportamento
entries.bad: Ele se sentiu envergonhado quando ela entrou.
entries.good: Ele abaixou os olhos para a xícara. A mexeu. Voltou a mexer. A xícara estava vazia.
entries.gloss_en: He lowered his eyes to the cup. Stirred it. Stirred it again. The cup was empty.
entries.note_pt: A ação compulsiva e sem objeto revela o estado interior sem nomeá-lo.

entries.principle: Gestalta känslor — inte berätta dem
entries.bad: Hon var ledsen.
entries.good: Hon lade ner sin gaffel utan att ha ätit. Tittade ut genom fönstret. Ingen pratade.
entries.gloss_en: She put down her fork without having eaten. Looked out the window. No one spoke.
entries.note_sv: Gestaltning snarare än berättande — specifika handlingar låter läsaren dra egna slutsatser.
entries.note_en: Dramatising rather than narrating — specific actions let the reader draw their own conclusions.
entries.source: Craft principle 'gestaltning vs. berättande' widely used in Swedish writing pedagogy; SkrivarSidan.nu

entries.principle: Toon emotie door gedrag, niet door label
entries.bad: Ze was verdrietig.
entries.good: Ze had haar jas nog aan. Ging zitten aan de keukentafel. Stond weer op. Zette water op. Vergat er thee bij te doen.
entries.gloss_en: She still had her coat on. Sat down at the kitchen table. Stood up again. Put the kettle on. Forgot to add tea.
entries.note_nl: De opeenstapeling van kleine, doelloze handelingen toont de emotionele verlamming.
entries.note_en: The accumulation of small, purposeless actions shows emotional paralysis.

entries.principle: Pokaż uczucia przez działanie, nie przez opis
entries.bad: Była smutna i tęskniła za nim.
entries.good: Wyciągnęła jego sweter z szafy. Przytrzymała chwilę. Złożyła z powrotem.
entries.gloss_en: She took his sweater from the wardrobe. Held it for a moment. Folded it back up.
entries.note_pl: Proste, konkretne działanie mówi więcej niż każdy opis emocji.
entries.note_en: A simple, concrete action says more than any emotional description.

purple_prose.description: Prose so ornate that the language draws attention to itself rather than serving the story.

entries.principle: Describe a mysterious stranger — precision over accumulation
entries.bad: The tall, brooding, mysterious stranger walked solemnly and silently across the desolate, fog-laced, moonlit street, his dark eyes burning with unspoken secrets and shadowed pain.
entries.good: The stranger drifted down the fog-laced street, quiet and unreadable.
entries.source: Becca Puglisi, Writers Helping Writers (writershelpingwriters.net)

entries.principle: Describe eyes — the 'glistening orbs' classic
entries.bad: Her eyes were glistening orbs of emerald green, shimmering with unshed tears like twin pools reflecting the sorrowful moonlight of her tumultuous soul.
entries.good: Her eyes were green. They caught light when she was angry, which was often.
entries.note: Two lean sentences do more work: appearance AND character.

entries.principle: Describing a sunset — serve the scene, not the thesaurus
entries.bad: The magnificent, resplendent, golden orb of fire descended majestically behind the undulating, violet-tinged mountains, casting its last, trembling, amber light across the shimmering, mirror-like surface of the serene, pellucid lake.
entries.good: The sun dropped behind the mountains. The lake went orange, then grey.
entries.note: Two clean sentences create mood more effectively than ten ornate ones.

entries.principle: Trust the reader to feel without being told what to feel
entries.bad: It was an impossibly sad, heart-wrenching, deeply moving, profoundly affecting moment that made every reader's heart ache with unbearable sorrow.
entries.good: He stood at her grave a long time. Then he drove home and couldn't remember the route he'd taken.
entries.note: The specific detail (forgetting the route) creates the feeling; the ornate version only asserts it.

entries.principle: Décrire la nuit sans surcharge d'adjectifs
entries.bad: La nuit était sombre, profonde, mystérieuse et impénétrable, enveloppant tout dans son manteau de ténèbres opaques et inquiétantes.
entries.good: La nuit avait effacé les couleurs. Il ne restait que les formes.
entries.gloss_en: Night had erased the colours. Only shapes remained.
entries.note_fr: Un seul verbe fort ('effacé') et une observation précise remplacent quatre adjectifs empilés.
entries.note_en: One strong verb ('erased') and one precise observation replace four stacked adjectives.

entries.principle: Evitare metafore stantie e cliché
entries.bad: Aveva gli occhi azzurri come il mare e i capelli giallo grano. Era bella come una dea.
entries.good: Aveva una faccia che faceva dimenticare quello che stavi dicendo.
entries.gloss_en: She had a face that made you forget what you were saying.
entries.note_it: Usare pensiero riciclato di un'altra persona significa non comunicare realmente. — scritturacreativa.org
entries.note_en: Using someone else's recycled thought means not really communicating at all.

entries.principle: Describir el amor sin grandilocuencia
entries.bad: La amaba con una pasión ardiente, inefable y desbordante que llenaba cada fibra de su ser con una intensidad que trascendía toda comprensión humana.
entries.good: La amaba. No tenía otra manera de explicarlo que aún no sonase a mentira.
entries.gloss_en: He loved her. He had no other way to explain it that didn't yet sound like a lie.
entries.note_es: La honestidad del narrador sobre la limitación del lenguaje es más potente que la hipérbole.

entries.principle: Adjektivsjukan — adjektivöverdrift
entries.bad: Den mörka, hotfulla, mystiska natten bredde ut sina svarta, ogenomträngliga vingar över den öde, karga, isande landsbygden.
entries.good: Det var den typen av natt som fick folk att låsa sina dörrar utan att riktigt veta varför.
entries.gloss_en: It was the kind of night that made people lock their doors without quite knowing why.
entries.note_sv: Effekten (beteende) är starkare än anhopningen av adjektiv.
entries.note_en: The effect (behaviour) is stronger than the pile-up of adjectives.
entries.source_term: Adjektivsjukan — 'adjective sickness' — a named concept in Swedish writing pedagogy

entries.principle: Wolligheid — overdreven bloemrijke taal
entries.bad: De avond daalde neer met al haar purperen pracht en glorie over de eindeloze, majestueuze vlakten van het slapende land.
entries.good: De avond viel. Ergens blaftte een hond.
entries.gloss_en: Evening fell. Somewhere a dog barked.
entries.note_nl: Het onverwachte, concrete geluid verankert de scène beter dan tien sierende bijvoeglijke naamwoorden.
entries.note_en: The unexpected, concrete sound anchors the scene better than ten decorative adjectives.

dialogue.description: Craft of written conversation — subtext, tags, rhythm, naturalness.

entries.principle: Dialogue that does double duty: character + tension
entries.bad: 'I have not forgiven you for leaving me,' Marcus said. 'I know. I feel terrible about it,' Elena replied. 'I still love you though,' Marcus admitted. 'I love you too,' Elena confessed.
entries.good:
'You look tired,' Paul said.
'I'm fine.'
'You've been saying that for three weeks.'
She looked out the window. 'I said I'm fine, Paul.'
entries.note: The good version contains: plot signal (something is wrong), character (she deflects, he notices), conflict (tension), and subtext (she is absolutely not fine).

entries.principle: Dialogue tags — action beats replace tags
entries.bad: 'Get out,' she exclaimed angrily. 'You don't mean that,' he pleaded desperately. 'Get out,' she reiterated furiously.
entries.good:
'Get out.' She pointed at the door.
'You don't mean that.'
'Get. Out.'
entries.note: The action beat and the broken-up sentence 'Get. Out.' carry the emotional weight without any adverb.

entries.principle: Voice differentiation in dialogue
entries.bad: 'We lost people,' said Marcus. 'Yes, we did,' said Elena.
entries.good:
Character A (soldier): 'Casualty count's low. Sector secure. We move at dawn.'
Character B (poet): 'Seventeen men. I keep counting. As though the number might change if I do it one more time.'
entries.note: Each character's vocabulary, rhythm, and focus should be unmistakably theirs.

entries.principle: Le dialogue doit faire avancer l'action, pas juste informer
entries.bad:
— Bonjour, Pierre. Je suis venu te parler de notre projet, comme tu le sais. Nous avons discuté de cela la semaine dernière.
— Oui, je me souviens très bien de cette conversation.
entries.good:
— Tu n'as pas l'air en forme.
— J'ai dormi.
— Combien d'heures?
— Assez.
Il n'insista pas. Mais il nota l'heure.
entries.gloss_en: 'You don't look well.' / 'I slept.' / 'How many hours?' / 'Enough.' He didn't push. But he noted the time.
entries.note_fr: Le silence, l'esquive et l'observation finale font plus de travail que toute exposition directe.
entries.source: Principle from jesuisauteur.com and concours-ecriture.com craft resources

entries.principle: Evitare l'uso eccessivo del punto esclamativo nei dialoghi
entries.bad: — Non ci posso credere! Sei pazzo! Come hai osato!
entries.good: — Non ci posso credere. — Si alzò, girandogli le spalle. — Non voglio sentirti.
entries.gloss_en: 'I can't believe it.' She stood up, turning her back on him. 'I don't want to hear you.'
entries.note_it: Un romanzo dovrebbe assomigliare alla vita reale. L'uso eccessivo del punto esclamativo dà un sapore adolescenziale alla narrazione. — chiarasolerio.it
entries.note_en: A novel should resemble real life. Excessive exclamation marks give the narrative an adolescent flavour.

entries.principle: El guión largo (raya) para el diálogo — uso correcto
entries.bad: "Estás bien?" preguntó María. "Sí, estoy bien", respondió Carlos. "No parece", dijo ella.
entries.good:
—¿Estás bien? —preguntó María.
—Sí —dijo él, sin mirarla.
—No parece.
entries.gloss_en: 'Are you all right?' asked María. / 'Yes,' he said, without looking at her. / 'Doesn't seem like it.'
entries.note_es: En español la raya (—) es la forma estándar para introducir diálogos en ficción literaria, no las comillas.
entries.note_en: In Spanish, the em-dash (—) is the standard for dialogue in literary fiction, not quotation marks.

entries.principle: Travessão no diálogo — pontuação correta
entries.bad: — Eu sei o que você está pensando. — Disse o menino.
entries.good: — Eu sei o que você está pensando — disse o menino.
entries.gloss_en: 'I know what you're thinking,' said the boy.
entries.note_pt: Não vai ponto final após a fala e nem letra maiúscula após o travessão do inciso. Erro muito comum em primeiros manuscritos. — viltoreis.com
entries.note_en: No full stop after the speech and no capital letter after the attribution dash. A very common error in first manuscripts.

entries.principle: Diálogo deve envolver ação e interação
entries.bad:
— Você está com fome? — perguntou ele.
— Sim — disse ela.
— Quer comer alguma coisa? — perguntou ele.
— Sim — disse ela.
entries.good:
— Você está com fome?
Ela olhou para a janela. A chuva tinha parado. — Estava.
— Tem sobras na geladeira.
Ela não respondeu.
entries.gloss_en: 'Are you hungry?' She looked out the window. The rain had stopped. 'I was.' 'There are leftovers in the fridge.' She didn't reply.
entries.note_pt: O erro mais comum: diálogos acontecem num espaço em branco, sem ação, ambiente, pensamento ou subtexto. — claudialemes.com.br

entries.principle: Trovärdig, spänstigt dialog — undvik stel exposition
entries.bad:
— Som du vet, Lars, har vi arbetat tillsammans i tio år på det här projektet som vi påbörjade år 2014.
— Ja, det stämmer precis.
entries.good:
— Du vet inte vad du håller på med.
— Nej. — Han tittade på sina händer. — Men jag vet vad det kostar om jag slutar.
entries.gloss_en: 'You don't know what you're doing.' 'No.' He looked at his hands. 'But I know what it costs if I stop.'
entries.note_sv: Spänst och underlighet håller läsaren engagerad. Undvik det som kallas 'maid-and-butler dialogue' — när karaktärerna berättar saker de redan vet.
entries.note_en: Tension and obliqueness keep the reader engaged. Avoid 'maid-and-butler dialogue' — when characters tell each other things they already know.

entries.principle: Informatie via dialoog, nooit dubbelop
entries.bad: De verteller legde uit dat de stad al twintig jaar in verval was geraakt. Later in de scène zei Karel: 'Je weet dat de stad al twintig jaar in verval is.'
entries.good:
'Wanneer is het misgegaan?' vroeg ze.
Karel keek om zich heen. 'Vraag het aan de gebouwen.'
entries.gloss_en: 'When did it go wrong?' she asked. Karel looked around. 'Ask the buildings.'
entries.note_nl: Vertel nooit iets dubbelop. Als uitleg via dialoog beschikbaar is, heeft dat altijd de voorkeur boven vertellersuitleg. — schrijvenonline.org
entries.note_en: Never repeat information. If explanation is available via dialogue, it always takes priority over narrator explanation.

pov_head_hopping.description: Maintaining a consistent perspective within scenes; the errors and fixes.

entries.principle: Head-hopping within a single scene
entries.bad: John watched her cross the room, wondering what she was hiding. She was nervous, Mira thought, and hoped he couldn't tell. John wondered what she was hiding. Mira felt exposed under his gaze.
entries.good:
John watched her cross the room, trying to read something in her posture. She moved like someone bracing for impact.

[Scene break]

Mira had felt his eyes on her from the moment she walked in. She kept her shoulders back, the way her mother had taught her.
entries.note: Two POV characters, two scenes — clean and clear. Head-hopping makes readers dizzy and distances them from both characters.

entries.principle: The first-person narrator cannot describe their own face
entries.bad: I walked to the mirror and stared at my large brown eyes, my sharp cheekbones, and my full lips.
entries.good: I'd been told I had my mother's cheekbones, though I couldn't quite see it. I mostly saw the bags under my eyes.
entries.note: Characters don't observe themselves the way an external camera would. First-person self-description via others' observations, or partial/reluctant observation, is more authentic.

entries.principle: Glissement de point de vue non intentionnel
entries.bad: Marc observa Julia avec méfiance. Julia, de son côté, pensait que Marc avait l'air fatigué. Marc ne remarqua pas qu'elle le regardait.
entries.good: Marc observa Julia avec méfiance. Elle paraissait à l'aise, ce qui n'avait aucun sens. Rien dans cette pièce n'aurait dû la mettre à l'aise.
entries.gloss_en: Marc watched Julia warily. She seemed at ease, which made no sense. Nothing in this room should have put her at ease.
entries.note_fr: On reste dans la tête de Marc. On infère l'état de Julia à travers son regard, pas ses pensées directes.
entries.note_en: We stay in Marc's head. We infer Julia's state through his observation, not her direct thoughts.

entries.principle: Salto di prospettiva (cambio di punto di vista)
entries.bad: Luca guardò Maria dall'altra parte della stanza. Maria pensò che lui sembrasse nervoso. Luca non capiva perché lei lo fissasse.
entries.good: Luca guardò Maria dall'altra parte della stanza. Non riusciva a capire cosa stesse pensando — non lo riusciva mai, e questo lo metteva a disagio.
entries.gloss_en: Luca looked at Maria across the room. He couldn't work out what she was thinking — he never could, and that unsettled him.
entries.note_it: Rimaniamo nella mente di Luca. L'incapacità di leggere Maria rivela sia il personaggio che la tensione.
entries.source: Principle discussed at sulromanzo.it and scritturacreativa.org

entries.principle: Demasiados puntos de vista — problema común en novelas iniciales
entries.bad: El primer capítulo está en la perspectiva de Ana. El segundo, en la de Luis. El tercero, en la del asesino. El cuarto, en la de la detective. El quinto vuelve a Ana, pero ahora en primera persona.
entries.good: Elige uno o dos puntos de vista y domínalos. Cada cambio de perspectiva debe tener una razón narrativa clara y estar marcado por un salto de capítulo o sección.
entries.gloss_en: Choose one or two perspectives and master them. Each POV shift needs a clear narrative reason and should be marked by a chapter or section break.
entries.note_es: El error del escritor novel: muchos personajes de punto de vista. 'Trop de caractères de point de vue' es uno de los errores más citados por editores españoles.
entries.source: aguycalledbloke.blog/fr (referenced in Spanish craft communities)

entries.principle: Veta inte i vilket huvud man befinner sig (perspektivhopp)
entries.bad: Eva tittade på honom och undrade vad han tänkte. Han kände hennes blick och ville fly.
entries.good: Eva tittade på honom och försökte läsa hans ansikte. Han verkade frånvarande — eller rädd. Det var svårt att säga.
entries.gloss_en: Eva looked at him and tried to read his face. He seemed distracted — or scared. It was hard to say.
entries.note_sv: Vi stannar i Evas huvud. Vi gissar om honom genom hennes ögon, precis som hon gör.
entries.note_en: We stay in Eva's head. We guess about him through her eyes, just as she does.
entries.source: SkrivarSidan.nu: 'Författaren vet inte i vilket av hens personers huvud hen befinner sig' — named as a common beginner error

entries.principle: Schrijven vanuit meerdere perspectieven — het beginnersprobleem
entries.bad: Caroline dacht dat hij liegt. Hij voelde dat ze het wist. Ze vroeg zich af of hij ook bang was. Hij vond haar vraag vreemd.
entries.good: Caroline keek hem aan. Er klopte iets niet aan zijn verhaal — ze wist alleen nog niet wat.
entries.gloss_en: Caroline looked at him. Something wasn't right about his story — she just didn't know what yet.
entries.note_nl: Vrouwelijk auteur Carolina Trujillo (winnaar BNG Nieuwe Literatuur Prijs) noemt dit de grootste fout van beginners: 'Ze maken het zichzelf vooral lastig.' — schrijvenonline.org
entries.note_en: Award-winning Dutch author Carolina Trujillo calls this the biggest beginner mistake: 'They make it very hard for themselves.'

cliches.description: Overused phrases that have lost their effect; language-specific examples and fixes.

entries.fix: His pulse was so loud he could hear it

entries.cliche: She had butterflies in her stomach
entries.fix: Something cold and knotted sat in her belly
The silence pressed against her eardrums
He didn't breathe. Couldn't. The second stretched.
She went very still
He'd been sitting in his car for forty minutes, key in the ignition, not turning it
