entries.note: Replace the metaphor with the specific situation.

entries.fix: Elle ouvrit la bouche. Rien ne sortit. Elle la referma.
entries.gloss_en: She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She closed it again.
entries.note_fr: Le cliché résume; la scène montre.

entries.fix: Elle sentait chaque battement jusqu'dans ses tempes.
entries.gloss_en: She felt every heartbeat up into her temples.
entries.note_fr: Localiser physiquement la sensation la rend concrète.

entries.fix: Plus rien ne bougea. Même la fumée de sa cigarette semblait suspendue.
entries.gloss_en: Nothing moved. Even the cigarette smoke seemed suspended.
entries.note_fr: Rend le temps figé à travers un détail observé, pas une affirmation.

entries.fix: Aveva una faccia che faceva dimenticare quello che stavi dicendo.
entries.gloss_en: She had a face that made you forget what you were saying.
entries.note_it: Il cliché dichiara; la sostituzione mostra l'effetto concreto sulla gente.
entries.source: scritturacreativa.org — 'Sei bello come il sole. Era bella come una dea.' — esempi di cliché da evitare

entries.cliche: Aveva gli occhi azzurri come il mare
entries.fix: Aveva occhi di un grigio-verde che cambiavano con la luce, come l'acqua di certi laghi.
entries.gloss_en: He had grey-green eyes that changed with the light, like the water of certain lakes.
entries.note_it: La specificità ('certi laghi') trasforma un cliché in un'osservazione autentica.

entries.fix: Sentía el pulso en el cuello. En los oídos. Hasta en los dedos.
entries.gloss_en: She felt her pulse in her neck. In her ears. Even in her fingers.
entries.note_es: Localizar el latido en partes específicas del cuerpo lo vuelve concreto y original.

entries.cliche: Un escalofrío le recorrió la espalda
entries.fix: Se quedó quieta. Muy quieta.
entries.gloss_en: She went very still.
entries.note_es: A veces el cliché puede simplemente eliminarse y reemplazarse con la acción subyacente.

entries.fix: Só havia o som do seu próprio ritmo cardíaco.
entries.gloss_en: There was only the sound of her own heartbeat.
entries.note_pt: Substituir o clichê por um detalhe sensorial específico do personagem.

entries.fix: Ela percebeu que estava segurando a respiração só quando começou a sentir tontura.
entries.gloss_en: She only realised she'd been holding her breath when she started to feel dizzy.
entries.note_pt: O clichê nomeia o estado; a substituição revela o comportamento inconsciente que o acompanha.

entries.fix: Sie bemerkte ihren eigenen Atem erst, als er zu laut wurde.
entries.gloss_en: She only noticed her own breathing when it got too loud.
entries.note_de: Konkrete körperliche Wahrnehmung statt abgenutzter Metapher.

entries.fix: Nicht mal die Uhr tickte. Er überprüfte sie. Sie lief.
entries.gloss_en: Not even the clock ticked. He checked it. It was running.
entries.note_de: Das Paradox des laufenden, aber nicht hörbaren Uhr macht die Stille spürbar.

entries.fix: Det enda hon hörde var sin egen andning. Hon försökte hålla andan. Det hjälpte inte.
entries.gloss_en: The only thing she heard was her own breathing. She tried to hold it. It didn't help.
entries.note_sv: Specifik fysisk detalj ersätter den slitna metaforen.

entries.cliche: Haar hart bonsde in haar keel
entries.fix: Ze kon haar eigen bloeddruk horen.
entries.gloss_en: She could hear her own blood pressure.
entries.note_nl: Vervanging via een ongewone maar nauwkeurige fysieke observatie.

entries.fix: Czuła własne bicie serca w uszach. W gardle. Nie wiedziała, że tak można.
entries.gloss_en: She felt her own heartbeat in her ears. In her throat. She hadn't known that was possible.
entries.note_pl: Odkrycie przez bohatera czegoś nowego o swoim ciele jest bardziej angażujące niż opis.

tense_consistency.description: A specific and frequently-marked error in most European language manuscripts.

entries.principle: Choose past or present — don't drift
entries.bad: She walked into the room. She looks around. The furniture was old. Everything seems dusty.
entries.good: She walked into the room and looked around. The furniture was old. Everything seemed dusty.
entries.note: Past tense, held consistently. Switching between past and present without intention is one of the most common manuscript errors globally.

entries.principle: Ne pas mélanger les temps — passé simple / imparfait (fiction littéraire)
entries.bad: Il entra dans la pièce. Il a regardé autour de lui. Il est fatigué. Il s'assit.
entries.good: Il entra dans la pièce et regarda autour de lui. Il était fatigué. Il s'assit.
entries.gloss_en: He entered the room and looked around. He was tired. He sat down.
entries.note_fr: En fiction littéraire française, le passé simple s'emploie pour les actions ponctuelles, l'imparfait pour les états et les habitudes. Mélanger le passé composé (il a regardé) avec le passé simple (il entra) est une erreur de registre.
entries.source: jesuisauteur.com: 'Les temps fonctionnent habituellement par binômes.'

entries.principle: Indefinido vs. imperfecto — uso correcto
entries.bad: El usurpador había derrotado al rey y había tomado el poder, así que no le fue fácil hacerse con el control del ejército.
entries.good: El usurpador había derrotado al rey, y tomó el poder del ejército en cuanto tuvo oportunidad.
entries.gloss_en: The usurper had defeated the king, and seized control of the army at the first opportunity.
entries.note_es: Pretérito indefinido = acción puntual posterior. Pretérito imperfecto = estado habitual o simultáneo. El error mezcla los dos en el mismo marco temporal.
entries.source: escueladeescrituracreativa.com — extensive treatment of tense errors in Spanish fiction

entries.principle: Verteltijd — verleden vs. tegenwoordige tijd
entries.bad: Julia en Tim staken de straat over. Even later buigen ze rechts af.
entries.good: Julia en Tim staken de straat over. Even later bogen ze rechts af.
entries.gloss_en: Julia and Tim crossed the street. A little later they turned right.
entries.note_nl: Één van de meest gemaakte fouten in Nederlandse manuscripten: onbewust wisselen tussen verleden en tegenwoordige tijd. — boekscout.nl, boekengilde.nl
entries.note_en: One of the most common errors in Dutch manuscripts: unconsciously switching between past and present tense.

entries.principle: Tempus — oavsiktligt hopp i tidsform
entries.bad: Hon gick in i rummet. Hon tittar sig omkring. Möblerna var gamla.
entries.good: Hon gick in i rummet och tittade sig omkring. Möblerna var gamla.
entries.gloss_en: She walked into the room and looked around. The furniture was old.
entries.note_sv: Välj presens eller preteritum och håll dig konsekvent. Oavsiktliga tempusskiften är ett av de vanligaste nybörjarfelen. — skrivarsidan.nu
entries.note_en: Choose present or past and be consistent. Unintentional tense shifts are one of the most common beginner errors.

entries.principle: Tempus — Präteritum vs. Präsens in der Prosa
entries.bad: Er betrat den Raum. Sie sieht ihn sofort. Ihre Hände zitterten.
entries.good: Er betrat den Raum. Sie sah ihn sofort. Ihre Hände zitterten.
entries.gloss_en: He entered the room. She saw him immediately. Her hands were trembling.
entries.note_de: Deutsche Prosa verwendet in der Regel das Präteritum als Erzähltempus. Mitten in eine Szene zu wechseln ist ein häufiger Fehler in Erstmanuskripten.
entries.note_en: German prose typically uses the past tense (Präteritum) as the narrative tense. Switching mid-scene is a common first-manuscript error.

entries.principle: Czas gramatyczny — konsekwencja narracyjna
entries.bad: Weszła do pokoju. Rozgląda się. Meble były stare.
entries.good: Weszła do pokoju i rozejrzała się. Meble były stare.
entries.gloss_en: She entered the room and looked around. The furniture was old.
entries.note_pl: Nieumyślne przeskakiwanie między czasem teraźniejszym a przeszłym to jeden z najczęstszych błędów w polskich debiutanckich manuskryptach.
entries.note_en: Unintentional switching between present and past tense is one of the most common errors in Polish debut manuscripts.

opening_lines.description: How to start strong. Common failures and successful approaches.

entries.principle: Avoid the 'throat-clearing' opening
entries.bad: It was a dark and stormy night in October. The wind howled through the trees. Sarah woke up from her alarm at 7am, got dressed, and made herself a cup of coffee before looking out the window and thinking about her life.
entries.good: The call came at 3am. Not the kind you sleep through.
entries.note: The bad example delays the actual story with weather, alarm clocks, and backstory. The good example begins in the middle of a moment that demands a response.

entries.principle: Four reader questions to answer by page 3
entries.note: 1. Why am I reading this? (What is the narrative drive?) 2. Whose story is this? (Who do I inhabit?) 3. What is the situation? (Ground me in the world) 4. What is at stake? (What will I lose if I stop reading?)
entries.source: Principle from Jorun Modén (Swedish) and multiple English craft sources — widely formulated as the 'four questions readers ask subconsciously.'

entries.principle: L'incipit — commencer au bon endroit
entries.bad: C'était un après-midi d'automne, et le ciel était gris au-dessus de Paris. Marie se réveilla et pensa à sa vie. Elle s'habilla lentement.
entries.good: Elle avait attendu cette lettre pendant dix ans. Maintenant qu'elle était là, elle ne l'ouvrait pas.
entries.gloss_en: She had waited for this letter for ten years. Now that it was here, she wasn't opening it.
entries.note_fr: L'incipit doit établir une scène, créer un conflit ou générer un mystère. La lettre non ouverte fait les trois.
entries.source: librinova.com: 'votre incipit doit établir une scène, créer un conflit ou générer un mystère'

entries.principle: Inizio forte — evitare la partenza lenta
entries.bad: Marco si svegliò quella mattina di ottobre sentendosi stanco. Fece colazione, guardò dalla finestra il cielo grigio, e pensò che quella giornata non sembrava promettere niente di buono.
entries.good: Quella mattina il corpo era ancora caldo.
entries.gloss_en: That morning the body was still warm.
entries.note_it: Iniziare con un fatto concreto e urgente è molto più efficace di descrivere la mattinata di routine del protagonista.
entries.source: storygenius.it: 'De longs débuts lents' among most common errors listed

entries.principle: Empezar en el momento adecuado — in medias res
entries.bad: Ana nació en un pequeño pueblo de Galicia. Tuvo una infancia difícil. Cuando cumplió dieciocho años, decidió marcharse a la ciudad...
entries.good: Ana llevaba tres horas sentada delante del teléfono cuando, por fin, llamó.
entries.gloss_en: Ana had been sitting in front of the phone for three hours when, finally, it rang.
entries.note_es: Empezar donde el conflicto existe, no donde el personaje nació.
entries.source: escueladeescritores.com; verbalina.com — standard advice in Spanish craft communities

entries.principle: Fånga läsaren från första raden
entries.bad: Det var en grå novemberdag i Stockholm. Molnen hängde lågt. Eva hade sovit dåligt och vaknade med en känsla av oro.
entries.good: Eva hittade brevet under dörrmattan. Utan frimärke. Utan avsändare. Med hennes namn i hennes egen handstil.
entries.gloss_en: Eva found the letter under the doormat. No stamp. No sender. Her name in her own handwriting.
entries.note_sv: Väck nyfikenhet kring din karaktär, ställ till med ett problem, låt något gå fel eller skeva. — forfattarkurs.se
entries.note_en: Arouse curiosity about your character, introduce a problem, let something go wrong or skewed.

adverb_dependency.description: Language-specific notes on adverb overuse and the fix of finding stronger verbs.

entries.stronger: 'Careful,' she said, her eyes on the door.
entries.note: The context and body language eliminate the need for any qualifier.

entries.stronger: He was already late — he sprinted the last block.

entries.principle: Les adverbes en -ment — le problème français
entries.bad: Elle lui dit doucement d'une voix apaisante qu'il n'y avait rien à craindre.
entries.good: Elle posa la main sur son bras. 'Il n'y a rien à craindre.'
entries.gloss_en: She placed her hand on his arm. 'There's nothing to fear.'
entries.note_fr: L'adverbe 'doucement' et l'apposition 'voix apaisante' sont remplacés par l'action physique et le dialogue direct.
entries.note_en: The adverb 'softly' and the appositive 'soothing voice' are replaced by physical action and direct speech.

entries.principle: Adverbios en -mente — el problema español
entries.bad: Caminó rápidamente hacia la puerta y la cerró silenciosamente.
entries.good: Cruzó la habitación y cerró la puerta sin hacer ruido.
entries.gloss_en: He crossed the room and closed the door without a sound.
entries.note_es: En la revisión, busca todos los adverbios en -mente y pregúntate si el verbo puede hacer el trabajo solo. — estandarte.com
entries.source: estandarte.com: 'Puedes escribir tantos -mente como quieras cuando estés creando. Pero después, en la fase de revisión, fíjate cuántos de ellos puedes eliminar.'

entries.principle: Adverbien als Notlösung — die -lich/-weise Falle
entries.bad: Sie sagte leise und eindringlich, dass er sofort aufhören solle.
entries.good: Sie beugte sich vor. 'Hör auf.'
entries.gloss_en: She leaned forward. 'Stop.'
entries.note_de: Adverbien kompensieren oft einen zu schwachen Ausdruck. Das Kürzen auf das Wesentliche ist fast immer stärker.
entries.note_en: Adverbs often compensate for an expression that is too weak. Cutting to the essential is almost always stronger.

entries.principle: Bijwoorden als vluchtroute
entries.bad: Ze liep snel naar de deur en sloot hem zachtjes.
entries.good: Ze was bij de deur voor hij zijn zin kon afmaken. Ze trok hem dicht.
entries.gloss_en: She was at the door before he could finish his sentence. She pulled it shut.
entries.note_nl: De actie (bij de deur zijn vóór hij klaar is) doet meer werk dan het bijwoord 'snel.'
entries.note_en: The action (being at the door before he finishes) does more work than the adverb 'quickly.'

info_dumping.description: Delivering background and world information in blocks rather than woven through action.

entries.principle: History told through a character's observed detail
entries.bad: The old religion was outlawed two hundred years ago when King Aldric the Third defeated the temple priests and converted the country to the new faith, which is why the temples are now used for storage.
entries.good: The temple had been repurposed as a grain storehouse. Someone had plastered over the fresco of the old gods, but the plaster had cracked, and three divine faces looked down at sacks of barley.
entries.note: History is delivered through a single observed scene; no authorial summary is needed.

entries.principle: World economy — revealed through transaction, not lecture
entries.bad: In this world, the currency system works as follows: three copper rings equal one silver arc, which equals one-tenth of a gold circle, established by the Council of Regents in Year 1204...
entries.good: She paid for her bread with three copper rings, checked that the stamping on the reverse matched the current regent, and moved on.
entries.note: One sentence reveals the currency, the political system, and a recent regime change through action.

entries.principle: Ne pas donner trop d'informations à la fois
entries.bad: Le royaume de Valdor était gouverné depuis 400 ans par la Maison Arkel. La capitale, Seirath, comptait environ 300 000 habitants. La principale religion était le culte des Sept Flammes, fondé par le prophète Aris en l'an 1204.
entries.good: Elle traversa la Place des Sept Flammes sans s'arrêter. Les pèlerins lui bloquaient le passage deux fois par semaine — aujourd'hui c'était leur jour.
entries.gloss_en: She crossed the Square of the Seven Flames without stopping. The pilgrims blocked her way twice a week — today was their day.
entries.note_fr: La religion, la géographie de la ville et la routine du personnage sont établies en deux phrases, sans exposé.
entries.source: librinova.com: 'ne donnez pas trop d'informations à la fois, sachez distiller le suspense'

entries.principle: Evitare la 'scarica di informazioni' (info-dump)
entries.bad: Il castello di Arken era stato costruito nel XII secolo dai Signori del Nord. Aveva resistito a tre assedi e ospitato quattro re. Le sue torri, alte quaranta metri, erano visibili per venti chilometri.
entries.good: Si fermò davanti alle torri. Suo nonno le aveva dette che nessuno aveva mai preso quel castello. Suo nonno non aveva mai visto quello che c'era dentro.
entries.gloss_en: She stopped before the towers. Her grandfather had told her nobody had ever taken that castle. Her grandfather had never seen what was inside.
entries.note_it: La storia viene filtrata attraverso la voce del personaggio e crea subito tensione narrativa.
entries.source: Principle from sulromanzo.it: world-building through narrative lens

entries.principle: Información como elemento de la acción, no como exposición
entries.bad: El sistema político del reino llevaba tres siglos en pie. Estaba basado en un consejo de doce gremios fundado en 1412 por el rey Aldric IV, que había fusionado los antiguos clanes...
entries.good: Doce sillas, doce gremios. Y un trono vacío en el centro. Siempre vacío. Ese era el acuerdo.
entries.gloss_en: Twelve chairs, twelve guilds. And an empty throne in the centre. Always empty. That was the agreement.
entries.note_es: Tres frases cortas transmiten la estructura de poder, la inestabilidad latente y la historia — sin ninguna explicación directa.

entries.principle: Bakgrundsinformation via handling och observation
entries.bad: Kungariket Valdor hade styrts av Arkel-dynastin i fyra hundra år. Huvudstaden hade 300 000 invånare. Kyrkan höll gudstjänst varje fredag.
entries.good: Hon pressade sig genom fredagsprocessionen utan att sakta ner. Prästerna blängde på henne. Det brydde hon sig inte om.
entries.gloss_en: She pressed through the Friday procession without slowing down. The priests glared at her. She didn't care.
entries.note_sv: Religionens närvaro, karaktärens personlighet och platsen etableras i två meningar genom handling.
entries.note_en: Religion's presence, the character's personality, and the place are established in two sentences through action.

pacing.description: Speed of information and event delivery. Techniques to accelerate and decelerate.

entries.principle: Short sentences for urgency — create physical heartbeat
entries.bad: He ran as fast as he could across the square, passing by the fountain that stood in the middle of the piazza, and then he entered the narrow alley on the far side, where he pressed his back against the cold wall and listened carefully to hear if anyone was following him.
entries.good:
He ran. Across the square, past the fountain, into the shadow of the alley — and stopped. His back hit cold brick. He listened.

Nothing.

Then footsteps.
entries.note: Sentence fragments ('Nothing.') and isolated paragraphs slow the reader's eye to a near-stop — creating silence on the page.

entries.principle: Scene vs. summary — when to expand, when to compress
entries.bad: The next three months were very difficult for both of them but eventually they managed to work through their problems and their relationship grew stronger. Then one morning she found the letter.
entries.good:
Three months. Silences at dinner. A toothbrush moved to the guest bathroom. A second key cut without being asked.

Then one morning she found the letter.
entries.note: The summary is compressed to specific, concrete objects — each one a tiny scene. Then the 'then' hits harder because we've felt the three months.

entries.principle: Slow down for emotional climax — let the moment breathe
entries.bad: She read the letter and started crying. It was very upsetting. She sat down and cried for a long time.
entries.good:
She read it twice. Then once more.

She folded it along the original creases. Placed it back in the envelope. Set the envelope on the table.

She didn't cry. That was the strange part. She just sat there, looking at it.
entries.note: Slowing down through specific physical actions gives readers room to feel what the character cannot yet articulate.

entries.principle: Ellipse narrative — accélérer en comprimant le temps
entries.bad: Trois semaines passèrent. Pendant ces trois semaines, il alla au travail chaque matin et rentra chez lui le soir. Rien ne se passa.
entries.good: Trois semaines. Le même trajet, les mêmes dossiers, le même silence du soir. Puis, un mardi, son téléphone sonna.
entries.gloss_en: Three weeks. The same commute, the same files, the same evening silence. Then, on a Tuesday, his phone rang.
entries.note_fr: L'ellipse narrative comprime le temps mort en quelques mots concrets avant de relancer l'action.

entries.principle: Tempo durch Satzlänge steuern
entries.bad: Er rannte. Er rannte schnell. Er war außer Atem. Er blieb stehen. Er hörte Schritte.
entries.good:
Er rannte. Durch die Gasse, um die Ecke, gegen eine Wand — Stopp. Stille.

Dann: Schritte.
entries.gloss_en: He ran. Through the alley, around the corner, into a wall — stop. Silence. Then: footsteps.
entries.note_de: Der Doppelpunkt vor 'Schritte' erzeugt eine dramatische Pause, die im Deutschen besonders effektiv ist.

entries.principle: Ritmo y ley de causa-efecto (motivación-reacción)
entries.bad: Oyó un ruido y salió corriendo por la puerta.
entries.good: Oyó el ruido. Se quedó quieta. Luego salió corriendo.
entries.gloss_en: She heard the sound. She went still. Then she ran.
entries.note_es: La ley causa-efecto en la escritura española exige que el personaje reaccione antes de actuar. Introducir la reacción interna entre el estímulo y la acción da credibilidad y controla el ritmo.
entries.source: escueladeescritores.com: 'ley causa-efecto' as a fundamental pacing principle in Spanish craft pedagogy

entries.principle: Gestire il ritmo attraverso la struttura del paragrafo
entries.bad: La scena del combattimento durò molto a lungo e fu molto intensa e pericolosa per entrambi i personaggi che lottarono con tutte le loro forze.
entries.good:
Il primo colpo la prese di sorpresa.
Il secondo no.
Al terzo, si mosse.
entries.gloss_en: The first blow surprised her. The second didn't. At the third, she moved.
entries.note_it: Tre paragrafi brevi con struttura progressiva accelerano la scena e la rendono cinematografica.

entries.principle: Tempo och spänningskurva — böja och sträcka
entries.bad: Scenen var spännande och intensiv. Det hände mycket. Alla var rädda.
entries.good:
Han bet ihop. Inte nu.

Sekunden drog ut på sig.

Sedan: skott.
entries.gloss_en: He clenched his jaw. Not now. The second stretched. Then: a shot.
entries.note_sv: Enordsstycken och ensamstående fraser skapar visuell och rytmisk spänning på sidan.
entries.note_en: Single-word paragraphs and standalone phrases create visual and rhythmic tension on the page.

entries.principle: Tempo variëren met zinslengtes
entries.bad: Ze rende door de straat en om de hoek en botste bijna tegen een fietser op maar wist hem te ontwijken en rende verder naar de brug.
entries.good: Ze rende. De straat. De hoek. Bijna de fietser. De brug.
entries.gloss_en: She ran. The street. The corner. Almost the cyclist. The bridge.
entries.note_nl: Losstaande zelfstandige naamwoorden als fragmenten creëren een filmisch, vluchtig ritme.

entries.principle: Tempo poprzez długość zdań
entries.bad: Biegła przez ulicę i skręciła za róg, gdzie prawie wpadła na rowerzystę, ale zdołała go ominąć i pobiegła dalej w stronę mostu.
entries.good: Biegła. Ulica. Róg. Prawie rowerzysta. Most.
entries.gloss_en: She ran. Street. Corner. Almost cyclist. Bridge.
entries.note_pl: Fragmenty rzeczownikowe jako osobne akapity tworzą filmowe, urywane tempo.

sentence_variety.description: Varying length and structure to create prose with musicality and momentum.

entries.principle: Monotony of structure creates monotony of feeling
entries.bad: She walked to the window. She looked outside. She saw the garden. She thought about her mother. She turned away.
entries.good: She walked to the window. Outside, the garden — her mother's garden, still, after all this time. She turned away.
entries.note: The em-dash and appositive break the drumbeat of Subject-Verb-Object. The emotional weight lands on 'still, after all this time' precisely because the rhythm shifts.

entries.principle: The short sentence after long ones — the punch
entries.bad: He had spent years trying to forget what had happened in that room, the way the light fell through the curtains, the sound of her voice asking him to leave, the long drive back in rain — and even now, decades later, it came back to him without warning. He hated it.
entries.good:
He had spent years trying to forget what had happened in that room — the light through the curtains, her voice, the long drive back in rain. Even now it came back without warning.

He hated it.
entries.note: 'He hated it.' earns its power from the long sentence that precedes it.

entries.principle: Varier les longueurs de phrases — le rythme de la prose
entries.bad: Elle attendit. Il arriva. Elle lui parla. Il écouta. Elle pleura. Il resta.
entries.good:
Elle attendit. Deux heures, peut-être trois — elle avait cessé de compter. Quand il arriva enfin, elle ne trouva rien à dire.

Il resta quand même.
entries.gloss_en: She waited. Two hours, maybe three — she had stopped counting. When he finally arrived, she found nothing to say. He stayed anyway.
entries.note_fr: La phrase longue au milieu crée une respiration avant la chute courte et émotionnelle ('Il resta quand même').

entries.principle: Die Kunst des kurzen Satzes im Deutschen
entries.bad: Sie wartete. Er kam. Sie sprach. Er hörte zu. Sie weinte. Er blieb.
entries.good:
Sie wartete zwei Stunden, vielleicht drei — sie hatte aufgehört zu zählen. Als er endlich kam, fand sie keine Worte.

Er blieb trotzdem.
entries.gloss_en: She waited two hours, maybe three — she had stopped counting. When he finally came, she found no words. He stayed anyway.
entries.note_de: Im Deutschen ist der kurze Schlusssatz besonders wirkungsvoll, weil deutsche Prosa tendenziell länger ist. Der Kontrast ist stärker.

entries.principle: Variedad rítmica — la frase corta como golpe final
entries.bad: Esperó. Él llegó. Ella habló. Él escuchó. Ella lloró. Él se quedó.
entries.good:
Esperó dos horas, quizá tres — había dejado de contar. Cuando por fin llegó, ella no encontró palabras.

Él se quedó.
entries.gloss_en: She waited two hours, maybe three — she had stopped counting. When he finally arrived, she found no words. He stayed.
entries.note_es: La frase aislada 'Él se quedó' obtiene su carga emocional del contraste con la frase larga anterior.

entries.principle: Rytmisk variation — den korta meningen som punch
entries.bad: Hon väntade. Han kom. Hon talade. Han lyssnade. Hon grät. Han stannade.
entries.good:
Hon väntade i timmar, kanske tre — hon hade slutat räkna. När han äntligen kom hittade hon inga ord.

Han stannade ändå.
entries.gloss_en: She waited for hours, maybe three — she had stopped counting. When he finally came she found no words. He stayed anyway.
entries.note_sv: Kontrasten mellan lång och kort mening ger den sista frasen emotionell kraft.

entries.principle: Zinslengtevariatie — de korte zin als klap
entries.bad: Ze wachtte. Hij kwam. Ze sprak. Hij luisterde. Ze huilde. Hij bleef.
entries.good:
Ze wachtte uren, misschien drie — ze was opgehouden met tellen. Toen hij eindelijk aankwam, vond ze geen woorden.

Hij bleef toch.
entries.gloss_en: She waited hours, maybe three — she had stopped counting. When he finally arrived, she found no words. He stayed anyway.

entries.principle: Rytm zdań — krótkie zdanie jako uderzenie
entries.bad: Czekała. On przyszedł. Mówiła. Słuchał. Płakała. Został.
entries.good:
Czekała godzinami, może trzy — przestała liczyć. Kiedy w końcu przyszedł, nie znalazła słów.

Mimo to został.
entries.gloss_en: She waited hours, maybe three — she stopped counting. When he finally came, she found no words. He stayed anyway.

character_depth.description: Making characters three-dimensional, believable, and capable of change.

entries.principle: Want vs. Need — the engine of character
entries.bad: Elena wanted to be a doctor. She worked hard and became a good doctor. (Want fulfilled; no internal journey.)
entries.good: Elena wanted to be a doctor — needed to be, so she'd never again be as helpless as she was the night her brother died in a corridor while they waited for someone who knew what to do. She became a good doctor. She still felt helpless. (Want fulfilled; need exposed as unresolvable.)
entries.note: The character's external goal is achieved but the wound beneath it is revealed to be deeper. This is the engine of authentic character.

entries.principle: The villain as self-consistent worldview, not evil label
entries.bad: 'I want to destroy everything because I am evil,' he said, laughing. He had always enjoyed causing pain.
entries.good: 'They called me a monster,' he said. 'But I watched my entire village starve while the city held grain back for profit. Tell me who the real monster is.'
entries.note: The antagonist's logic must be internally coherent. Readers should be able to see how someone might arrive at this position, even if they reject it.

entries.principle: Voice differentiation — characters must not sound like the same narrator
entries.bad: 'We need to address the situation,' Marcus said. 'Yes, we should deal with it carefully,' Elena replied.
entries.good:
Marcus: 'Eighteen hours. Then we move.'
Elena: 'Eighteen hours and then we move into what, exactly?'
entries.note: Same information, opposite personalities — Marcus thinks in logistics, Elena thinks in consequences.

entries.principle: Le désir vs. le besoin — moteur du personnage
entries.bad: Il voulait devenir riche. Il travailla dur et devint riche. Fin.
entries.good: Il voulait devenir riche. Ce qu'il voulait vraiment, c'était que son père le regarde une fois sans cette expression — celle qui disait que tu ne seras jamais assez.
entries.gloss_en: He wanted to be rich. What he really wanted was for his father to look at him once without that expression — the one that said you'll never be enough.
entries.note_fr: Le vrai désir (besoin intérieur) est presque toujours émotionnel, jamais matériel.

entries.principle: Il difetto che limita il personaggio — il motore dell'arco narrativo
entries.bad: Marco era coraggioso e intelligente. Non aveva paura di niente. Affrontò il problema e lo risolse.
entries.good: Marco era coraggioso — sempre stato. Il problema era che confondeva il coraggio con l'impossibilità di chiedere aiuto. Gli era quasi costato tutto, una volta. Stava per costarglielo di nuovo.
entries.gloss_en: Marco was brave — always had been. The problem was that he confused bravery with the inability to ask for help. It had almost cost him everything once. It was about to cost him again.
entries.note_it: Il difetto che limita il personaggio deve essere correlato alla sua virtù — non opposto ad essa. È più credibile e più tragico.

entries.principle: Personajes secundarios que no sean meros apoyos del protagonista
entries.bad: Carlos siempre estaba ahí para Ana, apoyándola y dándole consejos útiles cuando los necesitaba.
entries.good: Carlos estaba ahí para Ana, sí. Pero últimamente parecía que también estaba esperando algo a cambio — algo que ella no sabía si podía darle.
entries.gloss_en: Carlos was there for Ana, yes. But lately it seemed he was also waiting for something in return — something she didn't know if she could give him.
entries.note_es: Los personajes secundarios tienen sus propios deseos y conflictos. En cuanto un personaje solo existe para ayudar al protagonista, se vuelve plano.

entries.principle: Der Antagonist als Gegenpol mit eigener Logik
entries.bad: 'Ich bin böse, weil ich es liebe, anderen Schmerz zu bereiten,' sagte er.
entries.good: 'Ihr nennt mich einen Verräter,' sagte er ruhig. 'Aber ich habe dreißig Jahre lang für euch gearbeitet. Was habt ihr getan, als man mich fallen ließ?'
entries.gloss_en: 'You call me a traitor,' he said quietly. 'But I worked for you for thirty years. What did you do when they let me fall?'
entries.note_de: Die Logik des Antagonisten muss von innen heraus stimmig sein. Der Leser muss verstehen können, wie jemand zu dieser Haltung gelangt ist — auch wenn er sie ablehnt.

entries.principle: Planteringar — förebåda karaktärsutvecklingen tidigt
entries.bad: I kapitel 15 övervann Erik sin rädsla för vatten, vilket kom som en överraskning för alla.
entries.good:
Kapitel 1: Erik gick alltid runt dammen i parken, aldrig bredvid den.
Kapitel 15: Han hoppade in.
entries.gloss_en: Ch. 1: Erik always walked around the pond in the park, never alongside it. Ch. 15: He jumped in.
entries.note_sv: Planteringar (seeds planted early) gör karaktärsutvecklingen trovärdig. Utan dem verkar förändringen påklistrad.
entries.note_en: Plot plants make character change believable. Without them, transformation feels arbitrary.
entries.source: SkrivarSidan.nu: 'planteringar' as a named concept in Swedish craft pedagogy

entries.principle: Personagediepte — wil vs. behoefte
entries.bad: Anna wilde promotie maken. Ze werkte hard en maakte promotie. Ze was blij.
entries.good: Anna wilde promotie — maar wat ze echt wilde was bewijzen dat haar vader het fout had gehad. Dat ze wél goed genoeg was. Ze maakte promotie. Haar vader zei niets.
entries.gloss_en: Anna wanted a promotion — but what she really wanted was to prove her father wrong. That she was good enough. She got the promotion. Her father said nothing.
entries.note_nl: De externe doelstelling (promotie) bereikt; de interne wond (vaders goedkeuring) niet. Dit is het verschil tussen plot en verhaal.

entries.principle: Bohater bez wad = brak napięcia
entries.bad: Marta była odważna, inteligentna, piękna i zawsze wiedziała, co robić. Wszyscy ją lubili.
entries.good: Marta była odważna — zbyt odważna, żeby przyznać się do błędu. I to ją kosztowało. Znowu.
entries.gloss_en: Marta was brave — too brave to admit a mistake. And that cost her. Again.
entries.note_pl: Wada bohatera musi wynikać z jego cnoty — nie być jej przeciwieństwem. To czyni postać prawdziwą i tragiczną.

active_passive_voice.description: When passive weakens prose and when it is correctly deployed.

entries.principle: Passive buries the actor and weakens impact
entries.bad: The door was kicked open by the detective.
entries.good: The detective kicked the door open.
entries.note: Active voice: agent first, action immediate.

entries.principle: Passive used correctly — unknown actor
entries.bad: Someone who we do not know stole the painting during the night.
entries.good: The painting had been stolen during the night.
entries.note: The passive is correct here because the unknown actor IS the point. Naming 'someone' is weaker than letting the passive carry the mystery.

entries.principle: The 'decisions were made' passive — evasive and lifeless
entries.bad: Mistakes were made. Decisions were taken. Resources were allocated and deployed.
entries.good: He made mistakes. He made the decision. He spent the money.
entries.note: The passive without an actor is often used to evade accountability. In fiction it reads as characterless and vague.

entries.principle: La voix passive — affaiblissement du style
entries.bad: La porte fut ouverte par lui d'un coup de pied.
entries.good: Il enfonça la porte d'un coup de pied.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door in.
entries.note_fr: La voix passive en français littéraire est souvent signe d'un manque de confiance dans le verbe. Chercher le verbe actif précis.
entries.source: jesuisauteur.com and concours-ecriture.com — passive voice flagged as a style weakness in French craft guidance

entries.principle: Passiv im Deutschen — wann es schwächt
entries.bad: Die Tür wurde von ihm aufgetreten.
entries.good: Er trat die Tür auf.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door open.
entries.note_de: Das Passiv ist im Deutschen grammatisch vollkommen korrekt, aber in der Erzählprosa oft ein Zeichen dafür, dass man dem Verb nicht genug zutraut. Das Aktiv ist direkter und energischer.

entries.principle: Pasiva perifrástica vs. pasiva refleja — el uso correcto
entries.bad: La puerta fue abierta por él de una patada.
entries.good: Él abrió la puerta de una patada.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door open.
entries.note_es: La pasiva perifrástica (ser + participio) debilita la prosa narrativa en español. La pasiva refleja (se abrió la puerta) es más natural pero también debe usarse conscientemente.
entries.source: estandarte.com — voz pasiva in Spanish creative writing craft

entries.principle: Forma passiva — quando indebolisce la narrativa
entries.bad: La porta fu aperta da lui con un calcio.
entries.good: Lui aprì la porta con un calcio.
entries.gloss_en: He opened the door with a kick.
entries.note_it: In italiano narrativo, la forma passiva rimuove l'agente dall'immediato e appesantisce la prosa. Usarla solo quando l'agente è sconosciuto o irrilevante.
entries.source: scritturacreativa.org: passive voice as a style issue in Italian fiction

entries.principle: Passiv röst — när den försvagar berättandet
entries.bad: Dörren sparkades upp av honom.
entries.good: Han sparkade upp dörren.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door open.
entries.note_sv: Passiv i svenska är grammatiskt korrekt men försvagar energin i handlingsscener. Aktiv röst sätter agenten i fokus.

entries.principle: Lijdende vorm — verzwakt verhalend proza
entries.bad: De deur werd door hem opengeschopt.
entries.good: Hij schopte de deur open.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door open.
entries.note_nl: De lijdende vorm (worden + voltooid deelwoord) neemt de energie weg van handelingsscènes. Gebruik de bedrijvende vorm.

entries.principle: Strona bierna — kiedy osłabia narrację
entries.bad: Drzwi zostały przez niego wyważone.
entries.good: Wyważył drzwi.
entries.gloss_en: He kicked the door in.
entries.note_pl: W języku polskim strona bierna jest poprawna gramatycznie, ale w narracji akcji osłabia tempo. Strona czynna stawia agenta w centrum uwagi.

narrative_consistency.description: Tracking details, facts, and internal logic across a manuscript.

entries.principle: Physical continuity — impossible geography or timing
entries.bad: She left London at noon on Monday and arrived in Edinburgh the same morning. (London to Edinburgh is ~4.5 hours by train; arriving 'the same morning' after a noon departure is impossible.)
entries.good: She boarded the noon train from King's Cross and watched London dissolve into grey suburbs. She arrived in Edinburgh by late afternoon, stiff and thirsty.
entries.note: Editors track timelines. A simple calendar/timeline document prevents most continuity errors.

entries.principle: Character physical details — don't change mid-book
entries.bad:
Chapter 2: 'Marcus had brown eyes.'
Chapter 14: 'She looked into his blue eyes.'
entries.good: Keep a character bible: name, age, height, hair colour, eye colour, key physical traits. Refer to it before every physical description.
entries.note: Changing eye colour is one of the most frequently cited continuity errors in editor feedback.

entries.principle: Coerenza narrativa — i piccoli dettagli che i lettori notano
entries.bad: Cap. 3: 'La pistola aveva cinque colpi.' Cap. 7: 'Aveva sparato tre volte, e rimase con cinque colpi.' (5 − 3 ≠ 5)
entries.good: Tieni un documento di traccia: oggetti, munizioni, posizioni, orari. Aggiornalo scena per scena.
entries.gloss_en: Keep a tracking document: objects, ammunition, locations, times. Update it scene by scene.
entries.note_it: I lettori italiani, specialmente nel genere poliziesco e fantascientifico, sono particolarmente attenti alla coerenza narrativa. Gli errori di continuità distruggono la credibilità del romanzo.
entries.source: pennarigata.it and sulromanzo.it — continuità narrativa as a specific Italian editorial concern

entries.principle: Innere Logik und Widerspruchsfreiheit
entries.bad: Kapitel 2: 'Das Schloss hatte keine Fenster.' Kapitel 11: 'Sie schaute aus dem Fenster des Schlosses auf die Stadt hinunter.'
entries.good: Erstelle eine Gebäudeskizze oder -beschreibung zu Beginn des Schreibprozesses. Notiere architektonische Details, die für die Handlung relevant sein könnten.
entries.gloss_en: Create a building sketch or description at the start of the writing process. Note architectural details that might be relevant to the plot.
entries.note_de: Lektoren und Korrektoren markieren solche Widersprüche routinemäßig. Ein einfaches Dokument mit Ortsbeschreibungen und Zeitlinien verhindert die meisten Fehler.

entries.principle: Streszczenie rozdziałów — narzędzie spójności
entries.bad: Rozdział 4: Bohater jest w Krakowie. Rozdział 5: Bohater następnego ranka jest w Warszawie (5 godzin drogi bez uzasadnienia).
entries.good: Prowadź streszczenie każdego rozdziału z: lokalizacją, porą dnia, obecnymi postaciami i kluczowymi faktami. Weryfikuj przed pisaniem nowego rozdziału.
entries.gloss_en: Keep a summary of each chapter with: location, time of day, characters present, key facts established. Verify before writing each new chapter.
entries.note_pl: Polskie poradniki pisania (born-to-create.pl, spisekpisarzy.pl) wymieniają spójność chronologiczną jako obowiązkowy element samoedycji.
entries.note_en: Polish craft guides list chronological consistency as a mandatory self-editing element.
entries.source: born-to-create.pl: 'streszczenie rozdziałów' as a tracking tool

rules_and_mindset.description: Understanding when to follow craft principles and when to break them with intention.

entries.principle: Breaking rules consciously is craft; breaking them accidentally is error
entries.bad: He was excited. She was nervous. They were both scared.
entries.good: He knew the rules of show-don't-tell, so when he chose to tell — 'She had been waiting her whole life for this moment' — the economy served the scene perfectly.
entries.note: Flat telling with no craft intention reads as error. The same gesture made deliberately becomes style.

reading_habit.description: Why serious writers must read voraciously — in genre and out.

entries.principle: Know your genre before you write in it
entries.bad: Writing a fantasy novel without reading fantasy. Readers will feel the ignorance — recycled tropes, wrong pacing, missed genre beats.
entries.good: Read 50–100 books in your genre before writing your first novel. Know what's been done, what readers expect, and where you can surprise them.
entries.note: Read the classics of your genre, recent bestsellers, literary fiction for prose style, and nonfiction in your theme area for authentic detail.

writing_habit.description: Building the daily practice that separates finished novels from perpetual first drafts.

entries.principle: The draft must exist before it can be good
entries.bad: Waiting for inspiration. Writing only when you 'feel like it' produces 3 pages a year and a lot of guilt.
entries.good: Write 500 words every morning before checking email. After 120 days, you have a novel draft.
entries.note: Put the work away for a while before editing. When you return with fresh eyes, you'll see clearly what needs to change. — Mary Simses

story_structure.description: How clear structural beats serve the reader's need for forward momentum and emotional investment.

entries.principle: Structural clarity serves story momentum — the inciting incident must arrive
entries.bad: 100 pages of fascinating world-building before anything happens that the protagonist must respond to. (Missing an inciting incident; readers abandon the book by chapter 3.)
entries.good: Chapter 1: Frodo lives peacefully in the Shire. Chapter 2: Gandalf reveals the ring's danger — the Inciting Incident. Chapter 3: Frodo commits to leaving — End of Act I.
entries.note: The reader's contract is set in Act I. Delay the inciting incident and you're spending goodwill you haven't earned yet.

flashback.description: Flashbacks earn their place only when they change how the reader understands the present moment.

entries.principle: A flashback must earn the reader's permission to time-travel
entries.bad: Chapter 1: The battle begins! Chapter 2: Flashback to protagonist's childhood (15 pages). Chapter 3: Flashback to protagonist's training (12 pages). Chapter 4: Back to the battle... which readers no longer care about.
entries.good: She stared at the man across the courtroom. The last time she'd seen that face, she'd been seven years old and running.
entries.note: Rule: a flashback should create a mystery or urgency in the present, then the flashback resolves it. The present scene must earn the permission first.

character_voice.topic: Character Voice — Making Everyone Sound Different
character_voice.description: Each character should be immediately recognisable by how they speak, not just what they say.

entries.principle: Show interiority through filtering — what a character notices reveals who they are
entries.bad: "You're late," she said. She was annoyed. She looked at him carefully.
entries.good: "You're late," she said. Not an accusation — just a fact she filed away alongside his crooked tie and the coffee stain on his left cuff.
entries.note: The same line of dialogue reads completely differently depending on what the character notices and how they process it.

entries.principle: Two characters discussing the same event should reveal entirely different worldviews
entries.bad: "We lost people," said Marcus. "Yes, we did," said Elena. (Both characters sound like the same narrator wearing different names.)
entries.good: Character A (soldier): "Casualty count's low. Sector secure. We move at dawn." Character B (poet): "Seventeen men. I keep counting them. Do they have names in your reports?"
entries.note: Pro tip: Give each major character 5 FORBIDDEN WORDS — things they would never say. This instantly differentiates voice.

character_arc.description: A character arc is not decoration. It is the story's proof that the events mattered.

entries.principle: The character must be meaningfully different at the end — or knowingly refuse to change
entries.bad: Character is kind at the start. Character is kind at the end. Nothing has changed. The plot happened to them; they didn't grow through it.
entries.good: At the start: Ebenezer Scrooge refuses to acknowledge others' humanity. At the end: He becomes the embodiment of generosity. Every story event forces the confrontation with his wound.
entries.note: The lie your character believes at the start of the story is the engine of their entire arc. Identify it in chapter one; resolve it — or not — at the climax.

iceberg_principle.topic: The Iceberg Principle — World-Building Through Detail
iceberg_principle.description: The reader infers the depth of a world from a single visible detail. The author knows ten things; the reader sees one and believes in all ten.

entries.principle: Let the reader infer the system from a single concrete detail
entries.bad: "In this world, the currency system works as follows: three copper rings equal one silver arc, which equals one-tenth of a gold circle, established by the Treaty of Veth in year 1204 of the Third Age..."
entries.good: She paid for her bread with three copper rings, checked that the stamping on the reverse matched the current regent, and moved on.
entries.note: Build outward from your protagonist's experience. What do they see, touch, and bump against? Start there.

setting_as_character.description: Setting is not backdrop. It carries theme, mood, and history. A scene's environment should tell us something that couldn't be said any other way.

entries.principle: Setting should carry history, theme, and emotion simultaneously
entries.bad: The hospital corridor was white and smelled like hospitals. She walked down it.
entries.good: The hospital corridor smelled of floor wax and old coffee and something medicinal that never quite cleared. It had the permanent atmosphere of waiting — as if the building itself had learned to hold its breath.
entries.note: The best setting descriptions are never neutral. They are experienced through a character's state of mind and shaped by the story's themes.

entries.principle: Setting can carry backstory that dialogue or narration would over-explain
entries.bad: "As you know, the old religion was outlawed two hundred years ago when King Aldric the Third defeated the temple priests and converted the holy sites."
entries.good: The temple had been repurposed as a grain storehouse. Someone had plastered over the fresco of the old gods, but the plaster had cracked, and through the gap a golden hand still reached toward the ceiling.
entries.note: The reader understands the suppressed religion instantly — without a word of exposition.

dialogue_tags.topic: Dialogue Tags — Said Is Not Dead
dialogue_tags.description: 'Said' is invisible to the reader. Adverb-loaded tags and exotic synonyms are not. Use action beats to replace tags wherever possible.

entries.principle: Action beats replace tags and add character simultaneously
entries.bad: "Get out," she exclaimed angrily. "You don't mean that," he pleaded desperately. "Get out," she reiterated forcefully.
entries.good: "Get out." She pointed at the door. "You don't mean that." "Get. Out."
entries.note: The action beat (pointing) does what 'angrily' tried to do, and the repeated word with a period does what 'forcefully' tried to do — at a fraction of the word count.

entries.principle: If you must convey tone through a tag, use a stronger verb — but sparingly
entries.bad: "I suppose," he said noncommittally. "Fine," she said dismissively. "Really?" he said questioningly.
entries.good: "I suppose," he said. "Fine," she said. "Really?" (No tag needed — the punctuation carries it.)
entries.note: Pro tip: 'she snapped,' 'he said quietly,' 'she laughed' are fine occasionally. But the default is said/asked. The moment tags become visible, they interrupt the scene.

subtext.description: The most powerful emotional content in dialogue is what goes unsaid. Characters who speak their feelings directly flatten the scene; characters who avoid them create tension.

entries.principle: Subtext lives in what characters refuse to say directly
entries.bad: "I have not forgiven you for leaving me," Marcus said. "I know. I feel terrible about it," Elena replied. "I still think about it every day," Marcus continued.
entries.good: "How long has it been?" he asked. She shrugged. "A while." "Right." They both looked at their coffee.
entries.note: The conversation about coffee is the conversation about everything. The reader fills in the wound; you don't need to name it.

working_with_editors.topic: Working With Editors — The Two Rules
working_with_editors.description: Receiving editorial feedback is a skill. The goal is to understand what the editor is responding to, not just whether to accept or reject the specific fix.

entries.principle: Understand the problem before evaluating the solution
entries.bad: Taking 100% of editor suggestions means you've surrendered your voice. Taking 0% means you've wasted the editor's time and your own money.
entries.good: When you receive an edit, first ask: WHY did the editor make this suggestion? What are they responding to? Even if you reject the specific fix, the problem they identified is almost certainly real.
entries.note: Rule 1: Take the edit seriously — the editor is responding to a real problem. Rule 2: You don't have to take the editor's specific solution. It's your story.

lore_writing.description: Lore earns its place when it invites questions rather than answering them. The reader should lean forward, not sit back.

entries.principle: Lore delivered through character voice invites curiosity; exposition shuts it down
entries.bad: "The mermaids of the Vethrian Sea were first documented in 1203 by the explorer Aldric of Casmoor, who recorded seventeen incidents of sailors disappearing under calm-water conditions..."
entries.good: "Old Mira used to say the mermaids took people who sang after sundown," the captain muttered, not looking at the water. "We don't sing after sundown."
entries.note: Lore as character knowledge and superstition creates world depth without stopping the scene. The reader asks the questions; you don't need to answer them all.

key_craft_challenges: Tense system: French fiction traditionally uses the passé simple (literary past) for narration and imparfait for background/description. Mixing passé composé and passé simple is considered an error in literary fiction — each belongs to a different register.

Adverb proliferation: French has a strong adverb tradition (adverbes en -ment), which parallels the English -ly problem. Editors flag overuse of adverbs like 'silencieusement,' 'rapidement,' 'soudainement.'
Noun-heaviness (nominalisation): Like German Nominalstil, French writers can slip into bureaucratic style — 'il procéda à l'ouverture de la porte' instead of 'il ouvrit la porte.'
Pronoun ambiguity: French gendered pronouns (il/elle) can create ambiguity when two characters of the same gender appear in the same paragraph.
Guillemets (« ») are the correct quotation marks in French fiction, not English double quotes.
recommended_resources: Stephen King: Écriture — Mémoires d'un métier (French translation of On Writing)
Anne Lamott: Tous les écrivains ou presque mentent (French translation of Bird by Bird)
Robert McKee: Story (widely used in French scriptwriting and adapted for novel writing)
Dominic Bellavance: blog at dominicbellavance.com (Québécois author, practical craft essays)

key_craft_challenges: Narrative consistency (coerenza narrativa): A major focus in Italian editorial feedback. Small continuity errors — character eye colour changing, impossible travel times, anachronistic references — are specifically flagged.
Exclamation mark overuse: Italian editors frequently mark manuscripts that use ! excessively. It reads as adolescent. Use it sparingly, only for genuine surprise or strong emotion.

Foreign words in italics: Foreign words not present in the Italian dictionary must be italicised. Words already in Italian dictionaries (film, file, computer, smartphone) are written normally and do not take a plural -s.
Numbers written in full: In Italian literary fiction, numbers should generally be spelled out in words — 'sette anni' not '7 anni' — except for specific dates.
Euphonic d (d eufonica): Italian style guides recommend adding the euphonic 'd' (ad, ed, od) only when the following word starts with the same vowel — 'ad agosto' is correct, 'ad ogni' is debated.
recommended_resources: Stefania Crepaldi: Lezioni di narrativa — Regole e tecniche per scrivere un romanzo (Italian editorial craft guide)
Sul Romanzo (sulromanzo.it) — Italian craft blog with deep POV and narrative technique articles
Genius Scuola di Scrittura Creativa (storygenius.it) — Italian creative writing school, publishes practical craft articles
PennaRigata (pennarigata.it) — Italian writing craft blog focused on common novel-writing errors

key_craft_challenges: Adverbs in -mente: The Spanish equivalent of the English -ly adverb problem. Editors flag overuse of 'rápidamente,' 'silenciosamente,' 'súbitamente.' The fix: find a precise verb, or restructure the sentence.

Cause-and-effect logic (ley causa-efecto): Spanish craft guides emphasise that every action must have a credible consequence. A character cannot simply do things; there must be a chain of motivation and reaction.
Dialogue punctuation with em-dash (guión largo/raya): Spanish uses an em-dash (—) to open dialogue, not quotation marks. Consistent use throughout the manuscript is expected.

Tense consistency: Mixing pretérito indefinido (hablé) and pretérito imperfecto (hablaba) correctly is a common beginner error. Indefinido = completed point-in-time action; imperfecto = ongoing state or habitual action.

Narrating in a falsely archaic or grandiose style: Some Spanish writing schools note that aspiring authors sometimes adopt an overly formal, rhetorical style mimicking 19th-century Spanish literature, making the text feel stiff and inaccessible.
recommended_resources: Stephen King: Mientras Escribo (Spanish translation of On Writing)
Escuela de Escritores (escueladeescritores.com) — Spain's leading creative writing school, publishes extensive craft articles
Muriel Spark's advice (cited in Spanish craft communities): 'Write as if you were writing a letter to a friend' — a key antidote to the grandiose-style problem
Oficina de Escritor (oficiodeescritor.com) — Alejandro Marcos's blog, widely recommended for Spanish-language craft
Howard Mittelmark & Sandra Newman: Cómo no escribir una novela (Spanish translation) — 200 common errors with explanations

key_craft_challenges: Dialogue punctuation: Brazilian Portuguese uses em-dash (—) for dialogue, same as Spanish. A common error is placing a period after the dialogue line and capitalising the dialogue tag: '— Eu sei — Disse ela.' is wrong. Correct: '— Eu sei — disse ela.'

Gerunds (gerúndio): Brazilian Portuguese has a heavy gerund tradition in speech ('estou fazendo,' 'estava comendo'). In literary prose, editors often prefer the simple past or imperfect: 'comia um hambúrguer' rather than 'estava comendo um hambúrguer.'

Pronoun overuse: In BP, subject pronouns (eu, tu, ele, nós) are often redundant because the verb conjugation already indicates person. Cutting them tightens prose: 'Olhei para o horizonte' rather than 'Eu olhei para o horizonte.'
Queísmo (overuse of 'que'): Repetitive use of 'que' in a sentence is flagged by Brazilian editors as a tic that makes prose sound machine-like.

Mostrar, não contar (Show don't tell): The principle is well-established in Brazilian craft communities. A specific example: ❌ 'Ela estava com raiva.' ✅ 'Ela fechou o punho com força, os olhos duros mirando o chão.'
recommended_resources: Stephen King: Sobre a Escrita (Portuguese translation of On Writing)
Claudia Lemes (claudialemes.com.br) — Brazilian fiction writing blog; widely followed
Vilto Reis (viltoreis.com) — Portuguese-language craft blog focused on common correction errors
Toma Aí Um Poema (tomaaiumpoema.com.br) — Brazilian creative writing platform with practical craft articles
NaNoWriMo Brazil community — large, active, and produces craft-focused content

key_craft_challenges: Gestaltning vs. berättande (Show vs. Tell): Swedish craft guides use 'gestaltning' (to dramatise/show) as opposed to 'berätta' (to narrate/tell). Editors mark: 'Författaren informerar istället för gestaltar' — the author informs rather than dramatises.

Tense consistency (tempus): Swedish writers often unintentionally shift between presens and preteritum mid-text. The advice is to choose one and be consistent. Presens creates immediacy; preteritum creates narrative distance.
Övertydlighet (over-explaining): Swedish editors specifically flag when an author does not trust their reader. If the reader feels talked down to ('hen känner sig dum'), you lose them.
Head-hopping: Swedish craft blogs call this 'oavsiktligt hopp i perspektivet' — unintentional POV jumping. Clear signals and scene breaks are the fix.

Plot planting (planteringar): Swedish editors check whether foreshadowed elements are followed through. 'Planterar inte eller planterar men glömmer bort vad som förespeglats' is a common beginner error.
Overly long manuscripts: Swedish craft guides note most books over 300 pages have sections that could be cut.
recommended_resources: SkrivarSidan (skrivarsidan.nu) — Iréne Johansson's Swedish craft resource; publishes practical lists of common errors
Skriva (tidningenskriva.se) — Swedish magazine for writers; free craft articles online
Författarkurs.se (Jorun Modén) — Swedish writing course instructor; detailed craft articles on POV, tempo, scene structure
Ingerlundin.se — Swedish writing tips resource; practical and widely used
Stephen King: Om Skrivandet (Swedish translation of On Writing)

key_craft_challenges: Tense consistency (verteltijd): Dutch editors list inconsistent tense as the single most common manuscript error. Writers mix verleden tijd (past) and tegenwoordige tijd (present) without intention. Rule: choose one and commit.

Compound words (samenstellingen): Dutch compounds are written as one word far more often than English writers expect. 'Koelkast magneet' is wrong; 'koelkastmagneet' is correct. This trips up writers who draft in English and translate mentally.
Numbers written out: In Dutch fiction, numbers under twenty (and multiples of ten/hundred) are spelled out: 'zeven jaar' not '7 jaar.' Dates are excepted.
Dialogue in quotation marks: Dutch fiction uses standard quotation marks (") for dialogue. Always place spoken text inside them for clarity.

Never repeat information (nooit dubbelop): Dutch editors flag information delivered twice — once in narration and once in dialogue. Dialogue delivery is almost always preferred because it reveals character simultaneously.

Multiple POVs: Dutch author Carolina Trujillo (award-winning novelist) specifically warns beginners against writing from multiple perspectives. 'Ze maken het zichzelf vooral lastig' — they make it hard for themselves, because everything must be internally consistent.
recommended_resources: Schrijven Online (schrijvenonline.org) — major Dutch writing resource; articles by working editors and authors
BoekenGilde blog (blog.boekengilde.nl) — practical Dutch manuscript tips
Schrijfvis (schrijfvis.nl) — Dennis Rijnvis's Dutch writing blog; focused on common errors
Lucia van den Brink (luciavandenbrink.nl) — Dutch writing instructor; tips from published Dutch authors
Carolina Trujillo — Dutch award-winning novelist; widely quoted on POV discipline

key_craft_challenges: Dialogue punctuation: Polish uses a dash (—) for dialogue, not quotation marks in most modern fiction. Correct formatting is essential and frequently marked by Polish editors.
Chronological consistency: Polish craft guides emphasise tracking a summary/streszczenie of your novel to avoid contradicting previously established facts — especially in longer works.

Craft vs. inspiration myth: Polish craft culture, like German, historically overvalued the 'talent' narrative. Modern Polish writing communities (Born to Create, Spisek Pisarzy) push back with the message that writing is craft that can be learned.
Pacing through structure (fabuła jako sceny): Polish craft guides emphasise building the novel scene by scene ('fabuła składa się ze scen') rather than writing summary-heavy prose.
Research accuracy: Polish craft guides specifically flag factual errors in crime, fantasy, and historical fiction. Research is considered non-negotiable professional discipline.

Waiting for inspiration (czekanie na wenę): A specific named failure mode in Polish writing communities. 'Nie traktuj pisania jako procesu oczekiwania na wenę twórczą' — don't treat writing as waiting for creative inspiration to arrive.
recommended_resources: Born to Create (born-to-create.pl) — major Polish writing blog by a published crime author; practical and prolific
Spisek Pisarzy (spisekpisarzy.pl) — Polish writing craft community and guide
PR Education (preducation.pl) — Polish illustrated writer's guide; course-based, professional
Stephen King: Jak Pisać. Pamiętnik rzemieślnika (Polish translation of On Writing)
Umberto Eco: 'Kto czyta książki, ten żyje podwójnie' — widely cited in Polish craft communities as the justification for reading as craft development

key_craft_challenges: Mesoclise (pronoun placement): European Portuguese uses mesoclisis in future/conditional — 'dar-te-ei' instead of 'te darei.' Literary fiction uses this; colloquial avoidance marks informal register. Editors flag inconsistency.
Dialogue punctuation: European Portuguese uses em-dash (—) identical to Brazilian standard. However, EP editors are stricter about not mixing the two regional standards mid-text.

Passado vs. pretérito perfeito composto: EP uses 'tenho feito' (I have been doing, continuous) where BP uses 'tenho feito' differently. EP 'fiz' is a completed action; BP 'fiz' = same but 'tenho feito' is far more common in BP speech. Mixing registers trips up EP literary fiction.

Register sensitivity: European Portuguese literary fiction is highly sensitive to register — academic/formal prose versus literary/intimate voice. Editors flag anachronistic informality or overcorrected formality.
Crase: Unlike BP, EP does not use the crase accent (à) in the same contexts. Writing à for contracted 'a + a' is BP-specific.
recommended_resources: José Saramago: any novel — for punctuation extremism (long sentences without conventional dialogue punctuation); study as counterexample to standard rules
Escrever Melhor (escreverbem.net) — European Portuguese writing craft resource
Clube dos Escritores (clubedosescritores.pt) — Portuguese writing community

key_craft_challenges: Two written standards: Bokmål (most fiction) and Nynorsk. Most mainstream publishers work in Bokmål; some regional publishers prefer Nynorsk. Mixing is seen as an error.
Dialogue: Norwegian fiction uses em-dash (—) for dialogue, same as other Nordic languages. New speaker = new line, no exception.
Tense consistency: Same issue as Swedish — mixing presens and preteritum mid-narrative. Choose one and commit.
Over-description (overforklaring): Norwegian editors flag the same 'author doesn't trust the reader' issue as Swedish. Trust the reader; resist the urge to explain what has already been shown.
Passive voice overuse: Norwegian passive constructions are easy to form and frequently overused by beginners, weakening the prose.
recommended_resources: Skrivekunst.no — Norwegian writing craft resource
Norsk Forfattersentrum (forfattersentrum.no) — Norwegian Authors' Centre; craft resources for authors
Stephen King: Å Skrive (Norwegian translation of On Writing)

key_craft_challenges: Dialogue: Danish fiction uses em-dash (—), same as Norwegian and Swedish. Quotation marks (") appear in some traditions but em-dash is considered more literary.

Compound nouns (sammensatte ord): Like Dutch and German, Danish compounds are written as one word. 'Kærligheds brev' is wrong; 'kærlighedsbrev' is correct. A common error in digital-first writing where spellcheckers don't always catch it.
Tense: Same Nordic pattern — preteritum for past narrative; presens for immediacy. Unintentional mixing is a common beginner error.
Modifying -ly adverbs (adverbier): Danish has the same -t form (hurtigt, stille, roligt). Danish editors flag adverb pile-ups the same way English editors flag -ly accumulation.
Small literary scene: The Danish market is small. Debut authors are advised to target literary prizes (e.g., Danish Radio's P1 Novel Prize) alongside traditional publishers.
recommended_resources: Skriv.dk — Danish writing craft platform
Forfatterskolen (forfatterskolen.dk) — Denmark's leading creative writing school
Litteratursiden.dk — Danish literature resource with author interviews and craft discussion

key_craft_challenges: Agglutinative morphology: Finnish builds meaning through suffixes on a single root ('talossani' = in my house). This gives Finnish writers extraordinary precision but creates specific beginner errors: overlong compound words, and awkward suffix-stacking.
Dialogue: Finnish uses quotation marks (") for dialogue in most modern fiction, unlike the Nordic em-dash tradition.
No grammatical gender: Finnish has no he/she distinction (only 'hän'). This eliminates gendered pronoun ambiguity but creates challenges when translating gendered English concepts.
Postpositions instead of prepositions: Finnish uses postpositions ('talon takana' = behind the house, lit. 'house's behind'). Beginners sometimes under-use this feature, creating unnatural prose.
Verb-focused style: Finnish prose tends to be verb-heavy and noun-light compared to English. Strong Finnish prose uses precise, concrete verbs rather than noun phrases.
recommended_resources: Kirjoittaja.fi — Finnish writing craft resource
Suomen Kirjailijaliiton (kirjailijaliitto.fi) — Finnish Authors' Association; craft resources
Teos Publishing craft resources — one of Finland's major literary publishers

attributions.text: Everything is worldbuilding. Worldbuilding has this negative connotation as sort of this homework that you have to do beforehand… Everything in a story is worldbuilding in the same way that everything about us is worldbuilding.

attributions.text: Show, Don't Tell: convey information through action, dialogue, and sensory details rather than direct exposition.

attributions.text: Filter words: words like 'felt,' 'saw,' 'noticed,' 'heard,' 'thought' that place a narrator between reader and experience. Removing them creates immediacy.

attributions.text: Purple prose: a type of writing in which the extravagant style and use of language gets in the way of the narrative. The work of a writer lost in the form of language, leading them to neglect the function of language.

attributions.text: Purple: 'The tall, brooding, mysterious stranger walked solemnly and silently across the desolate, fog-laced, moonlit street.' Better: 'The stranger drifted down the fog-laced street, quiet and unreadable.'

attributions.text: When you catch an adjective, kill it. Not always, not often, but whenever you can.

attributions.text: Head-hopping: when the Point of View (POV) changes mid-scene or mid-paragraph, confusing the reader by jumping between characters' internal perspectives without a structural break.
