attributions.notes: Recommends 'Rivet Your Readers With Deep Point Of View' by Jill Elizabeth Nelson as the primary Deep POV resource.

attributions.text: Das deutsche Literaturverständnis ist bis ins 21. Jahrhundert von der Genieästhetik geprägt — der Idee, dass echte Kunst nicht an Regeln gebunden sein darf.
attributions.attributed_to: Halupczok (cited in academic paper on Creative Writing in Germany)
attributions.source_work: Über die Bedeutung von Creative Writing im Land der Dichter und Denker
attributions.notes: Explains why the German craft-guide tradition developed later than the Anglo-American one and why 'Schreiben' was long considered unteachable in Germany.

attributions.text: Le descrizioni devono passare dall'emotività e dal punto di vista del narratore.
attributions.translation_en: Descriptions must pass through the emotional state and point of view of the narrator.
attributions.source_work: Scrittura Creativa — craft principles on POV-filtered description
attributions.notes: Core Italian craft principle: all description should be filtered through the narrator's emotional state, not presented as objective observation.

attributions.text: Mostrar, não contar: 'Ela fechou o punho com força, os olhos duros mirando o chão.'
attributions.translation_en: Show, don't tell: 'She clenched her fist, her eyes hard, fixed on the floor.'
attributions.attributed_to: Toma Aí Um Poema (Brazilian creative writing platform)
attributions.source_work: Show don't tell examples in Brazilian craft communities
attributions.notes: This specific example ('fechou o punho com força') is the canonical 'mostrar, não contar' illustration circulated in Brazilian writing communities.

attributions.text: Gestaltning vs. berättande — Swedish craft distinction between dramatising (gestaltning) and narrating/informing (berättande).
attributions.source_work: SkrivarSidan — Swedish writing craft resource
attributions.notes: The Swedish terms 'gestaltning' (to render/dramatise) and 'berättande' (to narrate/inform) are the established Swedish-language equivalents of 'show, don't tell.' Iréne Johansson's resource is the most widely cited Swedish craft site using this terminology.

attributions.text: Purple: 'The tall, brooding, mysterious stranger walked solemnly and silently across the desolate, fog-laced, moonlit street.' Better: 'The stranger drifted down the fog-laced street, quiet and unreadable.'
attributions.source_work: Writing 101: Avoiding Purple Prose
attributions.notes: Already cross-referenced as attr_022. This attribution records the specific canonical example used in pp_en_001 which was sourced from the same article.

attributions.text: Le dialogue doit faire avancer l'action, pas juste informer.
attributions.translation_en: Dialogue must advance the action, not just deliver information.
attributions.source_work: French craft writing resources on dialogue function
attributions.notes: Standard principle in French creative writing pedagogy; both sites are major French-language craft resources.

attributions.text: Salto di prospettiva (cambio di punto di vista) — POV shifting within a scene, a named error in Italian editorial feedback.
attributions.source_work: Italian craft resources on narrative perspective consistency
attributions.notes: Both sites are primary Italian craft resources. 'Salto di prospettiva' is the established Italian editorial term for head-hopping.

attributions.text: El error del escritor novel: muchos personajes de punto de vista.
attributions.translation_en: The beginner writer's error: too many point-of-view characters.
attributions.source_work: Discussed across Spanish craft communities including escueladeescritores.com
attributions.notes: Multiple POV as a named beginner error is consistent across Spanish craft pedagogy. The specific framing 'trop de caractères de point de vue' appears in aguycalledbloke's multilingual craft content referenced by Spanish writers.

attributions.text: Författaren vet inte i vilket av hens personers huvud hen befinner sig — a named Swedish craft error: the author doesn't know which character's head they are in.
attributions.source_work: SkrivarSidan — Swedish writing craft resource; list of common beginner errors
attributions.notes: Listed as a named, recurring beginner error in Swedish craft pedagogy. The phrasing is from SkrivarSidan's publicly available error list.

attributions.text: 'Sei bello come il sole. Era bella come una dea.' — cited as canonical cliché examples to avoid in Italian fiction writing.
attributions.source_work: Scrittura Creativa — esempi di cliché da evitare
attributions.notes: These phrasings are the canonical Italian examples of clichés in creative writing pedagogy, repeatedly cited at scritturacreativa.org.

attributions.text: Les temps fonctionnent habituellement par binômes — French tenses operate in pairs (passé simple + imparfait for literary fiction).
attributions.source_work: Jesuisauteur.com — French craft resource on tense usage in literary fiction
attributions.notes: The 'binômes de temps' principle is a standard teaching in French literary writing courses. The specific phrasing is from jesuisauteur.com.

attributions.text: Pretérito indefinido vs. pretérito imperfecto — correct use of Spanish past tenses in fiction; extensive treatment of tense errors.
attributions.source_work: Escueladeescrituracreativa.com — tense usage in Spanish fiction
attributions.notes: The indefinido/imperfecto distinction is a foundational point in Spanish creative writing pedagogy, treated extensively at multiple Spanish craft schools.

attributions.text: Four questions readers ask subconsciously on page 1: Why am I reading this? Whose story is this? What is the situation? What is at stake?
attributions.attributed_to: Jorun Modén (Swedish writing course instructor, forfattarkurs.se); principle shared across English craft resources
attributions.source_work: Författarkurs.se — Swedish writing pedagogy on opening pages
attributions.notes: This four-question framework is widely shared in both Swedish and English craft pedagogy. The Swedish articulation comes from Jorun Modén's forfattarkurs.se. The principle also appears in multiple English craft guides on openings.

attributions.text: Votre incipit doit établir une scène, créer un conflit ou générer un mystère — possibly all three.
attributions.translation_en: Your opening must establish a scene, create conflict, or generate a mystery — possibly all three.
attributions.source_work: Librinova — craft advice on the incipit (opening passage)
attributions.notes: 'Incipit' is the standard French craft term for the opening passage of a novel. The three-function principle is stated explicitly at librinova.com.

attributions.text: De longs débuts lents — slow starts are among the most common Italian manuscript errors.
attributions.source_work: Story Genius — Italian creative writing school craft articles
attributions.notes: Slow starts ('inizi lenti') are listed among the most common errors in Italian debut manuscripts. The French-language phrasing 'De longs débuts lents' appears in their multilingual craft content.

attributions.text: Empezar donde el conflicto existe, no donde el personaje nació — in medias res as the standard opening principle.
attributions.source_work: Spanish craft standard on opening placement; multiple sources
attributions.notes: In medias res as the preferred opening is standard advice across Spanish craft pedagogy. Both cited sites are major Spanish creative writing resources.

attributions.text: Puedes escribir tantos -mente como quieras cuando estés creando. Pero después, en la fase de revisión, fíjate cuántos de ellos puedes eliminar.
attributions.translation_en: You can write as many -mente adverbs as you like during the creative phase. But afterwards, in revision, see how many of them you can eliminate.
attributions.source_work: Estandarte.com — Spanish craft writing on adverb use
attributions.notes: Estandarte.com is a major Spanish craft and literature reference. This quote captures the practical revision approach to -mente adverbs taught across Spanish writing courses.

attributions.text: Ne donnez pas trop d'informations à la fois, sachez distiller le suspense.
attributions.translation_en: Don't give too much information at once; know how to distil suspense.
attributions.source_work: Librinova — French craft resource on exposition and world-building
attributions.notes: Standard French craft principle on controlled information release. Directly quoted from Librinova's craft guides.

attributions.text: World-building through narrative lens — il mondo visto attraverso gli occhi del personaggio, non esposto direttamente dall'autore.
attributions.translation_en: World-building through the character's eyes, not exposed directly by the author.
attributions.source_work: Sul Romanzo — Italian craft resource on world-building and POV
attributions.notes: sulromanzo.it is Italy's most widely cited craft blog for literary fiction. This principle is a recurring theme in their world-building articles.

attributions.text: Ley causa-efecto — the law of cause and effect as a fundamental pacing principle in Spanish craft pedagogy: every action must have a credible consequence before the next action occurs.
attributions.source_work: Escuela de Escritores — 'ley causa-efecto' as a core craft concept
attributions.notes: The 'ley causa-efecto' is the Spanish craft equivalent of Dwight Swain's Motivation-Reaction Unit (MRU). It is taught as a fundamental pacing principle at Escuela de Escritores, Spain's leading creative writing school.

attributions.text: Planteringar — Swedish craft term for plot plants: story details seeded early that are paid off later, making character development and plot turns feel earned rather than arbitrary.
attributions.source_work: SkrivarSidan — Swedish craft resource; 'planteringar' as a named concept
attributions.notes: 'Planteringar' (plantings/seeds) is the standard Swedish craft term for Chekhov's Gun and foreshadowing elements. SkrivarSidan lists 'planterar inte' (failing to plant) as a specific named beginner error.

attributions.text: La voix passive en français littéraire est souvent signe d'un manque de confiance dans le verbe — passive voice in French literary prose often signals insufficient trust in the verb.
attributions.source_work: French craft resources on voice and verb strength
attributions.notes: The principle that passive voice signals 'manque de confiance dans le verbe' is consistent across French creative writing pedagogy.

attributions.text: Pasiva perifrástica vs. pasiva refleja — the distinction between the two passive constructions in Spanish and their correct use in literary fiction.
attributions.source_work: Estandarte.com — voz pasiva in Spanish creative writing
attributions.notes: The distinction between pasiva perifrástica (ser + participio) and pasiva refleja (se + verb) is unique to Spanish and a specific editorial concern. Estandarte.com is the primary Spanish source cited.

attributions.text: La forma passiva rimuove l'agente dall'immediato e appesantisce la prosa — passive form removes the agent from the immediate and weighs down the prose.
attributions.source_work: Scrittura Creativa — passive voice as a style issue in Italian fiction
attributions.notes: The principle that passive voice 'appesantisce la prosa' (weighs down the prose) is the standard Italian craft formulation.

attributions.text: Continuità narrativa — narrative continuity as a specific and frequently-cited Italian editorial concern, especially for crime fiction, fantasy, and historical fiction.
attributions.source_work: PennaRigata and Sul Romanzo — Italian editorial resources on narrative consistency
attributions.notes: Italian editors are particularly attentive to 'coerenza narrativa' and 'continuità narrativa.' Both sites list continuity errors as top manuscript issues in Italian debut fiction.

attributions.text: Streszczenie rozdziałów — chapter summaries as a tracking tool for chronological and factual consistency across a Polish manuscript.
attributions.source_work: Born to Create — major Polish fiction writing blog
attributions.notes: 'Streszczenie rozdziałów' (chapter summaries) as a self-editing tool is specifically recommended at born-to-create.pl, a major Polish craft resource run by a published crime fiction author.

attributions.text: Blake Snyder: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need (2005)
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need
attributions.notes: Original source of the 15-beat sheet. Snyder died in 2009; the method has since been expanded by successors including Jessica Brody for novel adaptation.

attributions.text: The beat sheet is most useful when it helps you see the shape of your novel, not when it starts bossing you around like a tiny clipboard-holding tyrant.
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat Beat Sheet: All 15 Beats
attributions.notes: Used in Chapter 10 section 10.8 common planning mistakes. Captures the essential caveat about framework compliance vs. storytelling authenticity.

attributions.text: If a beat is only 'the reader learns something,' you have information. If a beat forces a choice and changes the protagonist's options, you have drama.
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat for Novels: Beat Sheet Template and Chapter Outline
attributions.notes: Used in Chapter 10 STC beat design rules. Defines the distinction between informational and dramatic beats.

attributions.text: Once you begin drafting, the story should be primary. If the story demands a scene you didn't outline, that's what you need to do.
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat Beat Sheet: The Ultimate Guide (+ Template)
attributions.notes: Used in Chapter 10 common planning mistakes. Articulates the proper relationship between outline and draft.

attributions.text: The fix is usually missing thresholds, unclear stakes, weak escalation, or chapters that do not change anything that could not have changed without them.
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat for Novels: Beat Sheet Template and Chapter Outline
attributions.notes: Diagnosis of structural drift in novels. Used in Chapter 10 to characterise pacing problems.

attributions.text: Joseph Campbell: The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949)
attributions.source_work: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
attributions.notes: Original source of the monomyth / 17-stage hero's journey. Named to TIME magazine's list of 100 most influential books written in English (2011). Entered the NYT bestseller list in 1988, nearly four decades after publication.

attributions.text: Christopher Vogler: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers (1992); originally an internal Disney memo (1985)
attributions.source_work: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers
attributions.notes: Vogler distilled Campbell's 17 stages to 12 for working screenwriters and novelists. First circulated as a 7-page internal Disney memo in 1985. Campbell's 'belly of the whale' term cited in Chapter 10 Ordeal beat is from Campbell via Vogler.

attributions.text: The standard path of the mythological adventure of the hero is a magnification of the formula represented in the rites of passage: separation — initiation — return.
attributions.source_work: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
attributions.notes: Campbell's foundational summary of the monomyth's three-part structure. The 'rites of passage' framing is credited to Arnold van Gennep (Les rites de passage, 1909), whom Campbell explicitly acknowledged.

attributions.text: The Ordeal is a 'black moment.' It will inform every decision that the Hero makes from this point forward.
attributions.source_work: The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers
attributions.notes: Vogler's characterisation of the Ordeal as a 'black moment' that reshapes all subsequent choices. Paraphrased in Chapter 10 beat 8 craft note.

attributions.text: Start with the Resolution. Then figure out the starting state (Hook), because you want to start in a far — if not absolutely opposite — state and get a good arc. The purpose of the seven points is to help you move believably from one to the other.
attributions.source_work: Writing Excuses Season 7, Episode 41: Seven-Point Story Structure
attributions.notes: The reverse-design principle — starting with Resolution, working backward to Hook — is Wells's core methodological insight. Also documented in the Writing Excuses podcast transcript.

attributions.text: Plots, subplots and character arcs can each be mapped out with the Seven-Point System. Line them up — have more than one advancing in the same scene — to create powerful moments.
attributions.source_work: Writing Excuses Season 7, Episode 41: Seven-Point Story Structure
attributions.notes: Wells's specific recommendation to apply the 7-point structure independently to subplots and then align pinch points for structural power. Used in Chapter 10 section 10.4 subplot_usage.

attributions.text: Plot Turn 2 is 'The power is in you!' — the hero has a moment when they realise their inner strength and how to use it toward their ultimate goal.
attributions.source_work: Seven-Point Story Structure presentation / Writing Excuses
attributions.notes: Wells's characterisation of Plot Turn 2 as the 'power is in you' moment — a named concept in his framework. Used in Chapter 10 beat 6 craft note.

attributions.text: Nigel Watts: Write a Novel — And Get It Published (Teach Yourself Books, 1996)
attributions.source_work: Write a Novel — And Get It Published
attributions.notes: Original source of the 8-point story arc: Stasis, Trigger, Quest, Surprise, Critical Choice, Climax, Reversal, Resolution. Watts was a British novelist and creative writing teacher. The 8-point arc is distinct from the 7-point structure.

attributions.text: My stories have often lacked a strong quest or goal. If there isn't a clear quest, the resolution won't satisfy the reader. Each event must be caused by a previous event, then cause the next. If an event feels random, the reader loses interest.
attributions.source_work: The Eight-Point Story Arc: Worth Thinking About?
attributions.notes: Used as a craft reflection on the key weakness of stories that use the 8-point arc without maintaining causal chain between events. The 'every event must cause the next' principle is Watts's core contribution.

attributions.text: The Snowflake Method: begin with a one-sentence summary and expand outward in ten steps. Each step tests the coherence of the previous one.
attributions.source_work: advancedfictionwriting.com — The Snowflake Method (2003 onwards)
attributions.notes: Ingermanson's process is named after the mathematical fractal: each iteration reveals more complexity while maintaining the same fundamental shape. The method is particularly popular for complex fantasy and thriller writers managing large casts and intricate plots.

attributions.text: Gustav Freytag: Die Technik des Dramas (The Technique of the Drama, 1863)
attributions.source_work: Die Technik des Dramas
attributions.notes: Freytag was a German playwright and novelist who derived his pyramid from analysis of Greek tragedy and Shakespeare. The five-part structure — Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, Denouement — remains the standard model taught in European literary education.

attributions.text: Not all stories are hero stories. If your story lives in fragments, nonlinearity, or mood over plot, STC or the Hero's Journey may fight your intent.
attributions.source_work: Save the Cat Beat Sheet: Complete Guide — 15 Story Beats
attributions.notes: The recommendation to use Kishōtenketsu or other non-conflict-driven structures for non-Western or experimental narratives. Used in Chapter 10 common planning mistakes.

attributions.text: Howard Mittelmark & Sandra Newman: Cómo no escribir una novela (Spanish translation of How Not to Write a Novel, 2008)
attributions.source_work: How Not to Write a Novel: 200 Classic Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
attributions.notes: 200 common fiction-writing errors explained with satirical examples. Widely used in Spanish craft communities as a negative-example reference.

attributions.text: Write as if you were writing a letter to a friend.
attributions.source_work: Cited in Spanish craft communities as an antidote to grandiose prose style
attributions.notes: Muriel Spark's advice — 'write as if writing a letter to a friend' — is widely cited in Spanish writing communities as a counterweight to the tendency toward overly formal or archaic literary register. The exact original source is disputed; it circulates as a widely-attributed craft maxim.
attributions.example_application: Counters the 'estilo grandilocuente' (grandiose style) problem in Spanish debut fiction.

attributions.text: Stefania Crepaldi: Lezioni di narrativa — Regole e tecniche per scrivere un romanzo
attributions.source_work: Lezioni di narrativa: Regole e tecniche per scrivere un romanzo
attributions.notes: Italian editorial craft guide covering novel structure, narrative rules, and common errors. Recommended by Italian editors and writing instructors as a primary Italian-language craft reference.

attributions.text: Ze maken het zichzelf vooral lastig — beginners make it very hard for themselves by writing from multiple POVs.
attributions.attributed_to: Carolina Trujillo (Dutch author, winner of BNG Nieuwe Literatuur Prijs)
attributions.source_work: Schrijven Online — quoted on POV discipline in Dutch fiction
attributions.notes: Carolina Trujillo is the most-cited Dutch author quoted on the multiple-POV beginner problem. Her warning — 'ze maken het zichzelf vooral lastig' — is widely referenced in Dutch craft communities.

attributions.text: Kto czyta książki, ten żyje podwójnie. (Who reads books, lives twice.)
attributions.source_work: Widely attributed; circulates in Polish craft communities as justification for reading as craft development
attributions.notes: This Eco quote is widely cited in Polish writing communities (born-to-create.pl, spisekpisarzy.pl) as the foundational argument for reading as a craft discipline. The exact original source within Eco's work is disputed; it is treated as a maxim.
attributions.example_application: Cited in Polish craft pedagogy to justify the 'reading imperative' discussed in Chapter 1.

attributions.text: José Saramago's punctuation extremism: long sentences without conventional dialogue punctuation, used as a counterexample to standard rules.
attributions.source_work: All major novels including Blindness (Ensaio sobre a Cegueira, 1995), The Gospel According to Jesus Christ (O Evangelho Segundo Jesus Cristo, 1991)
attributions.notes: Saramago is referenced in the European Portuguese language notes as a canonical counterexample — a Nobel Prize-winning author who systematically violates standard dialogue punctuation conventions. His style is studied as a deliberate artistic choice, not a model to follow without understanding its intent.

attributions.text: Jorun Modén — Swedish writing course instructor at Författarkurs.se; widely cited for craft articles on POV, tempo, and scene structure.
attributions.source_work: Författarkurs.se — Swedish writing pedagogy
attributions.notes: Modén is one of the most widely cited Swedish writing instructors. Her four-question framework for opening pages (Chapter 10 open_en_002) and scene structure principles are sourced from Författarkurs.se.

attributions.text: Janet Burroway: Writing Fiction — A Guide to Narrative Craft
attributions.source_work: Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft
attributions.notes: The most widely used university-level fiction writing textbook in the United States. Referenced in Chapter 9 recommended resources for beginners. Covers all aspects of craft with exercises. Currently in its 10th edition.

attributions.text: Campbell borrowed the term 'monomyth' from James Joyce's Finnegans Wake (1939).
attributions.source_work: The Hero with a Thousand Faces; James Joyce: Finnegans Wake (1939)
attributions.notes: Documented at authorflows.com and scottjeffrey.com. Campbell explicitly credited Joyce for the term. The term 'monomyth' therefore has a dual origin: Joyce coined it, Campbell applied it to cross-cultural myth analysis.

attributions.text: Brandon Sanderson (author of Mistborn) has discussed writing extensive outlines, expanding a one-sentence premise into multi-page documents — consistent with the Snowflake Method approach.
attributions.source_work: Story Structure Guide: 10 Powerful Frameworks
attributions.notes: Sanderson is cited as a high-profile contemporary author whose outlining practice parallels the Snowflake Method, giving it professional credibility beyond academic craft contexts.
